BRITISH WORKMAN'S ASSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED. Established 1866. Incorporated under the Companies Act, 1862.

CIIIEF OFFICES: BROAD-ST. CORNER, BIRMINGHAM. EXTRACTS FROM THE DIRECTORS' REPORT for the year ending April 30th, 1888. Notwithstanding the liberal terms and conditions of the Company's Polieies„ and the heavy amount paid in claims, and for extension expenses (resulting in the largest increase of new business the Company has ever made in any one year), the Directors are pleased to state that after meeting all pay- ments and expenses, they have been able to carry forward a balance exceeding £15,000. Mr. James Sketchley, one of your Directors, retired in De- cember last for the purpose of travelling, when Mr. J. C. Fowke, who for upwards of twenty years had been Solicitor to the Company, was requested by the Board to fill up the vacancy, which we are pleased to say he consented to do, and he has proved to be a very important addition to the director- ate. Mr. Fowke is not a shareholder, but holds a Policy in the Company upon his own life for £l,OOO, and therefore may be looked upon as a more direct representative of the Policy holders. The total income of the Company for the year was £178,310 18a Bd, being an increase of £21,928 I.ls 9d. The total amount of Payments was £163,018 14s Id, leaving a balance upon the Year's accounts of £15,292 45 7d, making the total funds at the close of the year £96,302 195 Od. The amount paid in Claims during the Year was £17,479, inelUding £4,411 Se Surrender Claims. The total sum paid uP to the 30th April, 1888, was £469,261 Is 10d. The number of Assurants upon the Company's books on the 30th April, 1888, was 374,098, and their annual premium would be £198,420 18s 10d, showing a net increase of 39,070 Arturanta, and £27,820 lie 9d in Premium Income. HENRY PORT, Managing Director. D. A. BECKETT, Secretary. DISTRICT OFFICE: MAREET GATE CHAMBERS, WARRINGTON. S. GREEN, SUPERINTENDENT.

SISTER KATE. 06, she is a darling ! Sister Kate. Fair and sweet and loving! Sister Kate. Cheeks like the dawn, and lips which are ever Pouting for kisses, and yired never; Red-gold hair and deep-blue eyes, Bright as the stars in the wintry skies, Has Sister Kate.

Oh, she is a treasure!— Sister Kate. Witty, wise, and clever ! Sister Kate. She sings like a bird, and is ever trilling Sweet little songs, the old house filling, From morn till eve, with music bright; And is everywhere like a ray of light, Dear Sister Kate.

Oh, how I should miss her! ' Sister Kate. If ever I should lose her ! Sister Kate. The girls who will flatter, and smile in your face, And tell you they love you with a Judas' embrace— The fleeting enjoyments cf fond lovers' bliss— I'd barter them all for one pure, sweet kiss From Sister Kate.
Annitsford.
JOHN Braucit.

Trust not a man who promises with an oath. Gold in this world covers as many sins as charity in the next.. It is right to be contented with what we have, but never with what we are. The best portion of a good man's life is his little, nameless unremembered acts of kindness and of love. A sparkling young debater, in a flight of eloquence, exclaimed—" Mr. President, the world is divided into two great classes, the learned and the unlearned, one of whom I am which." "George, dear," said Mabel, "I thought you and papa were not very good friends." " Well, yes, that's so to a great extent, I'm sorry to say." "Why, then, did you send him that great handsome bulldog?" "Why did I send him that dog?" George smiled a tender, thought- ful, far-away smile. "You see, dearest, that dog and I are old friends." He: 'I tell you it's hard to have to move away from the house that has sheltered you for years—the house in which all your children have been born, and which you have come to look upon as your home for life." She: "Well, John, there are some bright things to think of." He: "Yes, Matilda; but if I didn't owe the land- lord two years' rent things would look pretty dark— wouldn't they?" THE Oen. MISSING Ltme—Sentimental Gaol Visitor: "Of what were you accused?" Interesting Bird: "Stealing a watch, sir. I proved an alibi with nine witnesses and had eleven witnesses for character, but they gave me four years all the same." S.G.V. (amazed): "I don't see why you were not acquitted.' LB.: "Well, sir, there was one weak point in my defence." S.G.V. "And that was—" LB.: " They found the watch in mv pocket." HE WAS "DANarnous.-9. big man and a little man entered a saloon on Michigan-avenue, near Third-street. the other day, and called for drinks. While the little man lingered over his, the big man called the bar-keeper aside and asked: '6 Ever see him before?" "No." "That's Texas Dick. He is the man who grabbed a grizzly bear by the ear and broke its neck. Don't rile him, for he is on a tear and very dangerous." When the little man received change for a quarter he !coked at it in surprise and said: "I gave you 2 dols." "No, sir." "What? Call me a liar! I want the change foe my 2 dots. bill." The big man winked vigorously at the bar-keeper not to engage in it dispute with the danger- ous man, and as a consequence change was made on the new basis and the pair went out to tackle another place. They found it not far away, and it was in charge of a consumptive-looking young man. Everything went smoothly until Texas Dick claimed to have laid down a 2 dols. bill. Then the young man fished up a club and went for the two, and they got out doors so fast that they unhinged the fly-screen. The other saloonist saw them as they went down the street neck and neck, flee- ing from the wrath of a 90-pound man, and he kicked himself and muttered: "Twenty years of experience and still a fool! It was a put-up job on use !" DIAMOND Carrulo.—Nearly 200 years ago Englishmen were the finest diamond cutters in the world, and the trade was nearly all carried on in London. and at the present time old English cut diamonds will:always fetch a very high price, as the cutting is still so much prized. Through religious persecution the cutters migrated to Amsterdam, where they have since remained. At the present time anyone vi-iting one of the largest diamond cutting factories in Amsterdam will be shown a model . of the Kolni-noor, and told that it was cut and polished at their factory, when it is apt undisputed fact that both her Majesty the Queen and the late Prince Consort took so great an interest in the cutting that Messrs. Garrard, the Queen's jewellers, had a room specially fitted up for it to be cut in. and it was all done at Messrs. Gerrard's present- establishment in Haymarket. The Duke of Wellington put the first facet on, and her Majesty. and nearly all the members of the Royal Family, assisted in putting on those most perfect facets that it now has; and there are at least 72 of them on the stone. At the time that the African diamond fields were dis- covered, there was only one diamond cutter in London. Dutchmen were accordingly engaged to work in London from Monday morning till Friday sunset, and they were to receive £lO per week each man. There was a very Wee supply of rough diamonds to be cut, so they struck several times successfully for high wages. They would allow no person to be in the room that they worked in, being afraid that the secrets of their art might be dis- covered. At last they demanded £lB per week each man, when they were discharged and English precious gem cutters were put at the work. At first they were only able after a deal of trouble to cut a class of diamond in one month which they could now cut in about four days. As soon as it was clearly proved that English- men had once more gained the art, the Worshipful Com- pany of Turners had their attention called to it. They at once decided to give English cutters every encourage- ment, and have, with the valuable assistance of the Baroness and Mr. Burdett-Coutts, who are both members of this company, offered money awards in competition against the Dutch for the best cut diamonds. After several contests the Englishmen gained the first prize and most of the others. In 1859 there was only one diamond cutter in London. At the present time there are now a great number actually in full work. As a nation, the Americans are the finest judges of diamonds in the world. American buyers insist on getting the \ finest stones and the most perfect of cutting. It is a well known fact that where the British workman has mastered his art, no matter what art that may be, he is absolutely unsurpassed. THE iNEWALITIES OF MEN.—M. Lapouge, of Mont- pellier, has recently delivered before the Faculty lof Natural Sciences in that town a series of lectures on in- equalities among men, in the course of which he said that the political dogma of equality rested on hypotheses which were utterly false. He distinguished four social types among mankind :—(1) The initiators, who show mankind the way into the region of the unknown, and who go in front. Restless and daring, with an intelli- gence which is at least equal to the average, men of this type do not travel readily along beaten tracks. "New ideas are the breath of life to them. They spend their lives in new creations; they are often wrecked, but the true genius represents the most perfect form of this type. (2) Men of spirit, of intelligence, who, possessing no creative power themselves, yet carry out and perfect the ideas' and discoveries of the first type, to which they are really the complement. (3) Men who, with much or little intelligence, can work only with others, who mistrust every new idea not accepted by all the others, but who seize it with avidity when their neighbours adopt it. If intelligent, these men are docile, but they dislike every change ot routine, and they represent the dullness of the mass in the face of every reform. (4) Men of this type are not fit to attain even the smallest step in culture. Evidently every man cannot be clamed under one or other of these divisions. .In human societies clear lines of demarkation do not exist, but for general purposes the distinction is sufficiently .evident. The superiority of a race or nation depends on the greater or smaller number of men of the first two classes. The race which is richest ia the first type is the bit:eel° dolichocephalic, and this has been the case even when the people among whom they lived were not of this kind. In Egypt, Chaldea, Assyria Persia, India, and even in China men of this type ruled. In the Greek and Roman world it was the some, and is so still. In our own day the rank of a nation corresponds with the strength of the blonde dolichocephalic element. The Crallie and Frank elements which made France great sere of this.type, and it plays the same part in England, Germany, and America. Near these came the Semitic • and Mediterranean races, who had reached a high grade of civilisation when the blonde dolichocephalic peoples were still savages. The remainder of mankind must be reckoned the Passive races. The brachycephalic races of Europe, the Celto-Slays, rarely produced men of the first intellectual type. In the social changes of recent Years brachycephalic men, who form the lower classes, have been elevated and brought forward, and herein, the lecturer thought, lies the great danger of the future de- terioration of the French nation. The existence of the superior blonde dolichocephalic type is threatened by amalgamation with the dark braehycephalic and inferior races. - -

PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. By Ffuou BErrE.
XXIV.-ON CHIMNEYS-ESPECIALLY OLD BOB'S.

Some people might think that because a man was neither an architect, a bricklayer, or a chimneysweep, he couldn't know anything about chimneys; but with all due deference to the opinion of such people, I am going to run in a claim to the knowledge upon no other basis than that the chimney has been forced upon my notice under many varying conditions. The chief use of the house chimney is to collcet soot in readiness to surprise any man who fools with the chimney. It also furnishes a vast sea of enterprise, to the suffering sweep. The chimney is also useful as a sort of gymnasium for the sportive starling, who finds through it the only means of sailing around your bedroom at 4-0 a.m. on a summer's morning. I have heard my grandmother say that the chimney was originally erected for the specific purpose of con- veying the smoke from the house fire to a fair elevation in the open air. This may have been so, but I have ho doubt that before long great results will be. obtained in the beef-curing line by a reverse state of things, i.e., by simply hanging the beef somewhere near the chimney- piece .for a few hours. The chimney is also a source of unfailing entertain- ment and fun to anybody who has leisure and per- severance, Before I say anything further it will perhaps be as well if I explain what is meant by a smoky chimney. All chimneys in active use are smoky, but conventionality has allotted the term chiefly to the direction pf the smoke, and to elspecial circumstances connected with such direction. You will therefore understand, by the rule of para- doxes, that if you see thick volumes of smoke issuing from the top of a chimney, that chimney doesn't smoke by any means. On the other hand, if you want to thrash one of the children,and you have to grope around the house till you feel him in one corner before you can do it, you may safely conclude that your chimney is a smoky one. In.speaking of the entertainment tote derived from a smoky chimney, I have in my mind's eye one par- ticular chimney, which, in the days of my boyhood, did duty as a lightning conductor for the house of a good- natured cobbler whom we knew solely by the name of old Bob. Old Bob's domicile was situated at one end of the village, and the back portion of the roof was so low that, by a very simple acrobatic feat, which consisted in one boy standing on another boy's shoulders, any two naughty boys maliciously inclined could easily have placed a large sod upon the top of old Bob's chimney- pot, thereby stopping the escape of too much heat, and literally making it warm for old Bob. I make this note en passant, because sometime after the remarkable phenomena which I shall ha % e occasion to allude a ury large sod was dislodged from old Bob's chimney, where it had evidently stuck and crimpled up on some ledge, and been the nightmare of old Bob's existence for a considerable time. lam sure the impartial reader will not suspect for a moment that knew anything about that sod previous to Its dis- lodgement. It might have been placed on the chimney- pot by some wicked boy, and not being arranged with mathematical precision, it might have slipped down; but I incline rather to the theorythat in the days of old Bob's grandmother, when chimneys, according to tradi- tion, were of good service, the powerful drawing power of the chimney had sucked the aforesaid sod out of the common, through the back door, and up the chimney, where it had got crimpled up on some ledge as before stated; but this is pure conjecture. Anyway, the chimney, or the sod, or both, were the means of old Bob commencing to study the natural sciences at a fairly 'advanced age. The furniture in old Rob's front parlour consisted of his cobbler's stock-in-trade, a 'three-legged stool, and a long form, which latter afforded a free seat to anyone who could either tell a stor,y or listen to one, no matter what were his age and condition.

As far as I can remember, old Bob's capabilities were three, to wit, mending shoes, spinning and listening to yarns, and acting on the most reckless advice. Old Bob's chimney was decidedly a smoky chimney if it has to be-gauged by the definition we have agreed upon; and if you had sat with me, reader, upon the form before spoken of, and listened to the astounding cures propounded for smoky chimneys, you would un- doubtedly have been overwhelmed at the contemplation of your own ignorance of the subject. The young men who congregated at old Bob's, when giving their advice, needn't have winked so often at one another if they did know so much People who are theoretically well up in chimneys ought to give their advice to less instructed people with la-coming modesty. One night young Saville would give a long and intricate explanati, at as to how an inflated !ladder, suspended by a string midway in the chimney, caused a rush of hot air past the bladder, and made the draught perfect. A few nights after this, old Bob would describe how ho had tried to push a bladder down the chimney with a clothes-prop, and failed. Then Blair would tell how they always put a large pile of shavings on the fire at their house, and burned all the soot out of the chimney. After a few more sittings of the form, old Bob would inform us that he hadn't been fined half-a- crown for having his " chimbley" on fire, but that the blaze from the shavings had broken the glass face of his clock on the mantlepiece. . . . .

One young man showed by the clearest logic that a large hole cut into the room door would at once put an end to the nuisance, and illustrated his point by vigor- ously opening and shutting the door in question, at every movement wafting immense volumes of smoke from the fire. Several days after, old Bob explained 1 that the huge piece of rough wood nailed on the door I was to ease a growing apprehension of lumbago. I forget how many times old Bob had had that " chimbley" Swept, but the sweep always told the same tale—that there was a bend somewhere in it that he couldn't get his brush round. One night a young fellow named Charlie—an especial favourite of old Bob's told how, to his certain know-. ledge, some score of smoky chimneys had been remedied by simply firing a shot gun up them. The apparent feasibility of this made such an impression upon old ' Bob, that he at once candidly expressed his regret at not being the happy possessor of a gun. This misfor- tune was easily got over by Charlie, who not only offered to lend him a gun, but who forthwith went out and quicldy returned with an antiquated fowling-piee,e, the barrel of which might have been improvised out of a locomotive smoke stack. Charlie didn't evidently want a square foot to be blown out of anybody, nor even out of the house wall, for he asked, "Do you know how to handle a gun, Bob ?" Yes! Bob had fired a gun off several times. "Do you know how to load one ?" was then asked. Yes! he understood that. But Charlie was an exceptionally careful young man, and as he produced a flask of gun- powder from his coat-tail pocket, he explained to old Bob that he must not put more than half the contents of the flask into the gun; and then, producing a canvas bag full of small shot, he said, "About a quarter of a pound of this, not more; and you can ram as much paper in as you please." " All right!" said old Bob. "There will be enough ammunition for two discharges if it should be required," said Charlie, as he produced a few percussion caps from his waistcoat pocket. "I haven't time to wait any longer, for I have to meet Renshaw; perhaps you will tell us how you go on. , Ta-ta!" The other young man seemed also to be struck with sudden recollections of engagements, and with varied excuses they "sloped." I think there is some justification for my using the word "sloped," when we consider the downward course those young men were travelling. But to resume. I did think once of going outside to see how far the air would be darkened, but the rapidity with which old Bob manipulated the gun fascinated me, and I remained. I don't know much about the bore of guns, but experts will be able to form some idea of this one when I tell them that old Bob usV a good sized kitchen poker' for a ramrod. 1 As old Bob put the muzzle up the chimney, and the stock to his shoulder, I instinctively moved to the other

side of the room Poor old Bob! I don't like to see an elderly man knocked flat on is back, and never did. I should certainly have helped him up if I had been abV to find him; but if you were to put me under the mr solemn oath I should swear that at least two hundred eight of soot came down that chimney, as it 'appeared, for no other purpose than for old Bob's winding sbeet. But old Bob was a wiry old Bob; an extraordinarily tough old Bob, and the heap of soot moved, and old Bob crawled out like a Christy minstrel of the first blackness. But his chimney still smoked; such are the decrees of fate; and old Bob for a long time preferred to be blackened with smoke rather than with the actual soot.
able most

In course of time, however, old Bob was prevailed upon to pour water down the chimney, and the wonder- ful appearance of tufts of blackened grasa that were washed into the fire-grate led to the diplacetnent of the sod already mentioned. All the " chirnbleyis" enter- tainment and fun was at an end for old Bob, except that he could relate its dark history as well as anyone, although it told against himself; and. I might add, against the bad boy who planted that sod.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 25, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 25, 1888.
THE LICENSING QUESTION. BY KO-KO.

The Licensing Question, as it exists in Warring- ton to-day, will not favourably stand the calm re- view of an unprejudiced person. Ido not wish to look at the Tatter at all from the point of view of the teetotaller, who i 4 averse to the traffic in any shape or form. There are not many teetotallers who could look at it in a dispassionate and impar- tial spirit; and, on the other band, there are more than a few people whose interests, if not directly connected with the trade, are in various ways in- directly so connected, who would also find it impos- sible to be impartial when considering this matter. I stand between the two—the happy medium. I have nothingto gain by defending trade interests, and I have nothing to gain by opposing them. In fact, I have nothing to do with the matter at all, excein as a private citizen, and a ratepayer, who has a right to take some interest in local affairs. To my mind there can be no reasonable objection to a public-house, well-conducted, and in a neighbour- hood where it is solar called for as to be supported by the public of such neighbourhood. In Warrington, , however, it cannot be denied, there are really too many public-houses, and the magistrates, as the persons responsible for the good conduct of the borough, ought rather to think of decreasing the number than granting fresh licenses. A stranger, walking through any of the principal streets of Warrington is wont to exclaim—" What a drunken place this must be." Public-house signs catch the eye in every direction, and he finds himself wonder- ing how on earth they all exist in these days of competition. If the said stranger happens to he in town on a Saturday night, and has a look round the streets then, or has a glance into some of the drink- ing shops, his first impression will be confirmed. Warrington is a drunken place ; for its size dis- gracefully so. Police Court statistics prove it, and ocular demonstration proves it. Yet many of these houses do not pay—at least they do not pay the tenants—if the word of the tenants themselves is to be credited. Wages are not so ' high as they were in Warrington at one time, when working-men, atter providing for the wants of the week, had substantial amounts left to fritter away for the benefit of the publicans. It is about as much as a work- ing-man can do at the present day if he looks after the necessities of himself and family, and has left enough money for an occasional glass or two at the end of, the week—just to moisten his throat. Still there are the same number of houses of refreshment, whose trade must ix this way have been greatly affected. The tee- total mind will take it as a good sign that some of these houses languish, while others will simply regard it as an indication of the dullness of the times. Another sign, of the pre4sure of the times on publicans is the fact that some of them have had to call to their aid very question- able attractions in order to entice custom. When what have been known as respectablet N.vell-to-do houses have recourse to the engagement of singing-room artistes and dancers for the sake of attracting custom, it is evident that they are driven to it through a very pressing want of custom. The supporters of the trade themselves ad- mit that there are too many public-houses in Warring- ton. They point with some degree of satisfaction to the offer made by a great brewing monopoly to give up the licenses of certain public-houses in town if ,the erection of commodious hotels in the suburbs will be permitted. Most specious idea. They say, with much show of rea- son, that a well-conducted hotel is bound to be better, morally and socially, than houses in the centre of the town that cater for the rough, and perhaps the criminal classes—the sort of people who are almost certain to fall i into temptation if it s placed in their way. A far-seeing proposal this. The argument is a catching one, and has a sound that is pleasing to the ear, Taken off-hand, it is indeed convincing. But look at it in de- tail. Then it will be seen that the motives of the brewers are not, after all, so very dis- interested. What? Disinterested? They are just the other thing, and very much the other thing too. These brewers, these monopolists, these spongers on the drunken portion of the human race, have long-headed business men and cute lawyers at their command, and they know very well what they are doing. Their plausi- ble proposal is only a plan to hoodwink the public. No one understands better than they do that, besides the effect of bad trade, their business suffers to some extent, if not much, by reason of the advancing temperance wave. That wave is slowly, gradually, but surely, encroachingon the fore shoreof the liquortrade. Modera- tion is succeeding excess; may not total abstinence in time succeed moderation ? They know, also, that gradu- ally the people are getting more power into their own grasp. They can see looming not far ahead a time when they may be compelled with scant ceremony fo close some of the houses that are a disgrace to those who own them and the town that permits them to exist. And this, too, without receiving any quid Iwo quo in return. Hence their offer. If by giving up houses that do not pay, and may to a certain extent be considered doomed, they are allowed te erect houses on a larger scale, they in reality place themselves in a position of 'comparative security. It is only natural to think, that when the time comes for forcibly decreasing licenses, there will not be much pro- pability of a house being compulsorily closed that had only recently been built at great cost, and had only recently been licensed. Thus, though in the course of the inevitable they might be compelled to close old houses, they would have secured other houses to take their place, in wkich to build up a trade to replace what was lost.

• _ If the Licensing Committee will do their duty next month, they will not only refuse any new applica- tions, but they will refuse to renew some of the old licensee. Looked at from a moral and social standpoint, it is plainly their duty to put in force a weeding process. I do not for a moment suppose that such a thing will happen; but I do think it is only reasonable to expect that no new applications will be acceded to. A writer in your last issue, under the signature of "Orford-lane," very rightly observes that to "attempt to force any more houses upon us will be a public outrage that will meet with the re- sentment of all the respectable people in the district." I agree with him there. But he hits rather hard when he says—" If our magistrates were more manly and inde- pendent they would refuse to play into the hands of the church-building brewer of Walton Hall." That is hard on the Great Unpaid. They (the G.U.) all over the country do their duty, or they think they do it, which amounts to pretty much the same thing. True, some- times their ways are peculiar, and their decisions ex- traordinary, but as a rule their little vagaries only affect those who cannot help themselves. Occasionally some daring writer for the press endeavours in a feeble way to "show them up" when they have been more than usually particularly funny, bat as a magistrate is generally a man with a substantial banking account, a very thick skin, and a remarkable conceit of himself, such little references told§ failings are beneath notice. It is admitted that as a rule unpaid magistrates will pun- ish more severely a starving man who has stolen a loaf than an abandoned brute who has covered his wife with bruises, aid then how they do look after the rich man's , game? A perusal of the Press will show that the magis- terial bench, with honourable exceptions, " cottons " to the wealthy in a wonderful manner. The interests of the rich are well looked after, and, although there may be no distinction in the law, there certainly is one way of administering it for the rich, and another way for the poor. It is not unreasonable, then, to con- jecture that there may be magistrates who, if they happen to be on the Licensing Committee, and if they follow the natural bent of their inclination, would not be averse to favouring theinterests of an opulent brewer. , Magistrates occasionally de work for brewers, but that is a point I will not urge. They are open to fair criticism, but to impute mercenary motives to anyone would be an insult. There is nothing wrong in a rdagis trate having commercial dealings with 'brewers, but I refuse to believe that any such, at least among our , local justices, would lay himself open to a charge of hav- ing allowed that to in any way affect his decision in a public question like that of licensing. Should there be any magistrates on the local licensing committee so situated, I have no doubt that they will decline to take part in licensing business, and will retire in the same way that a magistrate who is a member of the Sanitary Committee usually retires when a prosecution is being conducted before the magistrates at the instance of that committee. Should the Licensing Committee recommend the granting of any new applications, it 4 will be for the public in meeting assembled to express their opinions, before the matter comes before the general body of the magistrates for confirmation.

Tng NEW WIMBLEDON.—The Council of the National Rifle Association have reported in favour of the Berkshire Downs ond Cannock Chase as offering the most eligible sites in substitution for Wimbledon, but a special meet- ing of the Council will be held on the 21st of December to make the final choice.

week a fine lot of five two-year-oh., _iirc entire colts for shipment to America. Mr. Parker, Simcoe, Ontario, got three, and Blair Brothers, of Illinois, two. They were all well bred, and, generally speaking, strong-boned colts, and well suited for crossing with the native mares. Turning to live stock and meat imports for the seven months, we notice an increase in cattle, after a steady decrease for the three years ending with 1887. Fresh beef, too, which fell off in 1887, has increased in quantity considerably, and salt 'beef slightly. Sheep and lambs have come in diminished number, while mutton has been imported more extensively than ever. Pigs have increased, while most of their products have suffered a decline. Butter has made an advance, margarine re- maining practically stationary, and cheese increasing. One of the most important land cases which has ever been before the Irish Land Commission was the subject of a judgment given by Mr. Justice O'Hagan a week ago. The farm, or to speak with more exactness, the territory in question, comprised an area of over forty thousand. acres, or sixty-two square miles. The tenant's applica- tion against the Marquis of Sligo to have a fair rent fixed was set aside on the ground that the farm was used purely for the purpose of pasture, and was not an agri- cultural holding within the Land Acts. Agricultural labour colonies, which have proved suc- cessful in Germany in relieving men out of employment, are not unlikely to be tried in this country. The first report of the Mansion House Conference on the Condi- tion of the Unemployed, while condemning ordinary relief works, mentions the report of a sub-committee in favour of trying an agricultural labour colony by way of experiment. A fresh sub-committee is now engaged in the investigation of the scheme, and matters have pro- gressed, as far as theconsideration of offers of farms and estimates as to the cost of the necessary buildings. After the recess, the main Committee will take all the details intb consideration, and probably base upon them' an appeal to the public for funds. TIIE PURCHASE Os' ARMY HORSES.—An important re- sult of the establishment of this reserve of horses has been that the Government have abandoned the experi- ment of importing animals from Canada, for Mr. Brod- rick said that as to the purchase of horses in Canada, he thought the impression that we paid a higher price there had arisen in this way. A Commission was sent out to Canada to purchase horses, and on calculating their ex- penses it was found that the cost of each horse was £52, whereas the sum allowed here for artillery and cavalry horses was £45. No horses were at present being bought outside the United Kingdom. The purchase of horses was now in the hands of a central organisation, with the result that the farmers knew where to take their horses at a definite time for sale. His right hon. friend was , anxious, as far as possible, to encourage the breeder at home. WHE RIGAIADF.N SHORTHORNS.—,At the Great York- shire Show at Huddersfield an announcement WES made which came with great suiprise to the horse-breeding and cattle-loving public, that Mr. Christopher Wilson intended to sell off his very famous herd of dairy cows, for which Rigmaden has a great reputationcin the north of England. Mr. Wilson takes as much interest in his herd of deep-milking cows as he does in SitiolGeorge and his famous descendants. He has been In the habit of attending the leading sales where Yorkshire dairy cows were to be found, and has made careful selections; but when the animals were brought home and placed along- side the:old stock gathered together by the late Mr. Wilton, they did not stand the comparison at all well. It has been decided to' sell the herd of Booth shorthorns, and the dairy cows, about eighty in number, in Septem- ber, two days before Mr. Foster's and Mr. Harris's sale at Calthwaite Hall, Carlisle. To FEED HORSES.—The heavier breeds are more liable to colic, because they are fed with larger quantities of food generally of inferior quality. A horse is worked several hours at a time, brought home, and has his manger filled with bulky and indigestible food, which he is'allowed to eat ravenously. The imperfectly masti- cated food goes into the stomach and intestines, whose vital energy has been impaired by over-exertion. Be- COMP a horse has done harder work than common lie certainly requires more nutriment ; but, then, this should be given by extra times of feeding and better food, not by increasing the volume of food at onetime. Horses in our large towns are often saved from colic, by being allowed to drink frequently at the public troughs and fountains. By doing this the horse becomes a good judge of the quantity he requires. If a horse conies home, from a hard journey, perspiring freely, do not al- low him to drink his fill of cold water. Let him stand in the stable till he has cooled somewhat, and is made comfortable. A little chilled water may be given, and a little good long hay be put into his rack to take his attention. It will require thorough mastication, and will have the effect of preparing the stomach for the reception of the more concentrated food which is to fal,low.—Report of Lincolnshire Veterinary Association. HINTS ON HARVESTING. Harvest will have already commenced in e ly dis- tricts south of the Thames, and will be gen( ra• in a fortnight. Careful farmers will be making ready for this principal effort of the year by getting forward with other descriptions of work, as well as by seeing that all is ready for action. Horse-hoeing and hand-hoeing of roots will ere long be interfered' with by calls to the harvest field, and should therefore now be pushed with all speed, and by the employment of extra hands. The last of the hay should be secured and the hay ricks pulled, topped up. and thatched. and, rick-yard should be cleared of weeds, and made ready for the reception of the crop. Stack saddles should he looked over and repaired, and harvest carts made ready to carry their precious burden. Harvesters, reaping machines, and elevators should be Overhauled by a skilled man, in order that they may work without interruption; scythes, horse-rakes, and hand-rakes should be properly ;fixed and prepared for work. Every requisite for harvest work should be thought over—files for sharpening the reaper knives, string for the self-binder, spars and tarline for thatching, straw ropes for corn ricks, drawn straw for thatching, beer (where beer js given) for the men, barracks or accommodation for travelling harvestmen, oatmeal and tea for harvest drinks, and many other small matters which, if left over until the actual "throng" comes, cause inconvenience, irritation, and delay. Among useful safeguards against the weather, the rick cover may well be classed. Certainly, an ample rick cover over a barley rick is a comfort, especially at the close of the day when the weather is "on the work." We speak from experience, and yet it is manifest to all observers that the neat rick cover, with its poles and pulleys, its stays and ropes, is an almost infallible sign of amateur, dilletante, or landlord farming. The rent- payer will have none of it. The hereditary farmer pre- fers to employ other means. He well fills up and tops up his ricks, covers it with straw, and waits for a favourable change of the weather—but patent rick• cloths he does not take into account. Why is this? The reason for this preference for old-fashioned and stereotyped methods is not easy to see, but it prevails throughout the whole practice of farming. A re- pugnance to increased expenses, a narrow margin of profitstreadily obliterated by prodigal expenditure, and the utter unfitness of agricultural labourers to be trusted with neat, valuable appliances are, no doubt, among the principal reasons. The valuable rick covet ik too often improperly used. It is thrown over the rick and allowed to lie upon it, instead of being so hoisted by its ropes and poles as to allow a current of air to pass underneath. Then comes a wet night; and the wet above, operating with the beat and damp arising from the rick, rots the canvas in 48 hours. That rick cover is ruined, and the farmer is not likely to try another in a hurry. Another objection to rick cloths is that they are made too smali for large farms where big ricks are put up. The fact is that, where farming business is carried on upon a large scale, and ricks are both large and numerous, the rick cloth will probably appear to savour somewhat of toy farming. We saw corrugated iron for thatching in use a few days ago upon a large farm in Wiltshire. It was de- cidedly too small, and the farmer had, with the aid of his blacksmith, tacked an extra width of iron to it on both sides in order to make it do. This did not look so neat as the drawings of these iron diatchings appear upon paper. If these novelties are to be generally used by large farmers, they must be made adaptable to big ricks, and not to little toy ricks, such as the one we in- spected was evidently meant for. The farmer expressed himself dissatisfied on account of the puny dimensions as to width of the covering sent out. He explained that, , although the stack bottom was made of the dimensions required, by the time the eaves were reached the rick had so increased in width that the iron was several feet too short for its purpose. A covered rick-yard may be constructed at very moderate cost on timber pillars carrying a wall-plate and light rafters covered by corrugated iron. Such perman- ent hay or corn houses will practically last for ever if firmly put up, and will always be a comfort for keeping hay, corn, or straw safe from injury. The precise stage for cutting corn will not be very easy to judge this year. The ear and the corn will pro- bably ripen before the straw, and, in fact, we must not look for the beautiful golden hue of last year, but judge by: other criteria. Wheat may be cut comparatively green. In the process of ripening there is a transfer- ence of material from the entire straw and leaves to

The advantages of early cutting in the case of wheat and oats may be thus summarised :—A better quality of wheat, without diminishing quantity; a better quality of straw for feeding purposes; less risk from weather:; a quicker clearance of the stubble, whether for the pur- pose of autumn clearing or for the early sowing of stebble turnips or other catch crops. Lastly there is the possibility of obtaining a good price for an early sample of new wheat brought into the market. COTTAGE GARDENING. Onions: This crop, which is usually a fickle one, perhaps never looked more promising this season of the year than it does now, and there is no sign of the mag- got, even in gardens where it has usually been so preva- lent. Some have to complain of too much top and too little bulb-growth, and so long as the weather continues moist this state of things is likely to continue. We have already 50 per cent, more weight of bulb than we had at the end of last season, and there is a possibility of yet greater increase if shortly the tops of those that are disposed to be bull-necked are pinched or twisted just above the bulb and bent over. The autumn sown may be served so now, and the sap will be checked in its up- ward course and will be diverted for the benefit of the bulb. Vegetable Marrow: If the growth is crowded thin out the shoots by cutting out the most barren, so as to let air and sun into the most fruitful ones. A mis- take is frequently made in allowing the fruit to remain on to get old, which has the effect of preventing the formation of others. The Dwarf French Bean will need a few short sticks now that the pods are forming and weighing them down, and if sticks are not at hand run a string along each side, twisted round a few sticks, firmly fixed in the ground. The Scarlet Runner is best stopped, to induce a bushy habit and fruitfulness. Left to grow higher than the stakes, they become top heavy, and are liable to be blown over by the wind. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Layering Carnations: One of the surest ways of propagating the Carnation is by layering the young shoots in the following manner:— Place the knife in a slanting direction below the third joint from the top and sever the shoot in half to the next joint, then direct the point of the shoot upwards and peg it into the soil, which should be introduced for the purpose—that which is light and sandy being the best. We generally use the emptyings of flower-pots, after it has been passed through a half inch seive, and this we place in a mound round each plant, or group of plants, and before the shoots are pegged we press it well down with the hand to prevent shrinkage. Scarcely a shoot fails to emit roots from the partly-severed portion if they are not allowed to get dry just at the first. Towards the end of September they may be expected to be sufficiently rooted to have a few of each sort taken up and potted, at any rate two good plants of each sort should be so served, OA they are liable to 80 many acci- dents in the open ground, and there is always danger of losing one or more of the sorts at all times. THE GREENHOOSE.—The early flowering Pelargoniums must be stood out in the open air, and in wet weather the pots must be turned on their sides, as if they are allowed to be constantly moist they will not rest, nor ripen their wood, and will be unfit for another year's flowering. 'They must be laid down with their tops away from the sun in order that its rays may play well into the centre of the plants, but if they show symptoms ! of the want of water the pots must be stood level and water supplied, but again withheld until the plant flags. After three inches of the base of the shoots have turned brown, each must be cut to within two or three joints ot its union with the elder growth. Water must now be more cautiously applied than before, and the soil must be permitted to get dry between each watering. EXTENSIVE ROSE GROWING.—It is not within the pro- vince of this column to make gentlemen's gardens sub- jects of comment, but now and then, when we observe any noteworthy circumstance or signs of rare cultural skill in the gardener in charge, we are tempted to record it as an incitement to those whom we endeavour to lead and instruct. This week we have to notice the finest private collection of roses for many miles round Preston that has been got together, by Mr. Came, gardener to George Dewhurst, Esq., Clayton Green, Chorley. There' ere b6O established plants, comprised of 400 sorts. Of ' course there are many of these that would be termed " weedy " by the professional rosarian, and there are many more of the most delicate constituted that will never develop their true character, and wilt not forgiVe MeCarne for introducing them into:such a bleak spot as Clayton Green, under the most favourable conditions. They are only fine weather roses, as many of the darker shades showed by the disfigured buds that the rainy, sunless weather was not at all to their liking. True, that many of the plants have to submit to the shade of trees, and their roots fight for food with the roots of other plants, planted as they are in the fruit tree and vegetable borders of the kitchen garden. One bed, in front of the carriage ring, containing 162 sorts whilst free from these drawbacks, is dreadfully exposed to the east and north winds, and roses that will do well here may be relied on as good doers. The bulk of the plants are, however, in beds on the lawn, and in the kitchen garden on the south-west side of the mansion. The best flowers at the time of our visit were Victor Verdier, Dupay Jarnain, Countess of Oxford, Baroness Rothschild, Fisher Holmes, Mrs. Caroline Swailes, Madame Sophie Fropot, Reynolds Hole, Madame Luizet, La France, Mu- veille de Lyon, Marquise de Castellane, Duke of Edin- burgh, Earl of Pembroke. Lady Mary Fitlwilliam, Prince Camille de ithoan, Clara Crotchet, Mr. Dudley Baxter. Captain Christy, and Ulrich Brunner, the latter having taken various prizes as the best rose in the show. All the above are exhibition sorts, and had we selected another score out of the 400 growing at Clayton Green, we would be in possession et the cream of those suitable for the climate of this district. Mr. Carne' ti object in getting so many sorts is to test this matter for himself, and his experience will be freely given to others.

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. TH' OWD TALE TOWD O'ER AGRON. (HEARD TH' OWD ',DYNE). .Neaw, Molly, stop—aw prithee, do ! An' hear wod aw've to say; Aw korn'd abide this warchin' deawt Another dreary day. Mi mind's filled up wi' gentle thowt, Mi heart's a treasury 0' t' best an' purest Luv ther is, Au' lass, it's o for thee ! Just speyk a word, an' dunnot screen Thi breet, bewitchin' face : WS one o' t' prettiest seets ther is Abeawt this lonesum place. Aw've thowt abeawt thee mony a day, An' dreamt o'er thee at neet ; Come, Molly, bee to nowt to say To melt uu sad heart lest ? Last Sunda', when aw went to t' Church, An' see thee set i' th' pew, Aw'm blest iv aw could keep mi een Off thee, o t' sarmon•thro';• Th' owd preycher towd o'er th' Hooam aboon, An' th' angels purity; But th' ngel as aw thowt abeawt Wur,—come, aw'll whisper—thee !” Sin' then, aw'ye thowt o scoarts o' thowts, Till aw con lierdly bide ; An'—Molly, arta willin', lass, To ho a poor mon's bride. Aw've no gret wealth to otter thee, Aw'm one as hates o sham ; But o ats mine thart welcome to, Wilt ha' me as aw aui ? God bless thee! Lift thi bonny een, An' look i' these o' mine;' There nowt but th' leet 0' goodness tileer To thee, an' o at's thine. Here tek mi hand, mi heart tha Iles, An' let me hey one cuss; Th' moon's flung id beet ire' t' cleawds to show As Heaven's blessin' us. Do, Molly, set mi heart at rest, An' ease mi troubled brain ; But, 0, dorn'd use me scornfully, An' aggravate mi pain. Dorn'd let's keep shilly-shallyin'— That's nayther moss nor sand; But speyk thad word, an' mek me one 0' th' happiest men i' th' land. Tha'rt studying o'er a tooathry things, An' wern'd be rash—to rue; Ther's mony a chap aboon my stamp, But nooan wi' heart mooar true. "Aye!" dosta say? div.head: • CHAPTER VII. ON THE HOUSE TOP.
div.p: • CHAPTER VII. ON THE HOUSE TOP.

Ursula, after taking her modest tea at a restaurant, sauntered on to the thoroughfares she loved, walking quickly when she reached them, as if with a set purpose, as a girl who respects her- self needs to walk in Paris. Her costume, which was neat in all respects, was not superior to that of an ordinary Parts maniere. The black straw hat drooped modestly over the young face, which was somewhat pale from constant work, and the black jacket and alpaca dress, with the well-mended gloves, were not calculated to at- tract attention. , Bhe in on unmolested. It was a lovely after- noon m that spring of the year which was the time she had always loved best. The ground was strewn with the pink and white blossoms of the chestnut trees. There was a delicate scent of acacias on the air, and thelimes were blossoming on the boulevards. For a little while he lingered by the Jardin des Plantes, and then quickened her steps as she returned to the bustle and stir, of life.

If a moralist could have followed Ursula Campion to her unpretending home he might have specu- lated as to whether there was reality in Spencer's dream. Was it possible that a pure-minded girl could put her delicate hand into the jaws of the lion, and sport unconscious of any mischief on a cockatrice den? Or was it that the loath- some Paris depicted in the pages of the older novelists, with all its Dante.sque horrors,had ceased to exist, with its traditional wickedness, though it is still described in the pages of Zola ? A believer in such constant and vicious degradation would have thought that the girl had pitched her nest on the very edge of a volcano where an outburst of de- structive lava from hidden revolutionary forces might at any time burst out and overwhelm her,"if he could have seen her turn into an unfashionable quarter, 'sacred to memories of religious struggles between Jesuits and Jansenists,and close to the old church of St. Medard.

She halted before a tall, somewhat dilapidated looking house, with a notice on a placard standing out from the door, " Grandes et petdes ap partemens a loner," and then began mounting 6. sistinte with a buoyant step which people getting into the forties and fifties might well have envied her. The stairs which she had to climb were smoke-blacked, and truth compels me to acknowledge that they were reeking with odours to which she was so accustomed that she took no notice of them.

A chord stirred in the memory of the fist asthmatic concierge, recalling a chapter long past in her life, as she watched the girl mounting the stairs, with her airy step, avoiding as if by instinct the blow which threatened her head, as she steered her way past the low ceilings and looked down laughingly at madame. "Ben soir, mademoiselle," said the concierge holding her stout sides and looking admiringly at the ascending figure, which laughed down at her hall- roguishly like Shakspere's Anel. "Ti-es gentils," she said they were loth, the brother and sister, with always a civil townie in their heads • and always paying their rent. Indeed Raymond's nuandif appearance, constantly excusing 'him from any vehement exertion, had roused her motherly sympathies, and heightened her admiration for made- moiselle, who seemed to have strength enough for both. Mademoiselle was like so many of her nation, never short of breath and never out of patience, even when she had to mount six storeys. And Mademoiselle was so well conducted, though she lived in the enceinte of an over-populated neighbourhood with not too savoury surroundings. Her smile and her bright greetings made amends for the poor young gentleman's muttered curse when he too had to toil up those rickety, flights of stairs. Well, well, he was not strong—there were excuses to be made for him, as madame said to herself, remembering her own Antoine; who would , have been near the same age, and whose grave was far away among the honest Alsatians. Antoine, if he had lived, might have been just such another with imagination, but no strength or force for the battles of life. 'Raymond, as she heard people say, was all brain and nerve. It flattered her to think that Antoine too; might have been a genius, and it was in defer- ence to this sort of castle in the air, which mothers are so apt to build about those children of whom death has 'deprived them, that she gave special in- structions to the little maid-servant—whose aprons and caps were more often black than white, in spite of a pension love for keeping clean the outside of the platter—to take exceeding care of the seventh-floor lodgers. T hus it was a cool, airy room whichUraula reached by thb last flight of stairs, which were nothing to the young limbs, though madame's stout legs seldom scale them—un garni with the furniture, a little cleaner and not more commonplace than usual, with fresh red tiles for the floor, which Ursula .herself often mopped; and what was better than all, a low window opening to the roof in which were' flowers in pots, carnations planted in sand, which bloomed every summer, chrysanthemums for the autumn, Lent lilies in the spring. The closed jalousies which protected the rest of the house with dim light did not exist in this attic. The clear sunshine streamed in by day, and at night the sunsets were beautiful from the roof. The weird- like dreaminess of the old city, with its churches; its bridges, its striking effects of light and shade, and its nver, with picturesque steamers, could be studied in a bird's-eye view from this height. All Gautier's , drearnseif enchanted palaces, lakes of lapislazuli, and the " barbaric gold and pearl of the Orient," could not beat the changing pictures to be seen from this attic—pictures not only bright, but redolent of the sad, still music of humanity. Need I say that Ursula only saw the brightnees,and had already forgotten her want of talent for painting, as she skipped about preparing supper, and watching at intervals the pageant of the sunset T She was essentially bright herself, opening like a blessom to the pure influences of air and sunshine, and with nothing, cold or repellant about her such as is generally associated in the Parisian mind with the English. And yet there was a piquancy impartNi to her companionship from the very fact that with all this she was queerly English in her downright ways. She had been so used to the company of men, that in all simplicity of heart she prided herself on being "a good pal," and—though she thought it her duty to stand up for women, and never would allow them to be run down in her presence—she could get on better with men than with friends of her own sex. And when her brother erune in, bringing, ae usual, some companions with him, no merrier party was to be found than the little one on that house-top, till it became too cold to sit on the roof, and- they drew their chairs into the room. Two other girls dropped in as the evening advanced —girls accustomed to work for their living as painters and musicians, and not to fidget the men by fastidious objections about trifles. There was no real harm in their laughter or in the good-tem- pered badinage with which they trifled with ideas ' which some of them ' called new, but which were really antediluvian. It never occurred to any of them that there was a necessity for chaperons. One of the girls—a Russian—who joined in the harmless chatter was prettier than Ursula; but prettyas she was, elle was practically extinguished by the remarkable. appearance of the English maiden. Leonard Campion had boasted a Castilian mother, and had always been inclined to make the most, not only of the high descent, but of the foreign element in his blood. It had been one of his little vexations that, ignore the Saxon character as he would, the English side was so clearly developed in his daughter. It was as if the in-. gredients had not properly amalgamated, and all the Spanish characteristics had gone to her brother. Ursula was English in her figure and complexion, if not in her dress. -

For the benefit of those of my readers who wish to realise with their senses as well as with their more spiritualised perceptions, I should like to make them see this figure modelled, so as to suit the artist eye, with gracious and not meagre proportions--a figure which had never been injured by the harmful and absurd practise of tight-lacing, with no high shoulders forced up in revenge for a contracted waist. What matter that the proportions of the face were by no means perfect? that the pretty nose was " tip- tilted " and piquantly rounded at the end, or that the tipper lip—coral in colour—expressed more in- dependence, more power. of saucy self assertion than was usual in a French girl. For the skin was lustrous in its fine texture and healthy transparency; the eyes were bright, and there was a rich abundance of red brown hair. There was something in the elasticity of the girl's youth and the freshness of her complexion which was like a blast of pure sea- air, and contrasted with the cadaverous faces and pulpy cheeks of most of the art students. And yet-4 must confess it—English mothers would

div.head: BROTHER'S KEEPER
div.p: BROTHER'S KEEPER

have been scandalised—her brother was =wall rolling a: cigarette for those red lips! But the Russian girl was also smoking, and so was the French one. To be bon eamarade, as Raymond declared, it was necessary for his sister to smoke. . Raymond was as sensitive on such points of etiquette, as he was to the slightest rise and fall in the social barometer. His sister was popular; be gloried in the fact, for they loved each other, th 9.. two, as brother and sister rarely love. But he iii We was too easily disturbed by the emotions Nakil; Atirred in him, like strange things that he could nel.t understand ; too easily inspired by the influences 01., poetry and melody—touching his sensibility like; I faint music far off—to be able to respond g'end'i' naturedly to the sallies of his rougher companions. 4 , "All the faults of the artist-nature with none el ( its •determination to conquer difficulties—ah, fellow I" as Desnoyers had said to himself witli 9 shrug, "he bad better get out of it !That sort of Sc sitiveness is beautiful to see, hua sure to be rubb'o off in the battle of life." They were chaffing him now for his laziness a WI his work. . , "He likes to do a little, but he will not finish," Said Ursula, displaying a remarkable sketch of a beggar,. woman and her child, the outlines of which were no very correct, but which someone said were like tbis! of a Murillo. "Some day when he will finish he .viii create a masterpiece." "If you can get him to say, like Corot—' c'a 01 amuse moi." " Ah, but he amuses himself by lying still. member when he was a little fellow he would liA the hour together hidden in ferns and deep grass, sr._ he told me that was the way lie amused hinisefl-- watching ,the animals and the insects." "Bali ! ' exclaimed a man of about five-and-twentl' the oldest in the room, with the benevolent intentioe of helping the elder sister to get some enthusiast° into the lazy boy, "Corot amused himself t 4. some purpose—and as for Millet—you should j 119" see his . portrait—looking determined as if he were 9 peasant leader standing to be shot." "I don't feel like being a peasant. I have no liking .for sabots, and I don't want to be shot," was Ear mond's answer to their banter. They laughed—laughter came very easily to these young people. There was a tap on the door. - "0, is it you ?" said Ursula, with. little change from her usually exuberant hospitality, as a y man entered, stooped and kissed her hand. -. seemed to be a regular part of the programme of ths evening, the others looking on interested. For this was Umula's fiance. It was as well ? have an accepted lover as well as a brother' Paris, when one had ' to live constantly in company of men, and to work for one's ch bread. It conferred a sense of protection, and s necessary to save appearances, just as the maidens ,-. certain towns of England like alwaya to have '-' solder with whom they can keep company, n: when there is no soldier to walk with them find necessary to hire one. Neither Ursula nor Louis Grandet attach importance to, the engagement. The ingcna, youth, who was as , pasty-looking as his felloei students, could boast a sweeping moustache, S° could play on the zither, which he had brought wIl him on this occasion. He adored Ursula, but content with his adoration. Neither did she see further into the future, content as she was with crust of bread, and sop of vegetables flavoured meat, in her six-storeyed sitting-room with adjacent . sleeping apartments, small as cubich. shut off from it by a couple of doors hidden by Mist curtains, and everything about it pretty and char', with a smartness which was inexpensive but ne disreputable. She had promised Grandet to marry him some without any serious intention of carrying out her mise—partly because there was no harm in him, ,he would help her to keep the gro-Wing-up Barn out of mischief ; partly on the system on which promises an organ-grinder sixpence,because Grar made himself a nuisance and had to be appeased- to really thinking about marriage, Ursula Cain] was much too busy to let such an idea enter head. Love seemed to be incompatible with "higher education" for which she had a cravini consistent with her diligence in making artit flowers. Most of the men whom she had seen del her father's lifetime were so van, so idle, 8,04 mindless, if not wicked. As to Grandet, he was bon enfant—a gentli by birth—who could not marry till he was n years older without his parents' leave. But he, well as his Ursula, seemed quite satisfied wit!' engagement which was apparently to end in sin( The young man was well content with present, for of all her comrades—and she had 1 —he was understood to be the most fav( And Ursula was the ideal of his ;cal dreams. Destiny, ho thought, liad brought to this English girl, and what was more - than that lie should worship at her was not aware that she had a unsettled ideas. The sovereignty which. st and which everyone accorded -to her, had been grudged to•her by Louis Grandet any than by her brother. He fell in like an obs slave with all her ideas. And though easy indifferent main:Ler made him feel for time, as he was, perhaps, intended to feel, that clarations of ardent love would be quite out of 1 ing with his usual inatter-of-fact reception, ITT' had a flexible mind, and fell in with his suggesit that she should start a lover, when there seem' be advantages in the plan. "I am so glad - you feel with me that " ought to be somebody else to help me to look i. Raymond. You see we don't know all the wsYs Paris, and my boy has no father," was her way of accepting his proposition. "flow can I guarantee what will happen te toe few years hence? how can I be quite sure I shall " change my mind?" she asked one day, with' open eyes. And when Grandet remonstrated with. on another occasion on her unnecessary kindne° the other students, she said, in the same fashio' "Why didn't you tell me, you foolish child ? I • never any idea of starting an English flirtation, you call it; and if I hail only known you were awfully jealous, I should have been afraid choosing/yon as my special eamarade—after all, are most of us good friends—comrades, are we not And he did not dare any longer to argue point. On sueh lines of policy did Ursula the empress. She did not flirt,. and not even know the meaning of love. was not aware that the subjugation of men ' natural to her. Most of her friends were poor, degraded they were not. The ideas of independ of fraternity and equality, influenced them witi their knowing it. They all had their rights—W' as well as men; all worked untiringly on days, and amused themselves on Sundays. (To be continued.)

TirE FRENCH ELECTIONS.—TRIPLE VIC- TORY OF BOULANGER. ?ARTS, MONDAY, 3 the Charente Inferieure, General Boulanger received '57,484 votes, and M. Lair 42,416; while in the Nord he was also successful, polling 132.152, against M. Neerlilin 128,567. In A miens, the streets were crowded, and there were some disturbances. IBeveral arrests were made at Lille. PAros, MONIpAY Nom—The final returns show that General Boulanger was yesterday elected for each of the ' three seats which he contested, viz., the Nord, the Somme, and in the Charente Inferieure. The result is a surprise to many in the capita BERLIN, MONDAY NlGHT.—General Boulanger's election excites great surprise here. It was thought that his downfall was complete. His present success is regarded ,as a proof that the French people are dissatisfied with the present state of affairs, and it causes here unmistak- able anxiety. The Vossiche Zeituag says that General Boulanger is no longer a personality. Reis the embodi- Merit of dissatisfaction with the inactivity of the Chain- hers and annoTaraCe at the uncertain position of the 'French Republic. ITALY, FRANCE, AND MASSOWAIL In his zeply to M. Goblet, on the subject of the Italian 'oecupatinn of Massowah, Signor Crispi denies that it was Ilecessary that Italy should notify the Powers of the step ha.s taken, inasmuch as the occupation was 'effected Prior to the act of the Berlin Conference which pre- scribes such notification. Signor Crispi complains of the action of the French Consul at Massowah in urging the People to refuse to pay certain local taxes—action which Was based upon definite instructions from Paris—and Insists that the French have no interests whatever at Massowah. The Note concludes with an expression of the Italian Government's determination to peacefully Pursue the policy which it has marked out, but, if occa- sion should arise, it will defend to the last its interests In the Red Sea. " WHITE MEN" IN THE SOUDAN. ALEXANDRIA., SA,TenDAY.—PiIgriMS who have arrived at Suakim from Shakotto, north-wen of Lake Nyassa. State that seven months ati...o;they RAVV, at Bongo, a large Party of white soldiers, commanded by white6men, and 'with no black troops. They wen armed with Reuling- tons, and marched mur.daysin camp with them. These Pilgrims speak a difficult 'language, and cannot be relied upon, as they might consider Zanzibars as white Then.

MERICA. —THE FISHERIES TREATY. FIGHT WITH NEGROES. NEW Yong, SATURDAY..--MT. Secretary Bayard, in an interview published this morning, vaguely hints that if The Senate postpones the vote on the Fishery Treaty, the President will withdraw it; thus 'throwing the responsi- bility of the failure to arriiv, at a =ohm vivendi on the Republicans. AS well as the blame for Canada revoking licenses. He also hinted that the President would then be compelled to apply the retaliation law. NEW YORK. SATURDAY,-Ts number of the negro in- babitants of Freetown, 'Louisiana, having become dis- orderly, the white portion of the population sought to expel them from the parish. A conflict ensued, with the result that 20 of the negroes were killed and several Others wounded. No otiestion of politics was involved in the dispute. TERRIBLE TIIIINDERSTORIVI..-LLT PERSONS KILLED. PHILADELPHIA. MONDAY.--A heavy thunderstorm passed over Eastern Ontario and Quebec on Sunday night, and iestroyed a number of houses and barns,.and hundreds tf horses and cattle. The storm was also attended with loss at life. At St.. lionis. De Goinagne, Captain Louis Sauvee, hit wife, and son, were killed. At St. Ignace Genres S. Loriller was ' killed by a falling tree struck by lightning. In St. Hyacinths the son of the proprietor of' the hotel was killed while closing a window, and also two lumbermen who were crossing the river. At. Chandee the lightning struck a canoe, and two men on board were lost. The hotel at Smith's Fall was set fire to. and the Wife of the proprietor lied from fright. At Lorigi nal the parish church WAS struck by lightning, while the building was full of people. A Panic ensued; and many persons were seriously injured by being trampled upon. The estimated damage by the Storm in Quebec alone is 51,500,000. Later reports from Valleyfield, Beaubarnaes County, state that five men were killed by liOltr;nv. TERRIBLE BOILER j',EXPLOSION :IN AMERICA. EIGHTEEN -PERSONS KILLED. NEW YORK, THURSDAY. A fire broke out to-day Oft the premises of Messrs. Whitney, paper manu- facturers, at - Neenah, 'Wisconsin. The conflagra- tion attracted a great crowd of spectators, who pressed RS close to the buildings,as they were able. Whilst the fu'e, was burning fiercely, some boilers belonging to the mill engines exploded with terrible force scattering des- truction right and left. Eighteen of the spectators in the crowd were almost instantaneously killed, and a large number severely injured. Of the latter at least Seven are so terribly hurt that there is no hope of their recovery. The pecuniary loss is estimated at 10,000 dollars.

TERRIFIC WEATHER AT SEA. WRECK Or A STEXMER AND GREAT LOSS OF LIFE. NEW Yonx, IVEDYESDIY.—A terrible storm of wind and rain has been raging along the Atlantic seaboard from Virginia to Massachusetts, and also for some distance inland. A perfect cyclone prevailed in Chesapeake Bay. The coasting steamer City of Chester has been sunk through coming into collision with the Oceanic, from song Kong, in San Frantisco Harbour' and it is reported that a large number of people were drowned in conse- quence. Naw YORK, WEDNESDAY NIGHT.—The shipping casu- alty in San Francisco harbour unfortunately turns out to be even more serious than was at first reported. Neit fifteen, but twenty-one lives were lost, and all the per- sons drowned belonged to the City of Chester, eighteen of them being passengers, and three members of the crew. SAN FaAarcisco, WRONESDAY.—Further particulars re- garding the collision between the Oceanic and the City of Chester state that the latter vessel was on her regular trip along the Northern Coast. A dense fog prevailed at the time of the catastruplie,.and the City of Chester was entirely cut through, and sunk in five minutes in fifty fathoms of water. At least thirty-four persons were drowned, including ten cabin passengers and three of the crew. The remainder were steerage passengers. The Oceanic stood by and saved between 50 and 60.

Potato blight has appeared in Kont. , Great damage has been caused by heavy rain in the lower Shannon Valley, hundreds of tons of hay and turf ing carried away, and the corn crop destroyed.
