LORD DIARTINGTON AND MR. AUSTEN CHAMBER-. LAIN.

Lad Harlington has written as follows to Mr. Craig-Brown in reference to MT. Austen Chamberlain's candidature for the Border Burghs :—" Bolton Abbey, Skipton, August 17, 1888. 'Bear Sir,-1 am extremely glad to hear that the Liberal Unionist Association of Selkirk has, in concert with the other burghs of the constituency, adopted Mr. Austen Chamberlain as candidate Tor the Border Burghs in the event of an election. Prom my acquaintance dtith Mr. Austen Cham- berlain, I feel convinced that he will fully justify the selection which you have made, and that he will deserve the confidence whichoto doubt, has been inspired by the courageous political 'conduct of his father and by the conspicuous service which the latter has rendered, to the Unionist cause."
THE NEW COUNTY COUNCILS._

The Local Government Board fit's issued circulars to the town clerks and•clerks of the peace in England and Wales, stating that, in pursuance of the powers conferred upon them, by the Local Government Act, 1888, they have issued orders determining the number of the county councillors for each county, and their appoint- ment between each of the boroughs which have sufficient population to return one councillor, and the rest of the county. The number of councillors so described does not, however, include the county aldermen. The'Board point out the duties that will now devolve upon the rourts of Quarter Sessions and town councils, so as to determine the electoral divisions for the first elections to the County Councils by the date prescribed in the Act. which is the Bth of November next. MR. GLADSTONE ON THE GOVERNMENT OF IRELAND.

Mr. Gladatone was on Monday presented, by working men Liberals of Burslern, with a handsome vase, as an ex- Pression of admiration, affection, and gratitude. Some 2,000 Liberals travelled by special train from Stoke in the early morning, and at noon a dermtation was received by Mr. Gladstone, in the library at. the Castle, when the vase, together with the address, were presented. Mr. GLAIISTONE, in reply, expressed his own thanks and those of Mrs. Gladstone for the 'kind feelings which had prompted the gift. He had always felt that in working men lay the nation's great,security in times of difficulty and political adversity. This had been specially marked during the Bulgarian atrocities agita- tion. Alluding to the particular district from which those present hati 'come, he spoke of the extraordinary progress madein the art of the potter. Thanks to the extraordinary .genius of Mr. Wedgwood. who successfully combined 'beauty of form with orna- mentation, porcelain manufacture has undoubtedly been a high characteristic of the progress of this country. In thanking those before him for the gift, he appealed to them, in a spirit of fair play, not to -unduly hamper the efforts of women and children In attaining excellence in the art. Subsequently Mr. GLADITON7 spoke for upwards of an hour from the terrace to nearly 1,000 persons, and after drawing a comparison between the cases of Ireland and of Poland, somewhat in favear of the latter, he pointed out that Ireland was oppressed by a nation, while Poland was oppressed by only one man; while further than that, Russis. laid Poland under subjection because the Polish were enemies, whose successful hostility would be fatal, whereas Ireland was invaded by England without cause, and for 700 years had been kept in subjection, and now the Irish were being denied equal rights with Englishmen, and subjected to coercion by a Government which obtained power under false pretences. Much would have to be said about the Parnell Commission, whose inquiry, he honed, would be of a judicial character; but it was well to point out that, instead of placing Mr. Parnell on equal terms with The Dines, the National League was to he subjected to an invest4gation ruinous in its Pecuniary effect. If the charges against him were declared proved, his political existence would also he killed, while his opponent, The Times, to whom the cost of the inquiry would be a mere flea bite, would not suffer by disproof, and would be secured against future proceedings. He approved Mr. Parnell's action in initiating proceedings at Edinburgh, where justice would he meted out fairly to both sides. Out of 85 Nationalist members, 21 had been sent to prison, not for ordinary crime—of which there was singularly little in Ireland—hut for conduct which had, done much to keep down crime; and they had been compelled to herd with felons and villians. Dealing with the Ridley and Mandeville inquests, Mr. Gladstone condemned the conduct of the Government in seeking first to evade the inquiry, then to slander the character of the deceased, and finally to accuse Mrs. Mandeville and the doctors of being perjurers. He pointed out that in the Mandeville case the jury, which included five Conservatives and-the sexton of a Protestant Church, were unanimous, yet Mr. Balfour declared their verdict, ought to he treated with contempt. He laid on the shoulders of the Liberal Unionists the blame for a system of government of which these instances were samples. He reminded them that. each voter shared the respon- sibility for the acts of the Government, and lie appealed to them to labour for time happiness and peace of the country, and for the relief of Ireland from the bonds which prevented her people cherishing those warm and unbroken affections which, since the Liberal party had taken up their cause, they had taken every opportunity of manifesting. . .

Durinz the delivcry of Mr. Gladstone's speech, a men in the audience fainted. Mrs. Gladstone, who hod been seated beside her husband, at once went to his as- sistance. sent to the Caste for pillows and restoratives, and did not leave the patient until he recovered.

MR. JOHN MORLEY ON POLITICAL TOPICS. On Saturday afternoon. Mr. John Morley Was present at a demonstration of Lincolnshire Liberals, held at Nocton Park, near Lincoln, the seat of the Marquis of Ripon. The 'weather twin., fine there Nve..s a large at- tendance, some thousands being present, with bands of music. At half-past three o'clock ther4 was an open-air meeting, at.which the Marquis of Ripon Presided, sup• ported by Mr. Morley, Mr. Waddy, Q.C.. M.P., Mr. Haney Stewart, M.P., Mr. W. Crosfield (candidate for Lincoln), Mr. W. .1. Ingram (candidate for Boston), Mr. W. H. S. Aubrey (candidate for Stamford Division), Mr. T. Bennett (candidate for (ainshorough Division), Mr. B. W. Perks (Louth Division),, Mr. J. W. Mellor (candi- date for Grantham). and others. Lord RIPON, in (melting the proceedings, said-that in 1886 they in Lincolnshire suffered not a few defeats, and the chancter of the representation of the County was very different from that which the Liberal,partv would , desire. They knew the false issues which were on that occasion placed before the country, and which led to • results which, he trusted, when the next contest came, I would be entirely reversed.' He trusted that great demonstration would be the starting of a revival of Liberalism in Lincolnskire. Mr. MORLRY, in the course of hiesneech. made allusior, to the Allotments Act, which lie understood had in Lin- • colnshire been practically a failure. By putting the clauses of the Parnell Bill without, debate the Govern- -meat had done one of the most revolutionary things in ! our time, Ile condemned the policy of insult to Irish members. As to the, Local Government, Bill, ho said their opponents would go about all the autumn declaring the bill to boa democratic measure, and that it was the last proof of the trust in the people for which, as they knew, the Tory party had always been so famous and so distinguished. The Government were doing nothinpfor the important.cause of temperance, and it was only owing to the .strenuous resistance of the Liberals that they were prevented from doing what they , intended to do by the compensation clauses, which if passed would have permanently and irretrievably put ' back the cause of temperance in the land. As to the in- fluence of the masses being given effect to by the Local Government Act; he tnaintitined that practically little had been done, anit. nothing would be done until power wasin the hands of bolder men than the present Govern- ment, with a truer faith in popular principles. On the motion cc Mr. Warmv, a resolution was carried expressing "condemnation of the actions of the Present Government in violating its pledges to grant to Ireland the same laws and liberties which are enjoyed in Great Britain."

Later in the evening, a second meeting was held, at which the speakers were Mr. Halle,/ Stewart, M.P., and Mr. T. D. Sullivan; M.P. A resolution was carried de- manding the immediate releos. of Mr. Dillon and other prisoners, and pledging itself "to 'leave no stone un! turned until those officials of the Government who have caused the death of John Mandeville are brought to punishment"

On Sunday afternoon, a shocking accident occurred to a child in Whitford-lane, Mitcham. Edward New, five years old, ran behind a trap and in trying to get on the axle his left leg slipped between the spring and the spokes, completely severing the limb from the body. The child was conveyed to Croydon Hospital. THE CHESS TOURNAMENT AT BRADFORD.—The Inter- national Chess Tournament at Bradford was brought te % close on Saturday evening.. The score stood as fol- lows :-Ist prize, Gunsberg. 13k, £80; 2nd prize, Mac- kenzie, 12, £5O; Mason and Bordeleben. 11, tied for £4O and £3O prizes; Burn, 10!z; £2O: Blackburne and Weiss, 10, tied for the £lO prize.

HORRIBLE DEATH OF A TEAM'S rEß.—A.coroner's quest was held at Alt rinchatn on Tuesday as to the death of a young man who had, been employed as a teamster by a hay dealer at Sale, and who tell from the shafts of his lurry when driving from Northwich early on Sunday evening. Some shocking disclostires were made as to the long hours which men of the deceased's class are required to work, and both Coroner and jury expressed their indignation at the existence of such a state of things. The Coroner remarked that the deceased had in the week preceding his death had only on an average three hours' rest each night, so that he must have been literally worn out when in his sleep he fell from his lurry. The jury requested the Coroner to bring the wetter before the Home Secretary with a view to legis- Wig, and the Coroner said he would do so. ;

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, ATTGUST 25, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, ATTGUST 25, 1888.
NEW TRADE ROUTE :TO SIBERIA.-AN

INTREPID ENGLISHMAN. In a despatch to the Marquis of Salisbury, dated June 30th last, and pul?lished on Monday, Sir Robert Morier, British Ambassadajr at St. Petersburg, gives an interest- ing description of an enterprise initiated by a British .'hipmaster, and carried out with intrepidity skill, and perseverance, with the object of opening up new channels, on a vast scale, for British imports and exports. Joseph Wiggins, a young English mate on hoard a brig connected with the Archangel trade, formed an idea, many years ago, of opening up a new waterway from the Arctic Ocean into the Kara Sea, by way of the Gates of Kara, then supposed to be ice- bound, and to enter by this means the Yenosei River, penetrating to the heart of Siberia and the northern con- fines of China. This idea never left him, and, in 1874, he fitted out a small Arctic-bailt steam yacht. of about 120 tons the Diana with which lie solved the problem brilliantly that year by asinine through the Kara Straits to the mouth, first of the Obi. and afterwards to the estuary of Yenesei. He established, beyond doubt, that the Gulf Stream moved eastwards elong the coast of Lapland, towards Novaia Zemba, and I hat this force, with the volume of the rivers Obi and Yenesei pouring through the straits of Kara, sufficed to drive the ice to the north of the Kara Sea, and thus kept the route through the Gates open during the summer months. Mr. Wiggins did not meet with much encouragement amongst the mercantile classes in England; but he made an attempt the next year, in a sailing cutter, to pass the Straits, and succeeded in making very valuable soundings. In 1876, with encouragement offered by a Russian mine proprietor. Wiggins fitted out a steamer, and ascended the Yenesei for nearly 1,000 miles. The ship was destroyed with the breaking up of tce next spring, but the problem had been solved that there existed a navigable waterway from the heart of Asia and the untold mineral and agri- cultural storehouses of Siberia, 2,000 miles inland, to the markets of Europe. In 1879, Wiggins successfully carried a cargo from Liverpool to the mouth of the Obi. and brought another back; and the following year five steamers were freighted from England for the Obi; but Wiggins condemned them as unfit for work, and refused to take charge of the expedition; and they all came to grief. The theory that the Kara sea was now and again free from ice was not believed in, but Wiggins stuck to his theory, and last year succeeded in finding a few bold spirits, who 'formed themselves into a limited company, called the Plicenix Merchant Adventurers; bought a steamer of 400 tons; freighted her with samples, and Wiggins started from Newcastle-on-Tyne with her for the town of Yeniseisk, 2,000 miles from the mouth of the Yenesei, and within a few hundred versts of the Chinese frontier. Wiggins had to pick his way, as best he could, and was piloted a considerable distance by a blind chief of a Samsyede tribe, whose accurate description from memory of the landmarks enabled the Plicenix to ascend in safety, and on the 9th October, 1887, for the first time, a seagoing steamship, carrying her own cargo from across the ocean, cast anchor, and landed her goods in the heart of Siberia., Sir Robert Monier describes the efforts he personally made on behalf of these stout-hearted and independent north countrymen to obtain for them some encourage- ment helm the " • ~'.lll Government for the enterprise, and says that he met with a very warm response from all officials concerned in getting the whole of the cargo admitted free of duty, and obtained a five years' con- cession for the free entry of certain classes of merchan- dise up the Yenesei, and a similar concession for the Obi. The Russian laws. forbid the navigation of the rivers by any but Russian stelajects, but per- missidn was obtained for the Phcenix to make a voy- age to Yeneseisk and back. If this year's operations succeed—and confidence !in the undertaking is firmly established—ft is hoped that the Siberia mine proprietors (an enterprising body of men), will organise an efficient steam system from Teneseisk to Goichika, at the mouth of the river, and establish warehouses there for storing goods, leaving to the Phoenix adventurers the task of transporting them across the Artie seas. Accompanying Sir. R. Morier's despatch, is a letter from Mr. H. N. Sul- livan, managing director of the Plicenix Co., Limited, bearing testimony to the great zeal, tact, and ability shown on behalf of the enterprise by the British Ambas- sador, and tothe courtesy of the Russian officials con- cerned.
THE COLLISION IN THE 'ATLANTIC.
'INDIFFERENT OFFICERS.

NEW YORK, FRIDAY NlGlM—NOthitiff could save a ship injured as the Geiser was. She rocked like a cradle and within seven minutes sank like a stone. As she settled more and more on the starboard side she careened so that some of the passengers rushing on deck stepped into the sea. Others dashing along blindly, fell into the hole made by the Thingvalla. Perhaps two score were crushed in their berths. The Geiser's second officer, sleeping in his berth, was awakened by the groans of his mangled shipmate, :and saw the Thing-. valla's prow thrtisting itself into the Geiser. Be seized the Thingvalla's anchor chains and when she drew away he clambered to the Thingvalla's decks and saw behind him his cabin close to a bole which two elephants driven abreast could have entered. The list of the saved is incomplete. John R. Dunlop, of Brooklyn, who was a passenger on the Thing,valia, says There was very lax discipline among the officers of that vessel during the voyage. The officers on the watch repeatedly left the bridge without an officer for four or rive minutes at is time. I particularly observed the lack of discipline." He says that when heavy rain or 'fog came the officers on duty did not seem to appreciate the importance of giving signals im- mediately. Consequently in this instance they delayed until too late. -"I, believe (he adds) that the accident could have been avoided had our ship given warning." Lloyd's agent at Halifax telegraphs that the ThAng- value had her tow carried away from the keel to the main deck by 'her collision with tho Geiser, and '2Bft. backward to the'forersost bulkhead. Shettad to jetsam about SO tons df,cargo. The captain reports that he saw the Geiser's lights ahead on the port bow and that the Geiser was struck about midships. The Thingvalla's repairs will take about 60 days. Only a small portion of the cargo is damaged. , Statements of-the cause of the collision of the steamers Geiser and Thingvalla are conflicting. The 105 human beings who went to the bottom of the sea with the ill- fated Geiser are believed to have lost their lives either through lack of judgment or criminal carelessness. Even Captain 3lilller, commander of the Geiser, vir- tually concedes that the collision was not necessarily the result of the prevailing weather. It is intimated that lie has a clear idea who is to blame, but he will not talk further on the subject except to the proper repre- sentatives of the 'Danish Government, who will make an investigation at 'Copenhagen. It was ascertained on ,Sunday that the vessels had sighted each other an hour before the collision, and in the intervals between showers of rain had obtained occasional glimpses later, but at the fatal moment the-rain was pouring down, and an ex- tended view could,not be obtained. There was no fog. The Geiser's officer Who was on the watch at the time of the collision perished. Captain Lamb, of the Thingvalla, does not express any opinion as to the cause of the dis- aster, and says that he will leave that to be found by the official investigation. The lights, he says, on -both steamers were burning all right.

div.head: 1.R131‘11.
div.p: A heavy rainfall took place on Sunday in West Cork, and much damage is reported to have been caused to grain and potato crops. The potatoes are in places affected with blight. On Sunday afternoon, a private soldier, named Thos. Willoughby, a deserter, while being pursuediby a military picquet, jumped from a bringeiinto the Shannon, at Athlone. and was drowned. Michael Walsh, the gamekeeper who was shot on Tuesday week, when the affray took place at Brandon Hill, New Ross, between Colonel Tighe's gamekeepers and some poachers, has died fronrhis injuries. The Orangemen of Tendragee, co. Armagh, have de- cided to offer £lOO reward for such information as will lead to the conviction of the persons who are supposed to have murdered the young man named Greenaway, on the night of the 13th ult., whose body, in a terribly mutilated state, was found next morning on the railway metals near Portadown.

div.head: PARNELL DEFENCE_ FUND.
div.p: THE PARNELL DEFENCE_ FUND.

Dr. Walsh, Roman Catholic Archbishop of Dublin. writing to the Freeman's Journal, enclosing £5O, to defray Mr. Parnell's costs, says: "The snloscription list that has been opened, will stand as an expression of confidence In Mr. Parnell, as a wise political leader of the Irish people, and also of the sympathy with him in the patient dignity with which he has, so long as it was pru- dent, silently submitted to the slanders of his political opponents." The London correspondent of the Irish Times of Satur- day says.:—According to report, The Times' counsel are satisfied that Mr. Parnell's action in the Scotch courts must collapse on a technical point, inquiries having established the fact that on the point Of property, which is essential, in the law of Scotland, there is no basis for procedure. The Edinburgh agents cif The Times have been questioned on the matter, and they have fully borne out the statement that the system on which 7he Times is marketed by them being such that the price of each day's simply of the paper is sent off before the paper is received by the vendor, the defendants are not possessed of property in Scotland RS the law demands. Mr. Parnell's legal advisers take a different view, and it may be remarked that the junior counsel engaged in the case isa Scotch Conservative of -strong political convic- tions. As regards the actions said to be entered against The Times by two of Mr. Parnell's colleagues, the Unionists are of ,opinion that the object is to subject the defendants to a repetition of the heavy costs incurred by the O'Donnell case, and it is circulated that the pro- ceedings taken by Messrs. Redmond and O'Connor will be supplemented by suits in which other Nationalist members will appear as plaintiffs. The London corre- spondent of the Dublin Express says it is said to be the intention of the Gladstonian party to defray the whole of ,Mr. Parnell's costs in defending himself and his friends from the attacks of The Times, and Mr. Brunner, it is alleged, has put down his name for £5OO. Archbishop Croke sends £5O to the National Indemnity Fund, and, in a letter to the Freeman's Journal, says: "It is incumbent on the people of Ireland to make known to all whom Malay concern that our staunch and generous English allies, no less than to our brethren beyond the seas, that ascur leaders cannot be intimidated by coercion, neither can they be damaged in the eyes of their country- men by such shameful and notorious calumnies as certain organs of the London Press have for some time past uttered against them."
END OF THE NAVAL MANCEUVRES.

The cruiser Calypso, of Admiral Fitzroy's Achill fleet, entered Mount's. Bay early on Saturday, and landed between thirty and forty men and a machine gun at Penzance. They captured the coastguard station an the post office, cut the telegraph wires, and took the commanding officer of the coastguard (captain Bolithorprisoner. There was a heavy mist at the time, and thenlace was taken by surprise. The Calypso re- mains off Penzance Pier.

The naval manceuvres concluded on Monday at noon, without the attack on the Thames and London (which Adnairarßaird had been so anxious about) taking place. In an address issued to the defending fleet before the ships dispersed, the gallant officer named referred with pride and satisfaction to the fact that the metropolis had been kept out of the hands of the "enemy ; but the rest oe the document was practically an admission of inability to contend with the opposing squadrons under the conditions laid down. It was found impossible to maintain the blockade, and with the force at his com- mand it was equally impossible for Admiral Baird to at- tempt the chase ot the escaped cruisers or to detach vessels for the defence of particular ports without laying himself open to a combined attack 'by the foe, a pro- ceeding which would have meant for him certain defeat in case his fleet had not been kept together. The diffi- culties of coaling, the strain put upon the officers and crews of a blockading force by constant watching, and the advantages enjoyed by the enemy in the way of communication were strongly and fairly urged by Admiral Baird, from whose account of the manceuvres it Seelll3 pretty clear that throughout the business all the fun has been on the side of the attacking party._

Her Majesty's ships Mercury, Collingwood, Hero, Iris, Severn, Rattlesnake, Active, Northumberland, Inflexible, Benbow, Hotspur, and Invincible, and seven torpedo boatsand the hired collier (NPssmore) arrived off Spit- head on Tuesday, and will discharge their ammunition and resume a peace rig. The Northumberland has de- fects in her boilers, which it will take two or three weeks to repair. The gunboat Hearty, on Tuesday, entered the Mersey in disguise, her funnels being painted black and her hull black, and white porta, to give her the appearance of merchantman. Her object was to recover two anchors which.Ohe left in the river on the 19th, when, by break- ing from her moorings, she caused much danger to shippicg.

div.head: WRECK OF A BRITISH SHIP.-LOSS OF 17 LIVES.
div.p: WRECK OF A BRITISH SHIP.-LOSS OF 17 LIVES.

A letter from Adelaide of July 16th describes a terrible shipping disaster in Australian waters, which occurred on the previous day. The Star of Greece, a magnificent full-rigged ship of 1,227 tons register, hailing from Belfast, got under weigh with a cargo of wheat for the United Kingdom. There were signs of rough weather, hut the captain (H. R. Harr°Well) thought he would he able to clear the gulf and get well nut to see without any danger. At one o'clock next morning all hands were called on deck, land having been observed on the lee bow. The storm was at its height, and the ship had hove to before the danger was perceived, and thus drifted towards the rocks. At two o'clock the ship struck within two hundred yards of the shore. Port Willunga, where she struck, is in a small bay on the pastern coast of St. Vincent's Gulf. A reef of rocks ex- tends to the south for nearly two miles. The men on board endeavoured to fire off rockets and show blue lights, but unsuccessfully. It was not until daylight that the people on shore saw the wreck, and then they were powerless to assist, for there were no appliance. The sailors tried to get lines ashore by floating sea- chests, but they were washed back to the ship by the current., At about seven o'clock in the morn- ing the ship parted abaft the mainmast, and the cap- tain, with three men who were standing on the poop, perished. A fifth man who was with them managed to swim ashore. Then followed most distressing scenes. The people<on the shore were unable to do more than help the brave .swimmers to laud and attend to their wants. Men intim act of making for the shore periseed before their ,eyes. They sent for help to Adelaide, hut unfortunately there were delays which were quite avoid - able. A very strong-feeling has, however, been aroused on this matter, the public demanding of the Government why help was not-sent at once. instead of a steamer being despatched immediately on hearing,:the news at 10 a.m. the tug did not get away until the afternoon. The rocket apparatus at 'Normanville, twenty miles from the wreck, was ordered to the scene, but it took five hours to get there and then it was too late. Just after midday the mate managed to get ashore after swim- ming for-about an bout. His example was followed by several men, some of whom were saved but others gave up. The bodies of R. Muir. G. Irvine, Welnerich, W. R. Waugh (second-ivate), IL I. It Cooke, F. C. Black- man, G. Carter, F. S. 'Carter, and D. Blair had been recovered, but there were still eight bodies missing. The first and third mates and eight seamen were saved, but 17 men, including the captain and second mate were lost. The incident has cast a gloom over the colony, where a subscription list for the bereaved familes has been opened.
THE GREAT ROBBERY OF BONDS. 'DISCOVERY AND RREST. •

The mystery of the Hatton Court bond robbery of last October is at length solved. Part of the stolen bonds— which were of the total value of nearly £ll,ooo—were two or three days ago presented for transfer to the sec- retary of an American railway company, who at once telegraphed to the London solicitors concerned for tha owners, and in reply to inquiries supplied the informa- tion that the American brokers who were acting in the matter were doing so on behalf of one Casey, "care of" an office owner in Winchester House, London. Win- chester House was watched, and on Monday morning Casey was arrested. He at 'once admitted that he was the person who robbed the youth who .had temporary charge of the bonds, and on the information he gave the police visited his lodgings at Bayswater, and found there another portion of the missing property. From a tele- gram received in London on Monday night., it appears that all the stolen bonls have now been recovered. Casey, ti e al'e;ed robber, was brought up ma r. esday at the Guildhall. Detective Taylor said he!found on him a crossed cheque on the Bank of England for £6OO, and a large knife, with curved blade. The accused, whose full name was Frank Morley R. Casey, of 39, Westmor- land-street, Bayswater, was charged with the robbery of bonds and securities, valued nominally at £lO,BOO, from a lad named James Watson, and with possessing an instrument for the purpose ot injuring Watson. Evi- dence was given of the arrest, and the discovery of a knife and documents on the accused, who said, "Seek John Abbot, and tell him he's my murderer. I shall not be alive in the morning to see the magistrate."—The pri- soner was remanded.

SMCIDE OF A Yount. —A youth named Farmer, 15 years old, son of a Poesmouth builder, committed suicide on Tuesday by shooting himself with a revolver. He had prevOusly taken landau am. There is no apparent Canso for the act.

div.head: ISLE OF. LEPERS.
div.p: THE ISLE OF. LEPERS.

Father Conrardy, who recently went out .from America to join Father Damien in his work among the lepers of Hawaii stationed in the island of Molakai, gives a terrible account of his surroundings. He says: ." The portion of Molokai thelepers,occupy is about three miles long and half or three-quarters of a mile wide; a perfect place of seclusion, for if the poor lepers thought of es- caping very few of them could do so, as very high cliffs separate us from the other parts of the island—so high that clouds most of their time cover their tops. As for leprosy, I don't think it can be avoided if it is contagious by contact or by inhalation, for any one who lives among them comes in contact with them in a thousand ways. I believe there is :no more possibility of re- maining uncontaminated than for a man to live in a fire without being burned. IWohave now some 89 boys. , I am most of the time with them, and besides live in the same house with Father Damien, who, as you know, is affected with the disease. The, disease has a peculiar smell, very offensive. In the beginning the sight of poor Father Damien, whose ears, face, neck, and hands are quite bad, was enough to take my appetite away.' and I was troubled with continual headache, but now I feel I am Used to those little inconveniences. Every- thing here is done and handled by lepers; cattle are killed, meat cut and distributed and brought by lepers, bread baked by them; but eggs are clean—yes, only the hens eat rotten flesh thrown to them by lepers. Poor Father Damien sometimes will speak to me in a confi- dential way, approaching very near. Many things that he and other lepers handle have also to be handled by me, but it seems to me that the smell is more injurious than the simple contact. How to live in the midst of them and not become one day a leper myself, I don't see; I leave that to God, happen what may." Since Father Conrardy's arrival about 90 lepers had died in the island.

FATAL RESULT OF RELIGIOUS DIFFERENCES.—A fatal quarrel took place at Clyde Ironworks, near Glasgow, on Monday. A gateman, named Wallace, ordered a man, named Owen Louley, off the road leading to the works, when, Louley attacked the old man with his feet and fists. Wallace waits found over the embankment with his neck broken. The men had religious differences. BURGLARY AT A RAILWAY STaTioN.,—Mold Railway Station was broken into early on Saturday morning by burglars. The booking office was successfully forced, and a considerable quantiity of jewelry carried off, in, eluding gold brooches, ladies' silver necklaces, gold ear- drops, Si.e. It is supposed to have been done by the same gang that successfully cleared out Saltney and Dunham stations, near Chester, and Gmnah's Quay Post Office.

CATHOLIC TEMPERANCE DEMONSTRATION.—The annual demonstration of the Catholic Total Abstinence League of the Cross was held at the Crystal Palace, London, on Monday. About 20,00 people, wearing the green and gold regalia of the order, marched past the Cardinal and a large body of London priests. At a large meeting held in the Palace Cardinal Manning condemned the drink traffic. Several sneakers from America, also spoke.
•NATIONAL CO-OPERATIVE FESTIVAL AT THE CRYSTAL PALACE.

It was estimated that there were over 50,000 persons Present at the Crystal Palace, London. on Saturday, on the occasion of the first National Co-operative Festival, which event obtained the official sanction and recogni- tion of the United Central Board of the Co-operative Movement and of the London Trades Council, and was welcomed and assisted by the Working Men's Club and Institute Union and various temperance organisations. The attractions of the festival, which brought together large numbers of excursionsts from some of the chief provincial towns, comprised co-operative productive home industries, and wholesale societies' exhibitions, and a co-operative flower, fruit, vegetable, and honey show, said to be one of the most comprehensive collec- tions—the produce of cottagers and artisans—ever held. The festival was formally opened in the morn- ing at a meeting at which Mr. Edward Vansittart Neale presided, and Mr. G. T. Holyoake and Mr. Maxwell (chairman of the Scottish Wholesale Society) spoke.— Mr. G. T. HoLYOAKE said this was the opening of the first national festival of labour in England, and visitors would see evidences worth looking at of handicraft, in- ventiveness, flowers and fruits, sports and song. The merits of the conception and organisation of this festival were due to Mr. E. Owen Greening, and to the zeal of the various committees in town and country. The festival was on behalf of a new condition of labour. The reason for it was that hitherto labour had had little about which to rejoice. Co-operators were Da enemies to capital, and all they asked for was that a moderate share of it should go into the hands of those who earned it. Were all persons who laboured to share in the profits they earned. onpitalists would be as rich as they ought to be, and every working man's family would be as rich. as they wished to be, and the poor would cease in the land. Whoever bought anything in store or market without first inquiring whether the workpeople who made the article had a living share of the profit of It, did nothing to improve the fortunes of labour, and silently connived at its precariousness and despair. If they had sympathy with industry it meant nothing Their sympathy was as barren as Indifference. Co- operators did not expect the principles they maintained to be accepted all at once. The millennium of capital came long ago—the millennium of labour was hardly yet in sight, and would come in unforeseen ways. Employers might, when they would, bind workmen to them by honourable concession, as some great employers had done. (Hear, hear.) Anyhow, the light of profit sharing was at last dawning on English workshops. That waS the meaning of their festival of labour. (Cheers.)— Mr. E. 0. GREENING (the chairman), alter alluding with satisfaction to the enormous gathering as a proof of the success of the first great national co-operative holiday, spoke of the progress of the co-operative movement. There were, he stated, 1,281 societies firmly established, having 'BBB,Bll members—men and women—who [with their families would represent a population of 4,000,000 or 5,000,000. The business transacted last year amounted to £31,283,222—a huge sum of money, and the profits arising from that busi- ness had reached £2,981.601. The share capital amounted to £9,247,435, and the average profits upon .the capital invested in the 1,281 businesses was over 30 per cent per annum. (Hear, hear.) The movement was at present only a shopkeeping movement, and they had really only touched the fringe of the question, which was a great social question; but it was the first step towards the emancipation of the workers in their work- shops. (Hear, hear.) In production they had as yet only invested less than £1,000,000, and that sum in- cluded all the workshops in the movement, whether they shared profits with the workers or not.— Mr. &purr TAYLOR proposed the first reso- lution as follows :—" That this great national gathering of members of co-operative societies, trades societies, working men's clubs, and other labour organi- sations recognises industrial co-operation carried out in the spirit of its founders as an effective means of raising the whole mass of our workers above the evils of poverty, debt., and overwork, as an effectual method of finally abolishing sweating, and bringing into the homes of our people the 'chance of enjoying reasonable leisure and something of the pleasures of art and culture."—Mr. ARNOLD FOSTER, M.P., secondimt the resolution, said that as the great co-operative movement extended there was a tendency to work simply as great capitalists, but if they abandoned the important principle of co-opera- tion, and simply went into the market as capitalists. they would be losing by far the greatest advantage which their co-operation would ever give them. (Hear, hear.) It would be necessary to guard against that. There was a danger of merely setting up great stores in which they were only imitating the example of the capitalists, and were not con- cerning themselves as to the lives of the Workers. (Hear, hear.) The people of England had the credit of being practical, and the strongest side of the co-operative movement was its practical side: but still they wanted to keep up the ideal side. (Hear, hear.) There was not quite enough done to make the productive movement popular and well known.—Mr. FIODOSON PRATT, who supported the motion, spoke of the day as being a most important one both in the history of the country and of the co-operative movement. It was a truly national festival, because the work represented at the Palace meant a change in the life of the nation, viz., that the social organisations of the people should be for the benefit of the whole and not of a part only. That which they wanted in human society was equity largely distributed. The world was made for all, and not for the few. The ca-onerative movement pointed out the way of a social evolution which if effected would 'prevent a terrible social revolution. The present conditions of society were not 90 equitable as they should be. In future the working men would not he the slaves of capital. but‘its hirers and masters, and then there would no longer be the strifes between employer and employed and capital and labour which now prevailed. They were that day cele- brating the birthday of co-operation. One and all should combine to bring about that peaceful transfor- mation of society, for if it was not carried out they would see terrible disasters and sufferings in this and in other nations.—The resolution was • carried. —Mr. HENRY HOLLEY (president of the Labour Asso- ciation) proposed. "That we welcome the organi- sation of a National Co-operative Festival as an effective means of bringing before new circles of our people the knowledge and conviction of the power of co-operation in the workshop, the store, and the home."—Mr. GRORGE TnoispsoN (of Hudders- field) seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. WILBERFORCH ,(of Leeds), and carried.—Mr. CRIMER,. M.P.. speaking to a resolution agreed to by the meeting, thanking the chairman and welcoming the co-operators present from France, said he hoped that their French friends would carry back with them some of the prac- tical lessons which they would doubtless learn at the festival, and during their visit to this country. Such lessons were needed. he knew, from many years' expert- &lce of the French workpeople.—The outdoor demon- stration was followed by organ performances and a grand fairy ballet. The whole of the palace and gardens were beautifully illuminated after dusk by electric light and many thousands of coloured lamps. An attraction in ,the grounds earlier in the day was the ascent of Captain Dale's balloon soon after five o'clock.

SHOCKING MURDER AND SUICIDE. A shocking tragedy has occurred at Nice. About two years ago Dr. Courseron was obliged, on account of ill- : health, to give up a good practice in Paris and remove with his wife and-two children to the milder climate of Nice. Unluckily he did not prosper as ho had done in Paris, and in the hope of supplementing a reduced pro- fessional income he had recourse to the gaming-table. Fortune refused to-smile on him, but he persisted. He ! sustained heavy losses, ran into debt, and finally , found himself on the brink of ruin. Ms last hopo ' was his wifes property, which that lady, very naturally and prudently, refused to hand over to him. Latterly -" scenes" were frequent between the couple, the 'lady obstinately declining to see hei husband make ducks and drakes of her money, as he had done with his own. At last, about ten days ago, there was a violent quarrel. Dr. Courseron threatened his wife with his revolver, and in terror and despair she left the house with their younger child, betaking herself to a hotel. Being unmolested she was under the im- pression that her husband had gone to Paris with the other child, a boy of eight; but on Friday, becoming alarmed, she went to the house in company with several police officials and found her husband and child lying on the bed quite dead, suffocated with the fumes of char- coal. It was ascertained that the little boy had first been lulled to sleep with injections of morphine, and that the father had then kindled the fatal fire and laid him- self by the child's side te await his doom. The dramatic suicide has created quite a "sensation," not only at Nice,-but in Paris, where the doctor had many friends.

A prize fight took place, on Monday, at Bedwilti, Monmouth, between Crowther, of Nevi/bridge, and Cooke, Of "Wordllery. After eleven rounds had been fought, Crowther was returned the victor. The police. saubse- quently appeared, and arrested Cooke. The others escaped.

! TrIAGIC SUICIDE OF LOVERS.—VERDICT OF FELO-DE-SE. —An extraonlinary double suicide was investigated by a Coroner's jury at Fisherton, De-la-Mere. Wiltshire, on ! Saturday evening, the deceased being Albert Sparey, of ! Warminster, and Elizabeth Ann Yeates; of Wylye. The bodies were found in a mill stream, clasped in each other's arms and tightly bound together. On the bank were letters addressed to their parents, stating that they had lived and loved together, and that they both wished to die together. The girl, in one letter, stated that they had drowned themselves through her sister and his brother. Nothine, transpired to throw any light on the .affair, and the jury returned a verdict of felo-de-se. REPRIEVE OF A MURDERER- —• The , governor of Kirkdale gaol has received a communication from the Home Secretary reprieving the condemned seaman, named Charles Arthur, pending the further pleasure of her Majesty. Arthur murdered Cap- tain Bailey, of the Dovenby Hall, while the latter was asleep in his bunk; but it was shown that there had been great provocation and cruelty on the part of the captain, and the jury recommended the prisoner to mercy, although the murder was of the most deliberate and horrible character. The prisoner, a coloured man, ! had been an assiduous attendant at the religious services lO ibe golLara!
GENERAL NEWS.
The King of the Belgians and suite started on Mon- :lay, in the steam yacht Cornelia, from Oban, tor a short cruise among the western islands of Scotland, including lona.
Jake Kilram, the American prize fighter, left Liter- pool, on' Saturday, for America. There was a large gathering of his "admirers" on the landing stage, to cheer him as he departed.

The 4,000 volunteers who have been manoeuvring with the regulars near Aldershot returned to London on ,';'aturday. Sir Richard Alison declares their work to have been highly creditable. NEW RAILWAY PROJECT IN THE ISLE OF MAN.—The registration of a company, under the title of the Douglas, Laxey, and Snaefell Railway Company, was announced in Douglas, on Monday. The object is to construct a rail- way from Douglas to Snaefell, rid Laxey, with stations at Onchan and other places. The capital is £70,000 in £lO shares.

On Saturday, at 10,30 am.. a man, named John Bela, a labourer, of no fixed abode, was drowned in the canal at Ince, near Wigan. He was helping a boatman, and while walking across the lock gate he slipped and fell into the water. No attempt, it seems, was made to save him. The police recovered the body shortly afterwards.‘ It is alleged that the deceased was drunk.

Mary -Connell was committed for, three months' im- prisonment, by the Manchester magistrates, on Monday, for a grievous assault on an old woman, named Catherine Tynan. The prisoner, having quarrelled with Tynan, beat her and, pushing her against a wall, held her head whilst she deliberately got her left ear in her mouth, and hit nearly the whole of it off. The severed portion of the ear was picked up by a policeman.

At Nottingham Police Court, on Saturday, Geo. Taylor. manager of a working men's club at Bulwell, was fined £2O for selling beer and tobacco without a license. The case against the defendant was that the club was a " bogus" one, established for the purpose of defeating the Licensing Act. A policeman in disguise visited the place, and, although a stranger, was served with beer and cigars, as if a member. BROACHING A OARGO.—At Port Glasgow, on Monday, Peter Dunn and David Thoburn, chief and second engineers respectively of the steamer Henry, which ar- rived from Bilbao with iron ore, were committed for trial on the charge of stealing 100 gallons of claret while the steamer was on the voyage from Algiers to Antwerp, between tho 18th and 28th July. On the discharge of the cargo the stevedore found minty casks and casks which had been tapped, and suspicion fell on the accused.

An important movement has been instituted among Cheshire dairy farmers by Mr. Gilbert Murray, agent of Lord Harrington. Believing that a factory conducted on co-operative principles, and turning out cheese and butter of uniform quality, would secure higher prices than by individual enterprise, Mr. Murray is establish- ing one to which farmers on the estate can consign milk. Fixed payment will be made for the milk, and the pro- fits are to be divided after meeting all outgoings.

THE WHITWORTH REQUESTS.—At a meeting of the Openshaw Local Board, on Monday evening, an offer was considered from the legatees of the late Sir Joseph Whitworth, to erect in Openshaw, fully equipped public baths for the benefit of the inhabitants of the dis- trict. An intimation was also given that the legatees were prepared to make a substantial contribution to the cost of carrying out a scheme, which the Board have al- ready had under consideration, for providing the town- ship with recreation grounds. The offer was unani- mously accepted. SWEATING IN THE CHAINUARING COUNTRY. —At a representative meeting of the chainmakers at Cradley Heath, on Monday, it was decided to request the Royal commission on Sweating to hold an inquiry in the dis- trict, with a view of legislation following to improve the condition of the chainmakers. It was stated that the operatives were in a deplorable state, that hundreds of them were undergoing great privations, and were without funds. Many of them declared they would die of starve- Han rather than resume work at reduced wages. It was decided to continue the strike. DARING ROBBERY AT NOTTINGHAM. —At Notting- ham, on 'Monday, two rough-looking men, named Wm. Waddington and John Brown, were committed for trial at the assizes charged with robbery with violence in an unfrequented street near the centre of the town. Four men, including the prisoners, were on tramp, and ap- pealed to William O'Connor, who treated them to half a gallon of ale and gave them ed. They afterwards fol- lowed him to a street where there were no houses, and while Waddington gagged him another held his arms, and Brown rifled his packets and then threw him vio- len.tly to the ground. An exciting scene occurred, on Saturday, on the Liverpool landing stage, when an ironworker from Lin- coin, named Collins, who had eloped with the wife of a fellow workman, was stopped by his Own wife, who carried a baby IV her arms. The wife had travelled from Lincoln, and she attempted to prevent her husband going on board the Nevada. He, however, made his escape with his paramour, the Liverpopl police being unable to prevent his departure. The wife returned to Lincoln, to apply for a warrant for desertion; and it is expected that the runaway husband will be arrested at Queenstown. Snocxrato STABBING Casa.—On Monday. Coroner Gra- ham held an inquest at South Shields on the body of William Smith Wilkinson. aged 17. who met his death by oeing stabbed with a butcher's knife by another youth named William Pickering. The prisoner and deceased quarrelled in a butcher's shop, when the latter struck the former twice. Pickering, becoming exasperated, seized a large knife and plunged it into Wilkinson's aide. He fell to the ground, bleeding. and his bowels protrud- ing. He was conveyed home and attended by three doc- tors, but he died a few hours afterwards from internal hemhorrage. The Jury, after an hour's deliberation, returned a verdict of manslaughter, and Pickering was committed for trial on the coroner's warrant. MYSTERIOUS DEATH Of' A PENSIONER.—The circum- P stances of the untimely end of a pensioner named Bran- , eigan, who was found dead in bed at his home in Glas- gow, on Saturday, having evidently been killed by blows 1 on the head with a coal hammer, are of a mysterious character. The man's wife, who is much younger than the deceased, made a statement when she was arrested .to the effect that ,the injuries were inflicted early on Friday morning by their son, a lad of 13, in revenge for a thrashing inflicted upon him by his father. She ad- mitted being aware on Friday morning of violence having been perpetrated, but gave no explanation why she afterwards washed and pledged some bedclothes which were found in pawn bearing traces of blood marks. The lad is also in custody. THE MYSTERIOUS POISONEcH CASE AT WALTHAMSTOW. —Wm. Barber was again brought up at Stratford Porte Court, on Saturday, on suspicion of having caused the death of Annie French at Walthamstow by administering a noxious drug.—Dr. Tidy, one of the official analysts, said the contents of the stomach showed no tntco of chloroform, but he found a small quantity of morphia in the bladder, which must have passed through the system. He had no doubt that death was caused by morphia poisoning.—Mr. Hamilton, prisoner's employer. deposed to missing Ithe prisoner and discovering a bottle containing a solution of hydrochloride of morphia in the shop, containing about nine grains of morphia.—The policeman who arrested the prisoner at Hounslow re- peated the statement made by him when arrested, and alread read a statement found on the prisoner, in which he said that Mrs. French swallowed a solution of morphia in his absence.—The prisoner, who said "I aec not guilty," was committed for trial. FOUR THOUSAND POUNDS SPENT IN GAMBLING.— A respectable-looking young man, named John Parker, who refused his address. was charged at the Mansion House, London, on Monday. with stealing, at 147, Cannon- street, a letter containing a cheque. for £4,000, the pro- perty of Mr. Edwards, of Birmingham. The prisoner is the son of a Mrs. Parker, who was housekeeper and care- taker at the offices of the Trust and Agency Company of Australasia at the address named. He had also about two years ggo been employed as a temporary clerk in the office, and he had opportunities of seeing the letters by the early post. On the day mentioned fur. Edwards sent a letter with the cheque enclosed, which letter and cheque had never been received by the Trust and Agency Company. It had recently come to the know- ledge of the company that the prisoner had paid the cheque into the Camberwell branch of the South- Western Banking Company, and from time to time he had drawn out all the proceeds except £3OO, all the rest being spent in betting.—Mr. Mullens, on behalf of the the Bankers' Association, said he expected to be able to prove the case of forgery, as well as of larceny and uttering, but as the prisoner had only been arrested that morning, Alderman Sir A. Lusk granted a remand.

CIRCULATING LIBRARIES AND THE SPREAD OF DISEASIL —On the question of books in circulating libraries, and the chances of their spreading infection, a great deal of discussion has taken place recently in continental towns. The Lancet states :—Tbe Dresden municipal authorities have had a thorough experimental investigation of this question conducted. A number of much-used volumes from the town library were taken for the purpose. The dust from the leaves and covers was sown in nutrient media and cultures reared. the result being that no mi- crobes belonging to infectious diseases were found—the dust being, in fact, nothing but ordinary dust of a harm- less character. Again, the dirti:st leaves in the books were rubbed first with the dry finger and then with the wet fin- ger. In the first case scarcely any microbes were found on the finger; in the second case plenty were found, but all appeared to be of a non-infectious character. Especially is it noted that there were no tubercle bacilli. Lastly, books were soaked for two days in spirit containing 10 per cent, of carbolic acid. This treatment destroyed all the bacilli, and proved harmless to the volumes. The conclusion arrived at was that the danger of circulating libraries spreading infection is very slight; but a re- commendation is given to dust books well before reading them, and never to wet the finger in the mouth for the purpose of turning over the leaves." We may add that the sanitary authorities of Preston have had in use for some time a large metallic safe, containing barred shelves, on which suspected books are placed on their front edges with the leaves well opened, and subjected to the fumes of sulphur and other reliable disinfectants. The whole of the books that have been in circulation during the past six months have passed through this process. The reading-room has undergone a prolonged and thorough cleansing and fumigation.

Mn. GLA DSTONE furnished further evidence, on ]Sionday, of his extraordinary versatility and vitality by delivering, at Hawarden, two important aPeeches of a widely different character. The first had relation to his knowledge of and interest in art as applied to pottery, and the second was an in- dictment of the Irish policy of the present Govern- Ment. The occasion was the presentation of an address, and of a porcelain vase, by the Liberals of /lurslem, who went in crowds from the Potteries to do honour to their chief. It must have been a rare treat to the representative men who pre- aented the vase to hear Mr. GLADSTONE discourse so learnedly and with such ample knowledge on the growth and development of artistic pottery; and it need hardly be said that the larger body of Liberals, who were after- wards addressed in the open air on the Irish question, had even greater occasion for satis- faction in listening to the eloquent denunciation of the authors of the injustice which is being done to the sister isle. The artist, with happy inspira- tion, had pourtrayed upon the vase "the figures of Ireland with bowed head, and Poland with znournful look and hair unbound." The great orator made use of this suggestive allusion with telling effect. He showed that the parallel, reflect- ing as it did upon Russia as a despotic country, toflected still more upon the United Kingdom, Which was a free country, governed by free insti- tutions. Further, Russia had the excuse that she 'fought Poland upon equal terms; but it could be said that there had ever been any danger of invading this country. Summarising the as to Ireland in a sentence or two, Mr. GLADSTON E said cannot undertake, gentlemen, to lay before you in rull to-day all that is to be said upon the great subject between England and Ireland, nor even all that may and ought to be said in relation to the Proceedings of the present majority in Parliament --a majority which, I must say, sits there upon 'false pretences—(cheers) —a majority which became a majority by promising the people of this country that, though they objected to Home Rule, they Would give Ireland equal rights, and they would tot subject Ireland to coercion, instead of which they have subjected Ireland to coercion without any outburst of crime to justify it, and they have de- ed to Ireland equal rights by making actions to be crimes in Ireland which are no crimes in Eng- land ("Shame on them") ; and they have under the Pretence of legislating against crime, legislated against lawful combinations of the people, and affainst those combinations which, though they "ought never to be resorted to except under strong 4lnd real necessity, yet constitute the only weapon 'of power and effect by which the Irish people are . able to set up a defence for their own dearest inter- eats. (Cheers.) -We should like to know what the accused—Liberal Irnionists as well as Tories—have to say of this Indictment of their conduct. Can they deny that its truth has been again and again proved up to 'the hilt ? To take the Tory representatives in the immediate neighbourhood, can Sir GILBERT 'GREENALL, Mr. SETON-KARR, Mr. T. W. LEGIT, or Mr. EDWARDS MOSS give a single quotation from their speeches, at the last election, to show that they meant, if the Tories obtained a majority, to resort to coercion in Ireland? Sir GILBERT GREENALL garnished his formal address with a 'reference to autonomy, implying that if Home Rule *to Ireland was not granted out-and-out, something in the nature of self-government would certainly be conceded. The suggestion that there was no kiddie course between Coercion and Conciliation Was laughed to scorn. Ireland should be treated as England was treated; if local self-government 14'ae given to the one, it should be granted to the Other; there should be equal laws between .Eng- land and Ireland; and than that what could be fairer? It was language of this kind which led °lazy who had their doubts as to the wisdom of Rome Rule to either give a Conservative vote, or to abstain from voting. The question of a parlia-

Itient for Ireland, they argued, required further con- 4lideration, and so long as Ireland was treated as • tngland was being treated, what harm, it was .aaked, Would be done? Men who reasoned in this 'may have been wof idly deceived; self-government is being granted to England, but Ireland is deliber- ately excluded from its benefits; while such a , 'savage Coercion Act is being enforced as makes it a hideous mockery to talk of equal laws. What makes the case all the worse against those who had equality on their 'lips whilst their hearts were fiit h.°lll it, is that they have not had the slightest instification in the conduct of the Irish people for thus turning on them. Coercion was introduced , When there was positively less crime in Ireland than there was when the Tory Government of 1885 41607E4:1 the Crimes Act to lapse because of the Pc'aeeful condition of the country. Mr. GLADSTONE is fully warranted, then, in saying that the present Majority in the House of Commons occupy their IGets upon "false pretences." But they know this without his telling them, and they dread dissolu- tion U.S the King of Terrors. div.p: greatest difficulty was with the rank and file of his followers. They were disposed to rebel against him; but he ruled them through their fears by in- timating that they must either yield in the matter or be prepared to go before the constituencies. They yielded instantly; they were not prepared for that. Nor are they prepared now in face of the terrible array of ugly facts phich, as Mr. GLADSTONE shows, is piling up against then; such for instance, as the imprisonment of over a score of representatives of the Irish people under conditions which are inhuman, and would have been a dis- grace to Naples and King BOMBA; the slow murder of Mr. JoHN MANDEVILLE and the sensational suicide of Dr. RIDLEY. These are the things which cause the Tories and Liberal Unionists to dread a General Election; they know what they have to answer for. But the election will come; they may delay but they cannot avert it, and when it does come there will, we suspect, be short shrift and sharp punishment for those who have broken their pledges and betrayed their constituents.

The expected has happened with regard to the Fisheries Treaty between England and the United States; it has been rejected by the American Sen- ate. It is true that the majority, on Tuesday, against the ratification, was one of three only, but it was a majority, and that disposes of the Treaty. In this country, the treaty-making power is con- fined to the Government; but it is otherwise in the United Statest" There, under a Republican form of government, it is left to the Senate to de- cide upon the acceptance, amendment or rejection of important engagements between the United States and 'other countries. There are 72 senators and, for confirmation, of a treaty it is required that there shall be a two-thirds majority. The number who took part in the voting, on Tuesday, was 57, and of these 27 Democrats voted in favour of the Treaty, and 30 Republicans against it. It will be observed that the division was in strict party lines) and, further, that the majority of two-thirds was a long way off being secured. It is deeply to be regretted in the interests, alike of this country, of Canada, and of the United States, that the Senate has not seen fit to confirm what was done by the plenipotentiaries of both Powers; but it is some- thing to know that the result, untoward as it may be, is not likely to cause any immediate difficulty, or terminate in war. A temporary arrangement is lat present in operation under which United States ifishermen, may, until the spring of 1890, ;obtain, by the payment of a small fee, the facilities which they desire. Meantime, the Presidential Election will have come and gone, and it is not unlikely that the people of America will be ma better frame of mind for favourably considering another treaty framed on similar lines: It is a matter of course to say that it is an umfortunate and mischievous thing when party politics interfere in this way with the public good. But that is only another way of expressing regret that human nature is not perfect—that men are not angels. We, in this country, may take credit to ourselves for having considered the question entirely on its merits; and yet we are not free from blame for the strong feeling which the Treaty has excited in the United States. To begin with, was it wise on the part of LORD SALISBURY, as the British Premier, to select Mr. CHAMBERLAIN as our representative, when it was known that the Irish voters in America would take a pleasure in marring any work he might try to do, because, as they perceive, he has stood in the way of Home Rule? Again, was it wise on the part of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, knowing this, to aggravate the feeling against him by attacking the principle of Irish Nationalism immediately before his depar- ture to the United States? He had become a dip- lomatist; but his speeches, to say the least of them, were at this period most undiplomatic. It is true, that when he set foot on American soil, his manner changed for the better ; but the mischief was done. He had sown tares, and he could not expect to reap wheat. It seemed in some quar- ters to be thought that because Mr. CHAMBERLAIN had succeeded, along with other representatives, in framing a treaty that ho had succeeded altogether; and when he got back to England a banquet was given him as one who had done great things. That banquet was premature; it does not appear to have been the right thing in view of the fact that the Treaty is now so much waste paper. It was injudicious because it was ill-timed, and calculated to stimulate, while the issue was still pending, the feeling of hostility in America towards the plenipotentiary who was beinglionised in England. We do not pretend to affirm that if, say, Mr. John MORLEY had been sent to America the Treaty would have been ratified—for a two-thirds majority would in any case be difficult to obtain—but we do say that it would have had a better chance of being ratified. It is, to be sure, no use crying over spilled milk, but we may at least look to the causes of the spill so as to avoid them in the fu- ture. There will be another Fisheries Treaty to prepare before long, and if it be taken in hand af- ter the Presidential Election, and if somebody less objectionable than Mr. CIUMBERLAIN be sent to negotiate it, there is reason to hope that it will be successful.

A shark, five feet in length, has been captured in the Dee. It has been placed in the Museum at Chester as a curiosity. But why ? ShNrks may be captured any day on the Stock Exchangt-- and most of them are more than "five feet in length."

I . According to the " Journal of Horticulture," over :20,000 persons recently attended a Flower Show, at Leicester, which was held with the object of obtaining funds for providing music for the peo- ple. Here is a hint for the enterprising in War- rington. Flowers and music—what could be nicer, •3pecially when they pay for each other?

German officers in the Turkish army were about tp strike because they did not receive their pay. But the Sultan has hit on a really "new way of paying old debts." He cannot pay his men, but he has undertaken to promote them. The Sultan is a genius; but it remains to be seen whether the officers will be able to live on compliments.

More evidence of civilisation in Japan—" The Japanese Government have decided to spend ten millions sterling during the next five years on fif- teen ironclads and thirty torpedo boats." They have only to enter upon a big war,, pile up a big national debt, and levy a big income tax, and they will be in the front rank of civilised na- tions.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, two men were sent to goal, and a third was fined 205., for helping themselves to a barrel of Wilderspool ale. There are men who will have it—right or wrong. As the ancient rhyme puts it : Back and side go bare, go bare, 80~..11 foot and hand go cold; But, belly, God send thee good ale enough, Whether it be new or old.

A French soliier has committed suicide because, by way of punishment, a foolish French officer ordered him to run fully equipped, for three hours. Ho dropped down at the end of two hours, and shot himself when denied a brief rest. The officer ought to be punished for his punishment. It is a pity that a man so lacking in common sense —to say nothing of physiology—should have any command over his fellows.

The cause of ,peace and of religious freedom has sustained a great loss by the death of Mr. Henry Richard, M.P. He was one of those of whom it may of a truth be said that "their works do follow them." He lived to a good old age, and has sown seed wkich is already bearing fruit. Disest thlish- ment is not far off; and it is to-day a commonplace with English statesmen to say, with Lord Derby, that "the greatest of British interests is peace."

The labourer or navvy, or whatever he may be, who has been hoaxing Warrington tradesmen by giving orders for coffins was a grim trickster. His object seems to have been to get meat or drink as a welcome messenger in that he came with " an order." He is a stupid sort of knave, or he would not have used the same name at each of the places he patronised. It is to be hoped his industry will be rewarded with a month or so on the tread- mill.

"Truth" says:—" Mr. Mahoney, M.P., has pre- sented Mr. Gladstone with a Kerry cow from his fine herd at Kilmorna. Kerry cattle are small in tize and very hardy, and they are not only most prolific milkers, but they make first-rate beef." Mr. Mahoney, it may be added, will be long remembered in Warrington for his excellent speeches. His last address, in the Public Hall, was one of the finest expositions of the Irish ques- tion ever delivered.

Mr. W. Hopton, of St. Helens, who has written so much and so usefully on the prevention of mining accidents, has not received a pension, after all. He has been given a grant of £lOO, not a pension of £lOO per year. It did seem as if the world was mending when a Pension was being given in a really deserving case. But the Government have not even stumbled on the right thing. 100 per year to the afflicted author would have been hand- some; £lOO for one year only is shabby.

Mr. J. B. Warren, of the St. Helens Cycle Club, is to be congratulated on doing his 700 miles in four days and ten hours, although he did not beat the record as he intended. It is noteworthy that although working so hard, he gained four pounds in weight. It is a popular opimon--and a popular error— that free perspiration greatly reduces weight. Those who have charge of Turkish baths know better ; they find that the rule is for patients to increase in weight after commencing to take three or four baths a week. The poet knew what ho was about who wrote—" A peasant's sweat is worth his lord's estate."

-- Mr. John Pierpoint does not often deliver him- self from the Warrington Borough Bench; but perhaps that is no great loss to the borough. On Monday, however, he remarked in the case of a woman who was summoned for using foul language that—" Bad language is worse than drunkenness." Bad language is undoubtedly bad; but it is not the means, like drunkenness, of filling our work- houses, gaols, and lunatic asylums. And, besides, if Mr. John Pierpoint will take the trouble to ob- serve, or inquire, he will find that bad language and drunkenness are very near relations; they are demons, but the demon drunkenness is the worst of the two.

At the National Co-operative Festival, which was held at the Crystal Palace, on Saturday, there was, naturally, a good deal said about the progress of Co-operation. But Mr. G. 0. Greening ad- mitted that they had not succeeded as producers. He said :—" The movement at present was only a shop-keeping movement, and they had really only touched the fringe of the question, which was a great social question; but it was the first step to- wards the emancipation of the workers in their workshops. (Hear, hear.) In production, they had as yet only invested less than a million, and that sum included all the workshops in the move- ment, whether thoy shared profits with the workers or not."

Londoners have a way of going to the police courts for cheap law. The other day a young woman inquired if her sister would be safe in marrying again, when she had not hoard of her husband for twelve years. Mr. Biron explained that in that case the sister, if she married again, would probably be acquitted if charged with bigamy. The Applicant: Then my sister's marriage may not be legal ?—Mr. Biron : No; and if her first' husband is alive any children by the second would be ille- gitimate.—The Applicant: She has a good offer of marriage now, and I think she will chance it. (Laugh- ter)" Chance it! How happily the phrase defines the situation. Marriage is a lottery where there are more blanks than prizes; but people will run the risk—they "chance it."

Mr. John Morley, speaking at Nocton Park, on Saturday, exposed Mr. Gosehen's most recent non- sense about restoring liberty to Ireland by enforc- ing the law. He said:—" Let them look at the atti- tude of the Irish clergy. Did they take the part of those emancipators and deliverers, or did they stand firm by their own people? They stood firm now, as they had nobly and splendidly stood, by their own people in many a clrear and, bitter year. One little lict he would mention without comment, because comment was needless. It was that the Papal reseript had, as he was informed, not been read from a.single altar in Ireland." That "little fact" is well worth remembering; it c,4nveys a world of meaning.

The Bishop of Liverpool has a way of looking facts in the face, however ugly they are. He has this week made a protest against the conspicuous omissions from the Lambeth Encyclical. He says: "I must, and will maintain that an important document like this, purporting to be the voice of a large number of Anglican Bishops, gathered to- gether on a very solemn occasion, ought to have contained some distinct reference to the unhappy divisions about the Lord's Supper which threaten to break up the Established Church of England, unless speedily healed. These divisions were specially noticed in one of the two former Lambeth

SUBSIDENCE IN THE SALT DISTRICT.—A serious landslip has taken place at Manton, in the salt district. The earth has subsided, forming a chasm five yards wide and fifteen yards deep, and a brook that ran over the surface has disappeared.

POSTAL CARD SRNT ROUND TIER WORLD. A Shepherd's Bush correspondent, despatched on the Bth of June a postal card from London, via the Brin- disi and Suez Canal route, to Hong Kong, with the request that it be then forwarded to the sender, via San Francisco and New York. This was done, and the card was duly received in London last Friday morning, the time taken in its transit round • the world being exactly seventy days, which is about forty days quicker than accomplished ten years ago. When the small cost cif postage for which the card was franked for its long journey—viz., 30., the number of hands through which it had to nass, and the enormous distance, upwards of 25,000 miles over ! hind and sea, are considered, the performance may be justly described as a marvellous one..
