div.p: LRDAY, AUGUST 25, 1888.

RESIGNATION OF THE REV. JOHN LOCEWOOD.—The Rev. John Lockwood, who was presented to the living of St. Mary's, Halton, in 1876, has sent in his, resignation of the benefice, which is the gift of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., Norton Priory, near Runcorn. LOCAL WORKMEN'S HANDICAP, WIDNES.—This handicap WM3 concluded at Millfield recreation grounds, Appleton, on Saturday, when about 400 persons were present. In the semi-final the result was—lst, J. Tansey ; 2nd, R. Parkinson; 3rd, 0. Jones; 4th, H. Scouts. Final :-Ist, J. Tansey ; 2nd, R. Parkinson, 3rd, H. Scouts. The dis- tance of the race was 120 yards, and the prizes were £5, £l. and 10s.

TILE REV. WATSON KING ORMSBY, formerly of Run- corn, and chaplain of St. Mary's Hospital, London, hav- ing sent to Canon Liddon a copy of his recently pub- listied sermon, " Preaching and its results," has received from him the following acknowledgment :—" 3, Amen Court, August 13th, 1888. My dear sir,—l am very much obliged to you for sending me your sermon. It contains a great deal of wholesome truth very well put, and I have read it with much interest.—l am, yours, very obligal, H. P. LIDDON." APP/lAL AGAINST TUE RUNCORN MAGISTRATES.—Before Mr. James Handley and Mr. G. L. Davies, at Runcorn [ Petty Sessions, on Monday, Mr. Joseph Jackson (Messrs. Marsh, Son, and Calvert, Bedford Leigh) gave notice of the intention to appeal to quarter sessions against the decision of the Magistrates in the case of the Police v. Snell. Snell. it will be remembered, is the landlord of the Blue Ball Inn or Golden Lion in Fryer-st.' and at the previous sessions was fined £4 and costs, for allowing his house to be the habitual resort of prostitutes. The house [ belongs to the Bedford Brewery Company: Snell was hound over in £lOO and Messrs Joseph Jackson and Charles Rowe in £BO each to prosecute the appeal at the next quarter sessions. PRESENTATION TO A WIDNES ORGANIST.—An interes- ting gathering took place in the cosrimittee-room of Lacey-st. School on Sat,rday evening. Mr Martin Tay- lor. who at one time took an active part in public affairs in Widnes, and who has officiated as organist at Victoria- road Chapel for 27 years. is about to sever his connection with the town owing to the demands of his business. The trustees of the chapel determined to acknowledge his long and able services, and in the presence of the choir and other members of the congregation. Mr. B. Brown presented Mr Taylor with a handsome and • vAluable timepiece. Mr. Taylor acknowledged the gift in a suit- able speech. The position of organist will in future be filled by his son, Mr. Chas. Nylon

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday, Mr. T. S. Timmis presiding. Present, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. H. Wade Deacon, N. Heyes, R. H. Davies, J. Bradshaw, J. B. Imison, and G. H. Danby (clerk.) The District Education Committee reported that during July (one week) there were 74 applications for the payment of school fees, which were recommended to be paid in 70 cases. For contravention of the Educa- tion Act 63 persons appeared before the committee and , were cautioned.—On the recommendation of the School Management Committee, Miss M. L. Harris was appoin- ted certificated assistant mistress in the senior girls' de- partment of Warrington-road School, at a salary of £55 per annum, rising according to the scale of the Board.— Accounts amoitntin; to £6ll 15s 41 were passed on the proposition of the Finance Committee. '

A Row AT Win:swot Poi/qr.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Emma Jane Evans, a young woman, was summoned for assaulting Elizabeth Tomlins, an elderly woman. The parties it appear live in the huts erected on the Weaver wharf by Mr.. Walker, contractor to the Ship Canal Company. On the evening of the 14th the chimney of the complainant's hut was on fire and a threat was used that Mr. Walker should hear of it. Next day a row occurred at the pump and it was alleged that the defendant followed the complainant into her hut, and struck her on the face with her fist, besides knocking her head against the wooden partition until she was insensible. For the defence evidence was called to prove that the complainant made use of most filthy language to the girl and threw a mop at her. The defendant returned the mop and it was denied that any violence was used. The Bench dismissed the case.

THE BILLPOSTERS' SQUABBLE.— At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before His Honour Judge Thom- son, Mr. Mearns applied for the committal of Mr. N. Ed- wards, of the firm of Abbott and Co., billposters, St. Helens. The proceedings were originally instituted by Mr. Jos. Smith, Raven-st., St. Helens, billposter in the employ of Mr. W. G. Deacle. Mr. J. P. Mearns appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. H. L. Riley defended. Mr. Mearns said that there was an order made for payment sonic time ago. His Honour would probably remember the defendant, who was becoming pretty well known to the court. Two orders were made against him, at the instance of the present plaintiff, for payment of £1 on each, and instalments became due on them last month. He had not paid anything towards them. He should not be using any stronger language than he was war- ranted in using in saying that the defendant had recently absconded, or was keeping out of the way, and he should be able to prove by the plaintiff that he still had an in- terest in the business in St. Helens, for the reason that he sent one of his men his expenses to meet him at Liver- pool last Saturday, and the man was .there paid his wages. He would prove to the court that he had kept out of the way. The plaintiff was then called in confir- mation of Mr. Mearns' statement. Mr. Riley said that he had only received instructions from Mr. Edwards that morning by post, and he suggested that His Honour should act on Judge Ffoulkes' method, and allow an ad- journment. He submitted that even if Mr. Edwards had gone to Liverpool and carried on his business in that secret way, it showed that he was pressed in other ways. No evidence had been given that Mr. Edwards was able to pay. His Honour granted a committal.

DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT WIDNES.—About an hour after midnight on Sunday last P.C. Thompson discovered that the oil and grease works of Messrs. James White and Co. were on fire. He immediately gave, information at the police station, and Inspector Keighley and about 14 con- stables were quickly on the scene, and used every effort to quench the flames. Owing to the inflammable nature of the material in the works the fire soon got a firm hold, and despite the energetic exertions of the constables, the flames spread and shot to a great height in the air. A he was obtained and fixed, but the water did not flow at all adequately to the occasion, and water was carried in buckets from the neighbouring houses, and thrown upon the fire, while a valiant attempt was made to re- move a large number of the barrels. The works were in close proximity to the back of the Temperance Hotel, In Victoria-road, and:the adjoining shops, and the ten- ants became alarmed, as the intense heat took effect upon the woodwork of the houses, and they commenced to pack up their furniture, &c. Happily the flames were prevented from spreading to the property. The door of die yard of the shop of Mr. Thomas, the ironmonger, did become ignited, and a cry Was raised that there a quan- tity of gunpowder' cartridges, and paraffin oil was stored in the back premises. Constables Mait- land and Worsfold. and Mr. E. Martley, and others at once smashed open the doer and found the ; explosives in a safe, enclosed in paper wrapping. The Idangerous compounds were safely conveyed into Mr. Anderson's Railway Hotel. When the fire brigade ar- rived there was no hope of saving the burning building, but they set to work and prevented the flames spread- ing to the adjoining premises. The crowd of persons that were about did not approve of the manner in which the brigade was performing its labours, and some very' uncomplimentary remarks were passed with regard to Mr. I. Carr, the superintendent. The building was entirely gutted, and the damage is very heavy, but an estimate has not been arrived at. Fortunately the building and contents was fully insured in the Guardian Assurance Company. We understand that the confusion consequent on the fire was taken advantage of by some thievishly-disposed individuals to break into a saddler's van belonging to Mr. Kneen, saddler, Bridge-st., War- rington, which was standing on seine land near the Central station. The door of the van was broken, and some footballs and other articles were purloined. The petpetrators of the theft have not yet been dis- covered. ACTION AGAINST A KINGSLEY FARMER.—At Runcorn County Court, on Tuesday, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes and a common jury, Elizabeth Lloyd, domestic servant, sued Thdmas Spruce, farmer, Kings- ley, for .E 33 7s Bd, being the balance due for wages, from the 11th June,, 1884, until May 22nd, 1888, and also wages in lieu of notice.—Mr. E. Brassey, of Chester, was for the plaintiff, and Mr. T. Shepherd Little (instructed by Mr. Burton) was for the defendant. The case for the plaintiff was that after the death of the defendant's wife at the back end of 1883, he had first one girl and then another managing his house, and on the eleventh of June, 1884, he engaged the plaintiff, who is his great niece, at £l2 a year. She had to milk the cows, feed the pigs, churn, mend the defendant's clothes, help to get the potatoes, and do all sorts of outside work. In fact, she had the management of his holm, and the jury would see, said Mr. Brassey, that £l2 a year was not large re- muneration for such duties. The defendant had, how- ever, never paid her any wages, and when she asked for the money lie said he would invest th • money for her.% and he. bought a cow and some pip. The cows bad calves and the pigs young ones, but the defendant sold the lot, and put the money in his pocket. Eventually the plaintiff left through the defendant commencing to drink and to curse and swear a great deal. Evidence bearing out these facts was given by the plaintiff, Ann Cowman, Thomas Lloyd, and Ellen Lloyd. The latter , 'said the defendant had lent her £B, and on that occasion ' he wanted to take liberties with her in the pantry. William Stubbs and Thomas Atherton were also called, but Mr. Brassey remarked that the Runcorn air bad evidently not agreed with them, and he should not examine them.—His Honour said it was evidently something besides Runcorn air.—Thc witnesses, who were under the influence of drink, then left the court. —For the defence Mr. Little characterised the evidence for the plaintiff as a tissue of falsehoods. The plaintiff acted as the housekeeper for the defendant, and lived as his mistress, and there was never any engagement for Ll 2 'a year, or anything whatever. He kept her in food and clothes, and she had the keys of the cash drawer, and managed the business just as his wife might have done. A number of witnesses were called to prove this, and His Honour pointed out to the jury that the plain- tiff admitted that she had the ruling of the defendant's money, and if these four years' wages were due, why , had not she paid herself.—The jury, after a fewminutes deliberation, returned a verdict for the defendant.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

THE WIDNES JUVENILE RECHABITES.—About 30 cliii- dren and 12 adults of the Order of Rechabites spent a pleasant afternoon at Mersey View, Overton, Frodsham, lon Saturday. The weather was beautifully fine, and every arrangement had been made for the enjoyment of the party by Messrs. Edwards, Widders. and J. Gray. WIDNES SOAP WORKS VOCAL Usaoss.—The members of this union together with a number of lady friends, had a picnic to Chester en Saturday. The party departed from Runcorn by the 1-30 p.m. train and spent a pleasant afternoon in viewing the numerous " sights" of the ancient city. At half past five a capital tea was par- taken of at Messrs Nixon's refreshment room, and the Union afterwards rendered "The Lord is King" and "Sovereignty." Mr. William Jackson made an appropri- ate speech. After a further ramble on the rows the party departed for home, Runcorn being reached at 9 o'clock. Messrs. William Jackson and George Hamp- son had charge of the arranzements. EXTENSION OF THE CENTRAL HOTEL.—At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mr. Alfred Parkes, pro- prietor of the Central Hotel, Victoria-road, applied for an extension of his license. He was a wholesale wine and Spirit dealer ; and he wished to use two rooms between the hotel and the railway bridge as store-rooms. He had not sufficient accommodation in his cellar. He handed in a plan of the premises.—Superintendent Johnston said it would be as well to have the rooms under the license as Mr. Parkes was now the tenant.—ln reply to Mr. Lewin, Mr. Parkes said he did not intend the rooms to be used for people to it in and drink.—After a brief consultation the Bench granted the application. -ST. PAUL'S SUNDAY SCHOOL, WIDNES.— About 170 scholars and friends in connection with this school took part in a picnic on Saturday afternoon. The ground at- tached to Hale Hall, the residence of Colonel Ireland Blackburne, had been placed at the disposal of the party, who were conveyed to the charming spot in conveyances supplied by Mr. J. H. Lee. The weather was highly favourable for out-door amusement, and the young people enjoyed themselves to the utmost. During the afternoon tea was provided in an adjoining field. The arrangements were ably carried out under the direction of Mr. It. Hughes, the superintendent, and the Rev. Mr. Ardle was present. The return journey was accom- plished by nine o'clock. A VICTIM TO DRINK AT WIDNES. At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Mary Hall, of 4, High-st., was charged wit's stealing a pair of slippers, value is 6d, the property of Christopher Glynn, of 9, Wellington-st. Mrs Glynn said that from what she heard she went to Mrs Gill's beerhouse and saw the prisoner there. She was wearing the slippers, but she took them off her feet and returned them. She gave information to the police. P.C."Worsfold said the women was in a helpless state of drunkenness when he took her into custody. She had pawned a new pair of boots just before he arrested her. The prisoner said her husband was a boiler maker and worked at Mr. Ankers. On Saturday she had some drink but she would not have any more. Mr. Lewin advised her to sign the pledge, and she promised to do so. The magistrates fined her 10s, and allowed her until Saturday in which to pay the money. RUNCORN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY'S EXCURSION.—The annual excursion in connection with this society took place on Monday, when about 300 persons from Runcorn and Widnes travelled to Rhyl by special train. Messrs. Daniel Worthington, John Betity, and James Whinyates members of the Board of Direct Ors, and Mr. Evans, the manager, accompanied the trip, and made every ar- rangement for the comfort of the excursionists. Unfor- tunately rain fell somewhat heavily in the morning and also in the afternoon, and considerably interfered with the amusements of the party, but nevertheless the best was made of the circumstances, and considerable enjoy- ment was extracted from the surroundings. An incident occurred during the morning that might have had a sad termination. A young man named Williams was bath- ing on the beach when he got beyond his depth, and was being quickly carried out by the receding tide, when Mr. A. Ma,nard Hubener, of Great Eastern fame plunged into the water, and rescued the drowning man. Williams was in an exhausted condition when brought to land. The excursion gafely returned to Runcorn by ten o'clock. LAWN TENNlS.—Widnes v. Prescot : This match was played at Widnes on Saturday, and ended in a victory for Widnes by 9 events to 7, 19 sets to 16, 172 games to 140. Singles : Miss Oakden (W) beat Miss M. Doke (P) 6-4, 4-6, 6-1; Miss Maddiaon (W) beat Miss Barlow (P) 6-0, 6-2; Miss Baker (P) beat Miss Sherratt (W) 6-0, 6--3; Miss Brown (P) beat Miss E. Maddison (W) 6-4, G--2 ; Kershaw (W) beat W. Walker (P) 6-2, 6-2: C. F. Tomlinson (W) beat C. Barlow (P) 8-4, 8-6; G. E. Sayce (W) beat C. Wilkinson (P) 6-0 6-2; J. P. Kershaw (W) beat N. Silcock (P) 6-1, 6-1; ,T. Carr (W) beat F. W. Halsall (P) 6-0, 6-2; P. Twist (P) beat S. G. Webb (W) 6-1, 1-6, 6-4. Doubles: Miss Oakden and Miss E. Maddison (W) beat Miss Brown and Miss E. Doke (P) 6-4, 6-8, 6s--3 ; Miss Baker and Miss M. Doke (P) beat Miss Maddison_ and Miss.Shermtt (W) 6-3, 6-4; W. Walker and C. Barlow (P) beat C. F. Tomlinson and W. Kershaw (W) 8-4, 6-4; G. E. Sayee and J. P. Kershaw (W) beat C. Wilkinson and N. Sil- cock (I') 6-3, 6-3; P. Twist and F. W. Halsall (P) beat J. Carr and S. G. Webb (W) 6-3, 6-5: 5. D. Doke and G. Halsall (P) beat H. White and J. Latham (W) 6-3, 7-6. ADULTERATED LARD AT WIDNES. -- At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Joseph Clare, grocer, Gerrard-st, was summoned for having on the 30th July sold lard which was not of the nature and quality demanded.— P.C. Thompson deposed to purchasing a pound of lard at the defendant's shop. He paid his wife 6d for it.— Superintendent Johnston produced:a certificate from Dr. Campbell Brown, the public analyst, who stated that the lard contained 25 per cent, of fat other than lard— partly of animal and partly of vegetable origin.—The de- fendant put in a letter from Messrs. William Heapy and Sons, provision merchants. ' Temple Court, Liver- pool, who stated that they purchased the lard as pure and sold it as mire in the same good faith. They believed it to be pure and knew nothing to the contrary.—Mr. Gossage said the wholesale people were the responsible persons, and he advised the defen- dant that in future he should get a guarantee.—The de- fendant said he had only been In the business two months and he did not know anything about the matter.—Mr. Gossage said the magistrates were obliged to impose a fine, and defendant was ordered to pay 20s, and costs £1 2s &i, total £2 2,s 6d. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT NORTON.—A la- bourer named John Kitson was summoned before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday, to answer a charge of cruelly ill-treating a horse by beating it with a wooden rail. Mr. Knowles, farmer, Norton, deposed that on the 15th inst he was in his garden when he heard a noise, arid walking in the direction whence it procee- ded, saw the defendant beating a horse with a rail about six feet long and two inches thick. The defendant used all the force he could apply. The horse was attached tia a waggon, which was off the line leading from the quarry, and it was impossible for the horse to have moved it.—He told the defendant that he was liable to a heavy penalty for abusing the horse, and he replied that he only struck the harness and not the horse.—For the defence Mr. John Scott, agent and manager for Messrs. Snelson and Sons, contractors for the water tower at Norton, said the defendant and the horse were in his charge on the work. He was on the top of the tower, 350 yards away, and saw all that took place. The de- fendant did not ill-treat the horse. The horse had kicked the harness eiff and the. rail was merely used to push the harness off its legs.—Arthur Dawson, labourer, said he was in charge of the horse, which was very fresh and had jibbed.—lt was plunging and rearing, and it took him all his time to mind it. He did not see the rail used.—Mr. Percival, farmer, said the horse belonged to him and was rather queer to manage. She jibbed very much. When lie heard that the animal had been ill- treated he examined it but could not find any marks of ill-usage.—The magistrates did not think the evidence sufficiently strong to justify a conviction and the defen- dant was discharged. STUBBS' FURNITURE CREAM.—For giving a brilliant gloss to all kinds of mahogany and French polished furniture with hslf the usual labour, use Stubbs' Furniture Cream. Sold in bottles. Li.. 25., and 3d.—lsaac Stubbs, Lowlands-road. Rim corn.—Adot.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.—Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the School Board, on Thursday. at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, prosecuted a large number of persons for not send- ing ther children regularly to school. The usual fine of 55 was imposed in each ease. TRIP FROM HAvrox.—The twelfth annual parish trip, arranged by the Vicar, took place on Monday, the place selected being Llangollen. Unfortunately the weather was very unfavourable, but the various places of interest were visited, and the party, which:numbered 60 persons. had an opportunity of seeing the latest specimen of gold ore found in Wales. _ I

.„-. NELSON-ST. SUNDAY SCIIOOL, RUNCORN.—About 200 scholars and friends had a treat on Monday last, when they were driven to a field at Aston, kindly lent by Mr. J. Frodshain. Rain descended during the greater part of the afternoon, but the children extracted much enjoy- ment from the sports that had been arranged for them. Prizes given by the tradesmen were offered for competi• tion. Ample refreshments were provided. The scholars were driven both ways in busses and waggonettes pro- vided by Mr. S. Yarwood. RABIES AT ASTON.—A case of rabies is reported from Aston. It appears a strange collie dog was seen running wildly in the hay at Messrs. Percival's farm at Parkside, Aston. It was observed by Mr Percival, who obtained a gun, and seeing that the animal was mad, shot it. Mr. Percival subsequently reported to Sergeant Jones, who is stationed in the district, and the dog was afterwards examined by Mr. Lewis, the county veterinary surgeon, and Mr. Ferguson, veterinary surgeon, of Warrington, and it was conclusively proved that the animal was suf- fering from rabies. ELECTION OF A GUARDIAN FOR FRODSRAM.—In con- sequepce of an order having been issued by the Local Government Board, bearing date 2nd August last, directing that a special election of a Guardian should take place to fill up the vacancy caused by Mr. Thomas Hadfield having ceased to be rated in the Runcorn Union, Mr. H. Linaker, the returning officer, issued a certificate yesterday week stating that Mr. Henry E. Hey‘vood, of Bradley, had been duly elected Guardian of the Poor for the township of Frodsham. A contest has been avoided owing to Mr. Arthur J. Ashworth, the other person nominated, having refused to serve the office of Guardian.

..... WIDNES INTER•WORES FOOTBALL COMPETITION.—The first match in connection with this competition took place on Monday evening, when the Widnes Alkali team met a team from the Tharsis Works Company. The latter team turned up with only ten men, and played that number. As might be anticipated, they met with a severe defeat, the score at theconclusionreading—Alkali, three goals. twotries, and seven minors to Tharsis nil. The weather was very wet.—On Thursday evening a hard fought game was witnessed between Messrs. Pilk- ington and Sons' team and Messrs. Gossage and Sony team. The result was that the first mentioned team won by 1 goal and 5 minors to 1 goal or 13 points to 8 points. Mr. W. Kiddie, Victoria-road, was the referee. RESIGNATION OF MAJOR WAREING, OF WIDNES.— Captain and Honorary-Major J W Wareing, of I Com- pany 2nd Volunteer Battalion Prince of Wales' Volunteers (South Lancashire Regiment), has, we learn, resigned his commission. The War Office Authorities permit him to retain his rank and continue to wear the uniform of the regiment on his retirement. Major Wareing was one of the most popular men in the corps. He, in c junction with Major Cross and Major Brunner, were the principal means of the establishment of the companies in Widnes in 1873, and he was then commissioned as a lieutenant. He retained that position until about nine years ago when, on the retirement of Mr. Deacon, he was promoted to a captaincy, and in 1886 he received his last promotion. MILTON CHURCH CHOIR PICNIC, WIDNES.-0/1 Thurs- day the choir of Milton Congregational Church had their annual picnic, when a party of about twenty, including I a few friends, had a sail up the river Weaver, in the I steam yacht Estnav, whlth was in the charge of Mr. Thomas Gibson. The party left Runcorn Bridge at seven o'clock in the morning, driving in a waggonette to Weston Point, where they went on board the yacht, and steamed up the river to Winnington. On arrival at this place it was time for dinner, and an excellent repast was sp-ead by Mrs. Hirst, of Albert-road, after ' which the party were photographed by Mr. Gibson. I Subsequently the voyage was continued as far as North- with, and the sights of that place having been inspected the party returned to Winnington, had tea, and indulged in games until evening, when they returned in the yacht to Weston Point, then drove to the bridge in a waggonette, and reached Widnes shortly after nine o'clock, after having spent a most enjoyable day. PLezootNa /Dm HUSBAND'S CREDlT.—Before his Hon- our Judge Ffoulkes, at Runcorn County Court on Tues- day, Messrs. Woodroofe and Sons, jewellers, Church-st., Liverpool, sued John Lewis, who lives in a'court off Gilbert-st.. for £2 3s 6d, the balance due on a ring sup- plied to the defendant's wife, and also a chest of drawers.—Mr. Longton, of Warrington appeared for the plaintiffs.—The delivery of the goods was proved, and a traveller for the plaintiffs stated that he had received money on account both from the defendant and his wife. The amount of the ring was added to the sum the defendant owed for a watch.—The defendant denied any knowledge of the sale of the ring, and said when he discovered that the watch was paid for he declined to pay anything for the ring.—The wife was called, and said she purchased the ring without her husband's knowledge.—ln reply to Mr. Longton, she admitted that she had pawned the watch because her husband was out of work, and she wanted to get food for the children.— His Honour said he could not hold that the wife had her husband's authority to get this ring, and judgment was given for the defendant. _ RUNCORN IMPROVEMENT COMMISSIONERS. —Th annual election of membess to sit on this Board is fixed to take place on Thursday. the 6th September. There are six vacancies to, be filled up owing to the resignation of Mr. W. Farrell, and the names of the five retiring members are Messrs. J. Pritchard, J. W. Lightburn, W. Mellor, James Dobson, and E. Itnison. As yet there are no signs of a contest, and it is highly probable that the five gentlemen will be returned unopposed. No gentleman has yet been named for the sixth vacancy. BEECHAM'S PILLS Fon AbtEnrcA.—The proprietors of Beecham's pills having decided to invade America with their medicine, which has become so popular at home, and having made arrangements to com- mence advertising in both the United States and Canada in somewhat the same spirit they have al- ready advertised here, have just forwarded such an American mail from St. Ilelens as deserves a passing word. It consisted of over 7,000 letters, which were delivered to the post master on Tuesday, ' the postage alone being .£74. Next week there will be forwarded from Liverpool by one of the At- lantic liners over 100 large cases of the world- renowned pills. Tan REPORTED PENSION TO Mn. HOPTON. —A general announcement was made last week that Mr. William Hopton. certificated colliery manager, St. Helens, had been awarded a Government pen- sion of .£lO9 per annum, in recognition of his ser- vices in the prevention of accidents in coal mines, but Mr. Hopton has since received a communica- tion from Downing-st., which says :—" lam desired by Mr. W. IL Smith to inform you that the .£lOO awarded to you from the Royal Bounty fund is not a pension, but a grant." This has naturally caused some disappointment to the many friends of Mr. Hopton, as efforts had been made to place his name on the civil pension list, and the receipt of an order for .£lOO led them to suppose that it was the first annual instalment of his pension. THE CYCLIST'S RIDE FROM LANDS END.—Mr. J. B. Warren, a member of the St. Helens Cyclists Club. who last. week attempted to beat the "record' in riding from Lands End to John o' Groats, arrived back in St. Helens last Saturday night, having tailed through unfortunate circumstances to accomplish his purpose. The previous "record "was established by Marriott, whose tithe was six days and fifteen hours. During his journey Warren missed his way three times, once between Penzance and Bodmin, again on the Welsh border, and a third time in the north, by which he !Jst considerable time. Warren and his friend, Fred Fothergill, pressed forward at a rapid rate on what they understood to be the road to Edinburgh, but after a night ride of several hours over a mountainous road found to their surprise that they were nearing,Glasgow. They bore to the right, as directed, and came within sight of Stirling. from which place they made a circuit back to Edin- burgh. The riders had spent the night in hiird work and had done 72 miles of road which they never intended. On reaching Edinburgh it was evi- dent that Warren needed rest, and as the end of the journey could not be reached in the time desired, it was decided to return to St. Helens. Although Warren did not accomplish what he hoped to do, he journeyed newly 700 miles in four days ten hours. Fothergill, who accompanied Warren, rode long distances, but occasionally took train to make arrangements for Warren at various places on the road.
FAREWELL OF THE REV. R. BURDON, OF WIDNES.

The Rev. R. Burdon, who has been superintendent of the Widnes NVesleyan Circuit for the past three years, preached his farewell sermon to a good congregation on , Sunday evening, in Victoril-road Chapel. Mr. Burdon has been translated to a circuit in Yorkshire, and he will be succeeded by the Rev. Mr. Law.;, of Ripon. The revd. gentleman took for his text Hebrews xiii, 8. "Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, and to-day, and for ever." Afterwards the sacrament of the Lord's supper was ad- ministered, and a collection was taken at the door in aid of the poor people of the district. Mr. Burdon de- parts for his new sphere With the good wishes of the Weslevans of the district, to whom he has endeared him- self by his amiable disposition and his earnestness as a preacher. On Wednesday ev:-.ning, a "surprise presentation"

was made to the Rev. R. Burden in Lacer-Bt. school- room. About fifty members of three classes that have been formed in connection with Victoria-road chapel during Mr. Burdon's ministration met in the committee room, and sat down to an excellent repast that-was served by Mrs. Davies, Mrs. Peet, and Mrs. Wood. Sub- sequently a meeting was held, and Mr. Burden occupied the chair, and delivered an address. After other addresses, Mr. G. Davies arose and presented the chair- man with nine volumes of Great Thoughts, which had been subscribed for by the classes. Each volume bears the following inscription:—" Widnes, August 22nd, 1888. Presented to the Rev. Robert Burdon, on the occasion of his leaving the circuit, by the three classes formed at the Victoria-roactSociety during his ministry, as a slight tokeu of the affection and esteem of the mem- bers." Mr. Burdon was much surprised at this unex- pected gift, and acknowledged it in a few sympathetic remarks.

On Thursday evening a number of the Cronton friends met Mr. Burdon at tea at the residence of Mr. Peter Glover, and after the repast Mr. Jack Kilvington, on be- half of the Cronton Wesleyans, presented the departing minister with a handsome silver-mounted walking-stick bearing an appropriate inscription on a silver plate. Mr. Burdon assured the company that it would be a valuable aid to him in his many long jonrneys. Mr. Michael Lancaster, of Albert-road Society, has also presented Mr. Burdon with a walking-stick of his own workmanship. On Thursday evening the members of Mrs Burdon's ' adult female society class at Victoria-road presented their leader with a lady's satchel, a glove box, and a handkerchief box, as a token of the esteem with which they regard her, and their appreciation of her services. Mrs. Forster formally made the presentation, and Mrs Burdon thanked the members sincerely for their kindneEED and beautiful gifts.

div.head: SERIOUS CHARGE OF WOUNDING AT W IDNES. _
div.p: SERIOUS CHARGE OF WOUNDING AT W IDNES. _

Before Mr. H. Wadt;lWaCrTnT'at Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, Barnett Cassidy, a married woman, of Ann-st. East, was brought up under a warrant, charged with unlawfully and maliciously wounding Catherine Bryson, a single woman, who lives at 64, Oxford-st.—The complainant stated that about 10 o'clock on Sunday night, the 19th inst., she was standing at "Kelly's door," in Ann-st. East, when the prisoner came out of her house, "calling her daughter." The prisoner had a broken bottle in her hand, and she struck witness on the head. The prisoner struck at her head again, but she warded off the blow with her right arm, which was very severely cut. , Afterwards the prisoner ran into the house. Witness I lost a great quantity of blood, and she went to Dr. I O'Keeffe's surgery, where the wound on the arm was stitched and dressed by the doctor. She still suffered pain and could not use her right arm. About half-past nine the same night, the prisoner had thrown two pop bottles at her, but they did not strike her; she did not know why the prisoner acted in this way; she had not had any quarrel with her that night.—The prisoner cross-examined witness to show that the latter had seized her by the hair and threateced to take her life. The prisoner alleged that she injured her arm by breaking a window with her hand, but witness denied this.— Elizabeth Ann Hampson, wife of Joseph Hampson, of Ann-st. East. deposed that she saw the prisoner raise her hand to strike Bryson, and then she heard the latter scream. She went to her and found her bleeding from the arm and head. She did not hear any words pass.— Dr. O'Keeffe stated that the wound on the arm was an inch and a half long, and might have been caused by a. knife or a piece of glass. It would be some Cite before the wound was healed.—P.C. Ratcliffe, a member of the St. John's Ambulance Corps, said lie bandaged thewound before the woman went to his surgery, and stopped the bleeding. He apprehended the prisoner on Wednesday, and in answer to the charge she said "All right, thank you." The prisoner was committed to the Quarter Ses- sions for trial.

div.head: DEATH OF AN OLD WIDNES RESIDENT.
div.p: DEATH OF AN OLD WIDNES RESIDENT.

Our readers will regret to learn of the death of Mr. Edward Roberts, of Frederick-st., Widnes. The deceased gentleman, who had attained the age of 69 years, had suffered for a considerable time from cancer in the stomach, and had been treated by eminent physicians in Liverpool and Manchester, but he died on Tuesday afternoon after a lingering illness. Mr. Roberts came to Widnes from Abergele about 40 years ago, to occupy the position of engi- neer at the Widnes Limestone Company, and he continued in that employ until he wa% incapable of fulfilling his duties. He laid down the limestone mill at Widnes, and invented a crushing machine. which was patented by another firm. Mr. Roberts was one of the chief supporters of the Welsh Wes- leyan body in Widnes, and took an active part in the erection of the new chapel, Lacey-st.. the foun- dation stone of which was laid by Mr. T. C. Ed- wards Moss, M.P., about two years ago. His re- mains will be interred at St. Mary's Church, to-day.

div.head: THEFT OF A BARREL OF ALE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: THEFT OF A BARREL OF ALE AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. James Handley, James Casey, Thomas Broderick, Thomas Ridyard, and William Ridyard, were brought up on remand charged with having stolen a barrel and 18 gallons of ale, value 18s, the property of John Finch, farmer, of Astmoor, near Runcorn.--The prosecutor was in the habit of getting beer from Wilderspool Brewery, and it was customary for the carter to deposit the casknear to Mr. Ackerley's farm. On Monday two casks were so left, and a neighbour signed the delivery book. Afterwards, from what William Ackerley told him, he went to one of his fields, and found the prisoners there with the barrel. They had taken the bung out, and were drinking the beer. Casey said if the prosecutor charged them with theft he would throw him into the canal, and Thomas Ridyard threatened to knock his eyes up. The prisoners then departed towards Norton, and the prosecutor and his son followed them. Subsequently the prisoners were given into the custody of P.S. Jones and P.C. Fryer.--Superin- tendent Hollingworth said Thomas Ridyard had just been released from gaol after serving a month for neglecting his son, and Broderick h .1d appeared before the magistrates at Warrington on several occasions.—Casey, whom the Bench said appeared to be the ringleader, was sentenced to a month's hard labour, and Broderick and Thomas Ridyard were each sentenced to 21 days' imprisonment with hard labour. William Ritlyard was fined 20a. in- cluding costs.

div.head: CATHOLIC REPOSITORY AT WIDNES.
div.p: A CATHOLIC REPOSITORY AT WIDNES.

-- The only case of public interest at Widnes County Court, yesterday, was one heard by His Honour Judge Thompson and a jury, in which Hugh Mc- (linity, schoolmaster, of 19, Farady-st., Liverpool, sued Miss Annie Muldoon and Miss Maria Muldoon. of 8, Lugsdale-road, Widnes, for the sum of £6, for good will and fixtures. The Misses Muldoon en- tered a counter claim for £B, for misrepresentation as to the business, and for £1 for fixtures taken away. Mr. Lynskey, of Liverpool, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. T. J. Peters was for the defendents.—Mr. Lynskey stated that the plaintiff's sister had managed a Catholic repository for him in Widnes for six or seven years. In Nov., 1886, tha contents of the shop were seized by the sheriff's officer. with the exception of what are known as tenants' fixtures. The defendants agreed to take over the business and the fixtures for the sum of £lO, and after many promises that the money should be paid the defendants for the first time alleged misrepre- sentation. The year previous to the sale, the busi- ness turnover was .£l5O IGs 11d, and upon such articles as prayer books, scapulas. beads, &c., there was a profit of 40 per cent.; and Miss McGinity in- formed the defendants that the business made from lOs to 15s profit per week.—Evidence was given in support of this statement.—The defence vk al that there was a guarantee that the business did not make less than 15s per week, and that for the first quarter the business, instead of making a mere living for the defendants, was carried on at a loss. he fix- tures included five glass cases, but when they took possession these were missing, and had to be pur- chased from the.broker who had carried them away. They also paid to the plaintiff .£4 to clear off the arrears of rent that were claimed by Mr. Manley, the landlord's agent.—Miss Annie .Muldoon said that through her own exertions the business now made about .£1 a week. - There was more profit on . the religious part of the business than on the news- papers and tobacco; and the profit was at the rate of about 4s in the £.—The jury teturned a verdict for the plaintiff on both the claim and the counter- ' claim.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

A DREADFUL CHARACTER Eliza Smith, an elderly woman, and William Wilkinson, a young man, were charged with having been drunk and guilty of dis- orderly behaviour in Dallam-lane on the previous night. They pleaded guilty. Alderman Burgess remarked that the • character of the woman was something formid- able," three sheets having been alreadyfilled in record- ing her offences. She nearly lived in gaol. Each of the defendants were fined 10s and costs. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alder- man Harrison, and Councillors S. Greening and John Pierpoint. The complainant's husband and the defendant's son had a quarrel, and whilst it was proceeding the defen- dant picked up a stone and struck Mrs. How- ard with it on the head. After hearing the witnesses the Bench imposed a fine of 2s 8d and costs 19s 6d.—The complainant said one witness named Hoffland, who had been employed by Mr. Quinn, pig dealer, Moss Bank, had been discharged because he had " spoken thetruth." —The magistrates requested Superintendent Johnstone to see Mr. Quinn and point out the hardships of this conduct, because the witness was summoned and was compelled to attend and give evidence.—Superintendent Johnstone said he would do so.

Lancashire defeated Surrey on Saturday by nine wic- kets. Notts inflicted another and very severe defeat on the Australians. and Yorkshire and Gloucester" drew,' when another half hour would have given the victory to the northern county. Lancashire beat Derbyshire on Tuesday after a well- contested game by four wickets. There seems to have been a regretable display of feeling .by the crowd. Kent achieved an easy victory over MiddlesPx on the same day.. .

A telegram from Kingston, Ontario, states that the team of Irish cricketers played their first match in Can- ada on Tuesday against an eleven of that district. The home team, winning the toss, went in first, and put , together 141 runs. The Irish team had made 96 for 1 the loss of five wickets when play was adjourned. The match between the Gentlemen of Cheshire and Yorkshire Gentlemen, which should have commenced at York on Wednesday, has been abandoned. Two important cricket matches were concluded on Wednesday. At Cheltenham the Australians were deci- sively beaten by Gloucestershire, this being the county's second defeat of the Colonials within a fortnight ; and at Bradford, Yorkshire—thanks partly to a difficult wic- ket and their own faulty fielding, but principally to the superiority of their opponents—were overwhelmed by Surrey, the latter having an innings and 228 runs in hand.

• THE TROUBLES OF A TRICYCLIN G . TOUR. BY "TOWNSMAN." Tiwreo were three couples of us casting about for a means of spending a holiday, and by way of joke I asked: " What do you say to a tricycling tour?" The idea seemed to commend itself immediately to all, and it was eagerly seized upon anti carried out in right good earnest. The girls, novices though they were to the cycling art, were far more anxious respecting the proposed tour than the men, and significant headshakes and doleful prognostications as to the outcome of the venture greeted them on all sides. Nothing daunted, they made the necessary pre- parations, and we men proceeded to fulfil our part of the programme. The first thing was to secure a trio of tandem tricycles, but trouble greeted us at the very onset, continued to attend its, and did not leave us when we had arrived home after our jour- ney. We scoured Manchesterdn search of machines, but without avail, and we were about to give up the quest in Liverpool in despair, when we cause across a shop, the proprietor of which offered to fur- nish us with the requisite machinery for a mode- rate sum. We agreed to the terms; and arranged to fetch the tricycles the following Saturday. Pro- curing the services of fourcyclists and two novices, we proceeded to the maritime city in the guard's van, the only available place in the train, on the day fixed; and, just as we were reaching our desti- nation, the depressing tidings went round the van —" it rains ! And rain it did ! With tropical rapidity the rain 'descended, clearing the streets with magical effect, and crowding every nook with dripping and disgusted citizens. We waited several hours for the atmosphere to clear, but as there appeared no prospect of its doing so, we determined to start for home. Fresh to the work, we rattled along in a style that astonished the Liverpudlians, but had scarcely got out of sight of the city when we were compelled to seek the friendly shelter of some overhanging trees. Down came the rain with pitiless persistency, wetting all of us through, and we saw clearly enough we were 'doomed to be belated. At the slightest intermis- sion of the downpour, we made the best of our way forward, but were forced again and again to run under the trees for shelter. The steeple of Prescot Church was just in sight, when the rubber of the front steering wheel of the machine which I and my comPanion rode, parted at the joint. We were the second on the road, and the riders of the last machine promised on passing us to go forward and bring us assistance. When they left us not a crea- ture was to be seen, and there we stood in pouring rain in the middle of a country road, gazing first at the disabled machihe, then at each other, and lastly at the rain. Nothing was to be seen or heard of our companions. and as night was fast approaching something had to be done. Get along we must, somehow. Taking the lace out of my shoe, I tied it round the rubber, and we moved forward a few paces, only to end the lace worn through. However, with various contrivances, we managed to reach Prescot, and there found at the Royal Hotel the companions who had promised to procure us assistance preparing to continue their journey with the aid of a good fire and refreshments. We vainly endeavoured to get our tricycle repaired, and after another patch-up we set our faces homewards. But it was useless trying to ride. That rubber would bother us. We therefore de- cided to walk thteremainder of the distance, and push the machine along. What a weary walk it was! The rain still descended, glueing our, clothes, to us on the weather side, anti trickling down us like a stream on the other. After missing trains at Rainhill and Sankey, we reached Warrington, at a late hour, like a couple of half-drowned rats. Late as it was we contrived to get our machine put right for the 100 milea ;tourney to War- , wick to be commenced on Monday Morning. Threb a.m, sharp was the hour fixed for the start, but when I and my partner arrived at the rendezvous, only a gentleman wise proposed to accompany us a short dis- tance was in attendance. It was five o'clock ere the other two conples put in an appearance, and at that hour we started for Knutsford. On entering into Lymns rain again began, and it caused us to lose three hours in sheltering at Hoe Green. At half-past nine the word for the start was again given, and we were going merrily over what would make a splendid racing track, when the previously troublesome wheel refused to revolve any further, and utterly. collapsed. Here was a fix. Five miles from the nearest town with a disabled ma- chine, the questions arose—how to get there, and how to continue eur journey? A hurried consultation resulted in a couple of the male riders being despatched to Allrin- cham to hire a new machine. Unfortunately, not a ma- chine of any description was to be obtained in the town, and as a last resort we took the Vain for Sale. Here all we could get was a bicycle, and as one of the gentlemen could ride we returned with it by train to Knutsford. Now, there was a lady'without a seat, so there was nothing for it but to borrow our friend's, tricycle. This course was at length decided upon, and about two o'clock in the afternoon we once more set out. Several times we pulled up to shelter, and found that the water in the roads was making havoc of our tyres. We stopped at the village smithy in Holmes Chapel for repairs, and the elderly smith proved fully conversant with the work, as it turned out he had a cycling son. A shower coming on, the ladies of the party were invited into the house, and there a surprise awaited them. The parlour was filled with cabinets containing silverware which had been won at athletic sports by the cycling son, whose prowess has earned for him the soubriquet of "the Holmes Chapel flyer." The smith's wife advised us, in- stead of continuing, our journey, to turn aside to Congle- ton, as it was the most likely place in which we should get lodgings for the night. We follawed the advice, and reached the town about half-past seven, wet through and worn out for want of food. Wearied as we were, we were more wearied still by a fruitless search through the wretched streets for lodgings. Neither public nor pri vate houses seemed to have a spare bed, and it was ten o'clock before we got a prospect of shelter for our ladies. A sympathetic creature kindly offered to take them in, but left us gentleman to take our luck.. Bad luck it was; and at last, thoroughly worn out, we returned to the ladies' lodgings. One of the luckless males offered to osleep on the sofa if allowed; another said he would be con- tent with the hearthrug, and the third thought the door- mat would make him a suitable couch. This arrange- ment quite overcame the landlady, and she gave up her bed to us. We needed no rocking that night, but before we fell asleep 3ve had briefly discussed the morrow's pros- pects. "Call this pleasure," said one of the men ; "I tell you what it it raine to-morrow I'm off home." "Well, yon may go," responded another; "I've started and I'm going through to the end, if I walk it." It was with no little misgiving that we opened our eye; next morning. Fortunately there had been a change of moon, and with it came a • change of weather. Mr. Faintheart was still for taking the first train home, but when he heard the ladies declare they were going forward his courage returned, and he consented, though some- what reluctantly, to go on with us. For six miles we had a grand run, and then we got in the wilderness known as the Potteries. So abominable were the roads that for another six miles, mostly we had to walk and push our machines. The afterneon was getting advanced when we began to feel the cravings of hunger. One of the ladies protes- ted she could not go further without food, and then com- menced a pilgrimage, the like of which I hope never to experience again. Public, farm, and private houses were visited in turn, where we stated our position, but the in-' mates, at one and all, "began to make excuse " for not assisting us. Had we been tramps demanding to be sup- plied we could not have received meaner 6treatment. Onepublic-house refused us on the ground that "the girl" had gone for a holiday! 'lt struck' me the, real reason was that the beer that was being consumed by a room- ful of men was more profitable than our custom would have been. Several farm houses were visited, and then I went to another where I was struck with the solitude of the place. A glimpse showed. the courtyard to be grass grown, the barns were crumbling to decay, the barn-doors hung threateningly, in their places, and the roofs of the outbuildings adulated the light of day. How- ever, a tidily dressed maid responded to my knock, and communicated my message to her mistress. The reply, however, was—"Misteess says this is a private house." I pleaded that we were faint. for want of refreshment and should be grateful for anything, but still the reply came "this is a private house!" I expressed myself somewhat freely in coming up the avenue, and I was overheard by a gentleman whom I took to be the occupier of the house. Seeing we were no ordinary ad- • venturers, he was softened to the extent of offering us each a glass of wine, but as we preferred bread we politely declined his offer. On we trudged, calling at every door' and reached another farm house, where we interviewed the mistress. She said they had what we wanted in the garden, but declined to provide for us. I offered to dig the potatoes and pluck the peas, and my fair companion proffered to prepare the meal, if only allowed. The mistress, how- ever, was immovable, and we left in disgust. At last we reached a publichouse where they agreed to provide food. It was an hour in preparation, and when it came the sight of it sickened one of the ladies and the writer. On the potatoes was a peculiar substance which one 91 our feminine companions declared to be black pepper, but which I submitted had come from the ash-hole. The rest and refreshment, however, did the party good, and when we again pulled ul at a farm house for tea we had added nearly 25 miles to the list. Here we got the first decent meal since leaving home, and we so worked upon the feelings of the inmates of the house that they agreed to lodge us for the night. The farmer had an ear for music, and, finding one of the ladies could play, conduc- ted us to the drawing-room, where we sat and sang our- selves away until nearly midnight. The excitement had the effect of keeping the whole house awake until the small hours of the morning, and as we contemplated an early start we got little sleep that night. The following morning broke rather showery, but we made good. progress, and reached Lichfield for dinner.

This meal was the best we had during our tour. I dined with my friends on the previous Sunday, and told them all to make a good meal, as they did not know where they would get the next. They looked at me with in- credulous eyes,but by Wedne.sday at noon they admitted my advice was good. This meal was, as the Yankees would describe it, the only "square meal" we had had since leaving Warrington. With renewed strength, on we went o'er hill and dale until nightfall, when we found ourselves at Stone Bridge, half an hour before closing time. Here again they offered to accommodate the ladies, but referred the gentlemen to another house several miles nearer Birmingham. Thither we trudged, only to find the house closed and the inmates in bed. A knock at the door brought a female's head out of one of the upper windows, with a query as to what we wanted. As soon as we mentioned "bed," the old woman asserted the house was full, and banged down the window in a hurry. Here was another 'ix! Five miles from any- where, and not a place to sleep in! We knocked at a lodge to ask for help, and the inmates kindly did their best for us. There was an old man who lived by himself whom they thought would allow us to shelter in his kit- chen. They commenced a wakening process which in the stillness of the night resenibled the bombarding of a town. At last a terrible growl announced their suc- cess.

"Who's there," roared a voice in tones of thunder. "Smith," was the reply. "What do you want." again thundered the voice. Smith explained that three young gentlemen were be- latPd, and would be glad of shelter from the heavy dew.

"I shall not have them," resounded from the upper room, and down went the window. As a last chance we knocked up the village policeman, and sought his help, but without success. It was past midnight now, and we were without hope. We re- traced our steps to the house where our companions had retired, but the place was as still as death. We felt chilly, and walked about to keep up our circulation. We walked miles in the opposite direction towards Coventry, when we came to a wood, and finding a dry spot, we lay down on the footpath. Mr. Faintheart was restless, and sleep became impossible. We walked aboutiagain until we came to a broad stone wall, where two of us again essayed sleep. Still we were prevented, this time by a straying horse which wandered up and down the road. Slowly the hours passed, and after miles of aim- less walking we were at length admitted to the shelter of the Village Inn. Once inside, my companions lay on the forms and were soon los; in slumber. I myself must have nodded; for when. I opened my eyes I noticed a cloth spread across the table, which cloth was not there when we entered the room. A basin of bread and milk each set us up, and when the ladies descended we were ready to resume our journey. I After about a four miles' spin we dismounted and called at a small farm for a second breakfast. The heat of the sun was now almost intolerable, and we took our food in rural style beneath the cool shade of the trees in the field. The whole party, having had really nothing since noon the previous day, ate with avidity, and the arms of the " cutter-up " nfust have ached severely, so great were the demands made upon her. Hours were spent in this sylvan retreat, where we enjoyed the signs of rural life—the busy haymakers tossing the dried grass in the air, a flock of plovers sailing away in the distance, and a herd of young swine poking their in- quisitive noses beneath our table. All day long we lin- gered amid the lovely sdenery of Warwickshire, and visiting Kenilworth Castle in the afternoon, we reached our destination the same evening without further mis- hap. After seeing the sight; of the neighbourhood, we called for our account and prepared to return. Expecting to be treated as friends, we gave our landlady as little trouble as possible, of which she showed her appreciation by charging us 5s for attendance for two days, and mak- ing other charges which are still enveloped in mystery. Our friends were as exactingas strangers were indifferent, and we were right glad to find ourselves bounding to- wards our native county. Saving that we got lost among the hills of North Stafford, in consequence of the ignor- ance of the inhabitants, we accomplished the return journey in half the time of the outward, and with far less adventure. The only notable incident lay in the fact that I again got 11(1 sleep—an army Of fleas having made a camping ground of me during the night. We were thankful to get through Staffordshire—the meanest county in England. Not a solitary finger-post anywhere indicates the road, not a single milestone could we anywhere discover within its borders; and a like ignorance and stolidity characterise the people. It was next to impossible to buy milk, and almost as diffi- cult to beg water. Grateful were we to reach Cheshire, with its more civilized inhabitants and its better defined roads ; and an hour after the shadows of evening had gathered round us we reached home,—sunburnt, travel- stained, and hungry. Next day we returned our tricycles, but disaster at- tended us in Bold, my companion being thrown to the ground through the breaking of a chain. An hour's de- lay sufficed to put matters right, and we made for Liver- pool, where we arrived safely about 7 p.m. After an experience of bicycles and tricycles, my predilection is strongly in favour of the two-wheeler, and I think it will be a long time before I again entrust myself to a tricycle.

AN EARLESTOWN STUDENT'S WALK FROM LONDON. Mr. Edward Corlett, son of Mr. Benjamin Corlett; tobacconist and builder, Market-st., Earlestown, re- cently accomplished the unusual performance of walking, with the exception of a few miles, from Lon- don to Earlestown. The pedestrian; who is a stu- dent at the British and,Foreign College, Borough- road, London, in company with a fellow student (Mr. Harold Payne, of Manchester), set himself the somewhat singular task as a pleasant variation in the ordinary custom of railway, travelling during the summer vacation. The couple started from the college about six o'clock on the morning of Friday, a week or two ago, walking along the beautiful Thames Valley, passing through Richmond, Kingston, and Windsor, and spending the night, after ac- complishing a distance of about 30 miles, at Eton Wick. Another journey of about similar distance on the 'following day took them through Eton, Maidenhead, Henley, and across the Chiltern Hills to Wallingford, where they stayed till Sunday. On that day they continued along the road through Wantage to Farrington, a distance of 25 miles. A heavy and continuous downpour of rain on the Monday drove the "pods." to seek the services of a railway train as far as Cirencester (19 miles), where they spent a couple of days with some friends in visiting the principal places of interest in the vicinity. On the Wednesday they pro- ceeded along the charming valley of the Severn, passing through Chepstow, where they visited the ruins of the famous Castle, and reached Warncliffe, where they ascended a high hill and were rewarded with a magnificent view of the Bristol Channel and the surrounding counties of Monmouth, Glamorgan, Somerset, and Devonshire. The same day they passed through Tintern and its historical abbey, and reached Monmouth -after a walk'of nearly 35 miles. Thursday saw the two friends on the road to the Cathedral City oi Here- ford, a journey of about 25 miles. They made a di- version from the road to ascend Symonds Yat, a prominent hill, from the summit of which they ob- tained a fine view of the surrounding country. Hereford was safely reached, and Thursday night was spent at that city., Next day they walked through Leominster and on to the ancient town of Ludlow (26 miles) but the walkers were not fa- voured with bright or cheering weather. On Satur- day their journey was again resumed along the road through Craven, passing Stokesay Castle, and Church Stretton, noted for the purity of its waters. No prolonged stoppage was made here, the night being spent at Shrewsbury after a walk of over thirty miles. That day's journey was one of the most tiring of the whole distance, owing to the dirty and sloppy condition of the roads after the recent heavy rain. Sunday was passed at Shrews- bury, and it Was then the intention oLthe pedes- trians to accomplish the remaining 60 miles to reach Earlestown on the two following days. Monday saw them at Whitchurch (about 20 miles), where friends prevailed upon them to stay until Tuesday. Early on the morning of the last-named day they commenced the task of walking the forty miles to their journey's end, and they walked rapidly through Tarporley and Wem, leaving Beeston Castle and Peckfor- , ton on the left. On their arrival at Acton Bridge they were drenched almost to. the skin • in a heavy shower of rain, and as the weather con- tinued very unfavourable Mr. Corlett and his friend prudently decided on completing their journey by train. This they did, and arrived at Earlestown about seven o'clock on Tuesday night. Altogether the young men walked about '250 miles and rode abhut 60 miles, in the twelve days occupied by the journey. They speak highly of the pleasant character of the journey, and Mr. Corlett informed our representative that they felt at the conclusion in far better spirits, health, and strength than when they started on the road.

div.head: TRE ROYAL VISIT- TO SCOTLAND.
div.p: TRE ROYAL VISIT- TO SCOTLAND.

Her Majesty Queen Victoria proceeded to Glas- gow on Wednesday, and discharged the double func- tion of formally opening the new Municipal Build- ings in George-square and making a State visit to the International Exhibition. It is 39 years since the Queen visited the west of Scotland, and if her reception was cordial then it was ten times more so on Wednesday, the scene in Glasgow being the most imposing ever witnessed. The weather was all that could be desired, and for -six hours before her Majesty's arrival in Glasgow the barricades were lined with crowds. The decorations were almost exclusively confined to the streets along which the procession passed, and as the colouring was chiefly crimson and gold, they had a brilliant effect in the bright sunshine.. As the Queen and Princess Beatrice drove through. Blythswood, there was no cheering except from the crowd outside the station. Her Majesty looked somewhat fatigued after her journey, but Princess Beatrice showed no signs of having travelled all night. The Queen wore a little black bonnet with net decorations, which were mixed with black feather flowers. Her hands were covered with black silk gloves, while her cloak was also made of black silk with crape stripes. Princess Beatrice was also attired in mourning, hel bonnet being much higher than Her Majesty's, and trimmed with ribbons and ospreys. Her thin black veil came to her lips. At Blythswood House her Majesty sat down to a dejeuner, and after resting for six hours she and Princess Beatrice, Princess Alice, the Grand Duke of Hesse, and other members of the Royal party entered the state car- riages to convey them to Renfrew station. About four o'clock the shouts of the Renfrew townspeople and the waving of handkerchiefs announced the arrival of the Queen. When the Royal carriage reached the Town Hall, Provost Wright, in the name of the Royal burgh of Renfrew, presented the Queen with an address of wel- come, which her Majesty graciously acknowledged. Miss Wright, a young girl, presented her Majesty with a beautiful bouquet made of orchids and white roses bor- dered with ferns. A reply was tendered to Provost Wright, couched in the following terms :—"lt affords me much pleasure to have this opportunity of visiting a Royal burgh so closely connected with the ancient his- tory of my kingdom in Scotland, and of seeing a district which has done so much in modern times for the pros- perity of my United Kingdom." Precisely at four o'clock the Royal train steamed out of the station, amid every demonstration of loyalty on the part of the thousands who had ay.ambled them - The arrangements for the reception of her Majesty and the Royal party at the Glasgow and South-Western Rail- way terminus were complete and satisfactory. The tram steamed slowly into the station at fourteen minutes past four. Her Majesty was accommodated in a semi- dress landau, and on her left sat Princess Beatrice tis-a- vis being the Grand Duke of Hesse and Princess Alice of Hesse. The other members of the Royal party occupied a vehicle of the same description and the suite were accommodated in, two- plain " sociable " landaus. Headed by an escort of the 15th Hussars the Royal pageant made its departure from the station and pro- ceeded amidst the cheers of the crowds to the new Muni- cipal Buildings. Here she was presented by the Corpo- ration with an address. In reply to the address the Queen said :—" I thank voq most sincerely for your renewed assurance of attachment to my throne and per- son. lam deeply touched by your reference to my pre- vious visit to Glasgow, when I was accompanied by my beloved husband. I gladly inaugurate these noble Municipal Buildings. which are worthy of the an- cient renown and the modern prosperity of your great city." Her Majesty then drove out of the quadrangle and pro- ceeded to the International Exhibition. At five o'clock the Northern Avenue was thoroughly cleared, the Royal Archers keeping guard. On her Majesty driving up to the gorgeously-decorated canopy, at the main entrance to the Exhibition grounds, the artillery on the neigh- bouring hills fired a salute of 21 guns. At each side of the porches were several hundred coolies attired in white. The audience, who rose on her Majesty's entrance, re- mained standing, but •after cries for " seats " were raised, the Lord Provost indicated that they might sit down. Her Majesty sat upon a beautiful throne, and had on her right hand the Princess Beatrice and Princess Alice, while the Grand Duke of Hesse and Prince Henry of Battenberg stood on the left. Sir Archibald Campbell read the address of the Execu- tive Council of the Exhibition to her Majesty. Her Majesty, in reply, said :—" It is with the utmost gratification that I receive the loyal and dutiful address which you have just presented, and I am greatly pleased by the warm manner in which I have been welcomed by the vast community of this great. city. I am deeply sensible of the advantages which the manufacturing and commercial interests of the whole civilised world have received from these exhibitions, which were first origina- ted by my beloved husband in 1851. I rejoice in the ; well-deserved success which has crowned your efforts, and I heartily offer you my best wishes for the continued prosperity of this great undertaking." Amidst cheers Her Majesty left the grand hall and visited the Women's Industries Section. She expressed herself highly gratified with the various departments. ' She also expressed her admiration of the pictures in the Art Galleries, and seemed much interested in the Artisan Court. Her Majesty then left the Exhibition and pro- ceeded to St. Enock's Station, where she entered the train which conveyed her back to Blythswood. Glas- gow was animated up till midnight, there being illu- minations and a grand firework display within the Exhi- bition.

Princess Beatrice and Prince Henry of Battenberg left Blythswood at 11 o'clock on Thursday, in the yacht Vic- toria and Albert, which was decked with bunting. A large company from Glasgow;including the civic autho- rities on board the steamer Dromedary, met the Royal yacht. Both steamers ascended the river and were greeted by crowds MI the bank. The Royal party landed at the Clyde Trust Docks in the presence of thousands, and amid a firing of guns from the Valorous, whose yards were manned. VISIT TO PAISLEY.

The Queen left Blythswood at five o'clock on Thursday afternoon and drove to Paisley, where her Majesty was enthusiastically welcomed. Elaborate arrangements had been made to give her Majesty a loyal reception, and the occasion was all the more auspicious as the towns- people celebrated the attainment by Paisley of its fourth centenary as a burgh. The royal carriage drove up at a platform upon which were gathered the Provost and magistrates of Paisley, and the Provost presented her Majesty with an address enclosed in a golden casket, and to which her Majesty, handed the Provost a written reply. The magistrates having been presented to her Majesty, the Royal party returned to Blvthswood. A Corporation banquet was subsequently held, and in the evening Paisley was illuminated.,

CADBURY'S caution the public against adulterated Cocoas, sold as pure Cocoa, to which about 4 per cent. of Alkali and other agents are added, to give appa- rent strength to the liquor, by making it a dark coiour. This addition may be detected by the scent when a tin is freshly opened. No Cocoa can be stronger than Cadbury's, which is guaranteed absolutely pure.—Advt. _ .

_ , A BOGUS CoNrEssioN.—A man named Thomas Wright, of Holloway, gave himself 'into custody a few days ago and " confessed " that he had murdered a woman in Hoxton in 1872. On Wednesday, at the Worship-street Police Court, the prisoner was brought up and dis- charged, there being no reason to suppose that his "con- fession" was true.

div.p: SERIOUS FIRE AT ST. HELENS: £3,000 DAMAGES. •An alarming fire was discovered on the premises of Mr. John Ball, pawnbroker. College-lane, early on Sundv morning, and before the flames were ex- tinguished the building was entirely gutted and its contents destroyed, and a considerable amount of damage was also done to the surrounding property. About half-past one o'clock Police-constable Hene- bury was on duty in College-lane. when he saw smoke issuing from Mr. Ball $ premises. The officer, with the assistance of a young man who was passing, got to one of the windows of an upper room, and gained admittance. The building was full of smoke, and as the crackling of burning wood could be heard downstairs, Henebury whistled for assistance, and Constables Gee ; and Pooley quickly appeared. In the zneantime a mes- senger had gone to the Town Hall, and given informa- tion of the outbreak. Inspector Steele, Sergeant Goodall, and a body of police at once started for the scene of the fire, and sixteen or eighteen members of the fire brigade, under Superintendent Birchall, took the hose and reel. On their arrival it was found that the flames had spread with alarming rapidity, and had secured a good hold on Mr. Ball's premises, the roof of which had fallen in. A plentiful supply of water was obtained from the Corpora- tion mains, and every effort was made to prevent the spread of the fire. Notwithstanding these exertions. however, the roofs of the adjoining shops and premises of Mr. Oliver Gregson, butcher, and Mr. James Gornall, tobacconist, were also destroyed. The flames shot up to a great height, and naturally occasioned considerable alarm in the neighbourhod, and some of the residents moved portions of their furni- ture and effects from their houses. The fire was ultimately got under in about two hours, but the brigade played upon the smouldering debris in the basement of Mr. Ball's shop for several hours afterwards. How the fire originated is difficult to ascertain. Mr. Ball does not reside on the premises and it is supposed that the fire was burning for over half-an-hour before it was dis- covered. Mr. Ball, Mrs. Ball, and an assistant named Thomas Marsh left the premises at half-past ten on Sat- urday night, when everything seemed safe and the gas was turned off at the meter. The stock, clothing, and drapery, which is entirely destroyed, was valued at £2,000, and many other articles of value were in pledge. It may be stated that a Chubb's safe in which about £5OO worth of valuables had been placed, was in the heat of the fire but its contents escaped damage. In Mr. Gregson's premises, next door, a bed and other i articles n the upper rooms were destroyed, and it is alleged that during the excitement a quantity of meat was stolen by persons who had congregated in the vicinity. Fortunately Mr. Ball's stock was insured in the County Fire Office. The property belongs to Mr. Joseph Marsh, of Boundary-road, and it is stated that it was not insured. The less in that respect will be about £5OO. The scene of th'e fire was visited by large num- bers of people on Sunday.

div.head: PRESCOT LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: PRESCOT LICENSING SESSIONS.

The annual licensing sessions for the Prescot Petty Sessional Division were held at the Prescot Police Court on Tuesday, when the magistrates on the Bench were Sir Thomas Earle and Mr. H. R. d'A Willis. The court-room was cr9wded, and considerable interest was manifested in the proceedings.-2-Superintendent Barker's report was submitted by Inspector 'Peters, of Wavertree, in Mr. Barker's absence. There were 42 licensed victuallers, and 24 beersellers on the premises, 2 off -leer licenses, and 3 other licenses. STRO?i'Ci OPPOSITION FROM HITYTON.

Mr. Thorn-as Swift (barrister, Liverpool, instructed by Messrs. J. 0. Swift, St. Helens) appeared to support an application by Mr. John William Lees for the grant of a provisional license for a house proposed to be erected on the south side of Huyton Quarry railway station. He said he understood it would be opposed by some temper- ance secretaries and clergy from Huyton, and perhaps his friends who represented them weuld say for whom they aptieared.—Mr. J. C. Eccles (solicitor) said he ap- peared on behalf of the 300 residents of Huyton Quarry; also on behalf of the Huyton Branch of the C.E.T.S.. the Huyton Park Congregational Temperance Society, the Welsh Presbyterian Church and Wesleyan Chapel, Huy- on Quarry, and also for Canon Holden, the priest in charge of Huyton.—Mr. W. Mackenzie (solicitor) said he appeared on behalf of Mr. Molyneux-Seel, the owner of a great portion of the land in the immediate neighbour- hood, and also for Mr. Thomas Rimmer, of Huyton Hey, who was the owner of the Seel Arms, and Mr. John Knowles, the owner of the dwelling-houses which are situated next to the proposed site of the public-house He also appeared for the mortgagee in possession of the adjoining property to Mr. Knowles.—Mr. Swift said if opposition of the character mentioned were to prevail there would never be any license granted at all, and the Act of Parliament for granting licenses might be re- pealed any day. The great bone of contention would be the locality, and with regard to that the owner of the land would not have sold it if he had not thought that it would be for the benefit of the neighbourhood. Really and truly there was no opposition in the immediate locality except from some clergymen, who always made it their business to oppose applications of that kind. There was the remarkable circumstance in that case that Canon Penrhyn, rector of Huyton, was asked by Messrs. Burton and Ball if he was opposed to the appli- cation, and Canon Penrhyn did not oppose it.—Mr. Ec- cles wished to correct his learned friend. He held in his hand a declaration signed by Canon Penrhyn that he did oppose it.—Mr. Swift said he was only sta- ting what were his instructions, and he was sorry if there had been any misunderstanding in that respect. They could all understand the nature of the opposition coming as it did from the temperance' societies and clergy and the owners of the rival public- houses. The whole of the neighbours, with one or two exceptions, were in favour of it and wished it success. The cost of the land was about £3OO, and the cost of the proposed building was estimated from £1,400 to £1,500. —Mr. Metcalf, architect, Mr. Ellis, the applicant, and Mr. Perrin, a solicitor's clerk, gave evidence in support of the application and in regard to the posting of the notices.—Mr. Mackenzie raised a tethnical abjection to the wording of the notices, but this was overruled by the Bench.—Mr. Eccles complained that the notice had ' not been posted in a conspicuous place, and that it had not been advertised in the local newspapers. He repre- sented all classes of clients and had petitions against the application signed by 300 persons.—The Magistrate' Clerk ruled that these petitions could not be put in as they were not evidence. Mr. Eccles said he also appeared for various temperance societies.—The Magistrates' Clerk said he could not repre- sent them unless they were registered corporations.—Mr. Eccles said he had received personal instructions from the clergy and ministers and trustees of the various places of worship, and he was astonished that anyone should think of erecting a public-house in the neighbour- hood. Within a radius of 550 yards there were four public-houses, and the proposed site was opposite the local cricket ground, which had been got up for the young men of the district. The temperance societies and the residents generally strongly opposed it, and he trusted the appeal to the Bench to refuse the application would not be in vain.—Mr. Mackenzie then addressed, the court against the proposal as affect- ing the interests of his clients.—Mr. William Bell, West View, Huyton.; Rev. H. J. Foster, of Liverpool, super- intendent minister of the Huyton Wesleyan Circuit; Miss Louisa Jane Booth, lady Wesleyan missionary at Huyton Quarry; the Rev. H. R. d'A Hubbard, curate of Huyton- Rev. A. W. Carter, Congregational Church pastor; Mr. Henry Capper, treasurer of Huyton Park Temperance Society; Mr. S. R. Jones, Huyton; and Mr. William Jones, fluvton Quarry, gave evidence against the granting of the licence.—The Bench retired, and after five minutes absence returned, and said the licence would be refused.

• Mr. W. Swift (St. Helens) applied on behalf of Alfrea Russell, grocer, 8. Beech-terrace, Tarbock-road, Huyton, for a license for the sale of wine and beer to be con- sumed off the premises, but the application was not granted.—Mr. Swift also applied for a wine and spirit license, for consumption off the premises, on behalf of John Bennett, chemist, 5, Raludah-terrace, Albert-road, Widnes. The applicant was possessed of a wholesale license, and the Bench granted the application. The whole of the old licenses were renewed, and this concluded the business of the sessions.

Two LIVES LOST IN A COLLIERY. On Wednesday evening, while some men were engaged in opening the old heading in George Inn Colliery, New Tredegar, be- longing to the Rhyrnney Railway Company, a huge vol- ume of water suddenly burst in upon them. A rush was made for the pit shaft, but two firemen, named David Davies and Ben Evans, were overtaken by the flood and drowned.
