(Applause.) What he was more concerned was that the eyes of the world were upon them. erms much controversy about them, both in and , Parliament, and inquiries were made by Special. ittees of the House of Commons, and others who" With no very particular favour upon friendly jes such as theirs. Therefore they should be pre- to justify the saying that they were so fond of alg, namely,. that the Manchester Unity was the luici wealthiest of all friendly societies. That could done by every member, lodge, and district con- ulg to the different rules and regulations of the so- , laid down at the various A.M.C.'s, by seeing that Member paid contributions according to his age mbilities, and that the capital of the lodges and. dis- Was well invested. (Applause.) They must re- that in the earlier career of the Manchester t 7 they had not the same scientific knowledge and to go upon they had at the present time, and their !athers fell into the error and mistake of promising '.benefits than the contributions could possibly pro- and the consequence was that upon a ttion of the assets and liabilities of the Order being , a serious state of deficiency was revealed, led to a strong determination on the part of the )era to reform these errors. and to endeavour, with better information possessed by them, to '"dde a more equitable scale of contributions and tefits. Accordingly, what was commonly known as! graduated scale," or "the 38th general rule," ia provided for menibers paying contributions accor- to their age on entrance, was passed by the Birken- I A. M. C, in 1864, and it was a matter of extreme ,et to him to find that some lodges and districts were yet complying with that very necessary and impor- ' rule, although it was passed over 24 years ago. The ' of Directors, feeling that the future prosperity and is of their great society was dependent upon lodges Mg out this rule in its entirety, had decided in all reported to them of lodges violating the same, to st them to conform to the same, or they would be with as severely as the rules would allow. (Hear, r.) It was all the, more necessary to do this at the Mt time when so many lodges were making applica- to the A'.3l.C. for some relief to be granted to them, they should be prepared to show that they had 1Y conformed to the rules of the society, and had 4mme m. 4t, their very best to correct the errors and mistakes e past by making some slight sacrifices, and thus Ilqw that they were prepared to help themselves first, N°l'e asking anyone else for assistance. He was, how- ttie,", pleased to find during his visits to the various dis- kcr that the more prosperous brethren were prepared thq lling to help, to the best of their ability, any of Emitlr More unfortunate brethren who, owing to misfor- eor unavoidable circumstances over which they had cOntrol, were not in as good a position as themselves, ..45Iding they were willing to make every effort on Part to better their own condition. He had been o, ed since his arrival in Warrington that they had 4t;,kled on complying with the graduated scale of bane- contributions as laid down in the 38th General ke`e, and that being so, from what he knew and had ttiet! of the officers and members of the Warrington Dis- abl'• generally, that notwithstanding a rather unfavour- *ee report of their position at the last valuation they peilre determined to place themselves in a sound and sol- t Position, and to become what he should be glad to ,i','2lamely, one of the most prosperous districts in the e Unity. (Applause.) "e Deputy Grand Master said that at the outset he l'jb•nht be permitted to say that he had the honour of be- ltilthe first representative from Scotland who had had t'Vat on the directorate during the past 35 years, and the still higher honour of being the first Oddfellow resenting a Scottish district who had attained to the qi,rl.l-ItY Grand Mastership of the Order. (Applause.) "Ped to be spared to fill the still higher position of ,I'd Master of the Order, when, should he receive an 4"tation, he should avail himself of it to pay a visit to 511aPlogton. (Applause.) Since his appointment he If:` Paid two official visits, the first along withthe Grand oTter to Dublin, and this formed the second ; and he every reason to feel pleased with the reception 'eh had been accorded to him on both occasions. With kiLrence to his colleagues on time directorate, whatever t la> ht be said of them, and however severely their de- ts ens and actions might be criticized, he was prepared 410 assert that no body of men could more earnestly or ta,„re assiduously attend to the discharge of the impor- tct business which was from time to time submitted to thl for their consideration. No doubt very much of r labour would be obviated were a little more charity CI forbearance evinced between members, lodges, and 7'4as, as it was no secret that many questions of dis- ' came before them which might properly be as frivolous and vexatious. There were, lie said, Noithee,ri three and four millions of members connected 'nese orders, and the amount expended annually

for sick pay to members, assistane,e to widows and or- phans, and for death claims was considerably over £3,000,000. In addition to that amount there were the moneys paid to brethren in search of employment, grants in special cases of distress, and the moneys paid through the juvenile societies, which would bring up the amount to over £4,000,000 per annum. If it were not for such societies the ratepayers would have to bear a much heavier burden than they did at the present time. He pointed out that it was most de- sirable to increase the efficiency of friendly societies— (1) by taking every cars that the contributions of the members should be able to meet the liabilities ; (2) by having a quinquennial valuation, and if the valuation disclosed a deficiency, the members should take steps at once to remove such deficiency ; (3) by providing a fund out of which the contribution of members out of employment should be paid so as to keep such members in benefit ; (4) by the formation of superannuation fund, so that members could insure against that time when, owing to old age, they were unable to follow their usual occupations. He stated that no friendly so- ciety was properly fulfilling its mission if it allowed members to lapse who were temporarily unable to pay their contributions ; or which did not keep its members from the pauper roll. (Applause.) The Oddfellows So- ciety- had no jealousy of any other well regulated so- ciety ; on the contrary, it held out the hand of friend- ship towards it, wished it success, and would, as far as possible, assist such societies in their endeavours to promote the general good of the community. There was room enough for all. (Hear, heiir, and applause). This toast was received with the ho.lours of the order,-, and was responded to by P.G.M. Holmes. A number of other toasts followed, and the evening was spent in a very pleasant manner. Several songs were given by Brother Henry T. Dean, and a selection of music, "The Fairy Bells," by Brother Sandal', Admiral Nelson Lodge, which were heartily encored. Mr. Geo. Riley' with his customary 'kindness, presided at the pianoforte.

The Life of Mr. William Congreve is published by Mr. Walter Scott in the Great Writers series. It is from the pen of Mr. Edmund Gosse, M.A.' and its value as a contribution to the biography of English literature may be in some degree estimated, when it is stated that this is the first time that any at- tempt has been made to write a detailed life of Congreve. It is highly creditable to the publishing firm that so much that is new can be given for a shilling in a substantial well-bound volume. Mr. Gosse clears away a good deal of rubbish which hau accumulated by the publication of certain " Me- moirs" containing certain lies; and he chronicles for the first time the exact date of the issue of al- most all Congreve's writings. The author of some of our finest comedies at last has justice done to him. • _ _ _ .

In the Canterbury Poets for August we have "El- fin Music; an Anthology ot English Fairy Poetry, selected and arranged, with an introduction, by Arthur Edward Waite." This is a unique produc- tion, and abounds in gems of poetry, ever great poet being Placed under contribution. Mr. Waite's introduction is a cireful historical treatment of the subject of fairy lore, which cannot fail to be of value to the student of literature. The belief in fairies is shown to date back to the very earlytimes, and to extend through the world from east to west. The elves are, of course, much superb," to mortals. As one of them is made to say—

Our shapes and size we ca,n convert To either large or small; An old nut-shell's the same to us As is the lofty hall. English Prose is the current volume of the Came- lot Series. It has been chosen and edited by Mr. Arthur Galton, and includes specimens—from Sir John Maundeville; of the fourteenth century, to Thackeray, of the nineteenth. Mr. Galton remarks that lie has not sought to supply a catalogue of English writers, but to give specimens of English prose. He has aimed in his extracts at complete- ness and interest, and in this it must be conceded, he has admirably succeeded. Mr. Galton shows himself, we think, too egotistical in his way of re- ferring to the weak points of his predecessors. But the specimens speak for themselves: and, while full of interest, they will aid in the acquisition of a good style, which is truly described as distin- guished by "directness, plainness, and simplicity." The Westminster Review for August leads off with a vigorous article on " lreland—a reply to an Irish Dissentient Liberal." This is followed by papers on "Both Sides of Jewish Oviiracter" and "The Indian National Congress." The article on " Memory " is especially interesting and instructive, but the paper which has caused the most stir is one on "Marriage,' by Mona Caird. "Mr. Whistler's Ten o'clock ' is thoughtfully criticised by Mr. Edmund Kelly; and science, politics, history, and belies lettres are dealt with under the head of Contemporary Literature, the magazine closing with the customary review of Home Affairs. Scribner's Magazine for August opens with a most valuable and interesting paper by N. S. Shaler on "Rivers and Valleys." It is profusely and power- fully illustrated. Another important illustrated paper bears the title of " American Locomotives and Cars." Mr. R. L. Stevenson supplies an "Epilogue to an Inland Voyage"; Mr. F. J. Stimson goes on reaping "First Harvests "; and there is, amongst other good things, a stirring complete story (illus- trated) by Maria Blunt—" The Fate of the Georgina." In part XXII of the new edition of the History of Lancashire, published by Mr. John Heywood, the pedigrees (eight in number) form an important feature. The one showing the connection between the families of Bexwicke,Oldham, Bradford, Hulme, Beck, Pendleton, and Crabtree, now for the first time drawn up, should have a special interest for Manchester people, as showing the close relationship existing between a group of Manchester worthies, which included the founders of the Grammar I School, Hulme's Trust. the Conduit, and the first I Free Library; also Bradford the martyr, and Crab- tree the astronomer. As showing how well Mr. Croston is doing his work. it may be stated that the I new matter in the text forms about one-third of the whole. The Tourist Guide to the continent, issued under the authority of the Great Eastern Railway Com- pany, is quite a wonderful sixpennyworth. Some of the illustrations are really charming works of art ; there is a good map; Mr. Percy Lindley has done his work well as editor; while the printing is all that could be desired. As much may be said of Walks in the Ardennes by Mr. Lindley. It is a bright, useful guide. with numerous clever pen and ink sketches by Mr. J. F. Weedon. Part 45 reaches us of Ward and Lock's Technical Journal. The present issue completes volume 5, and is accompanied by an exhaustive index. The work maintains its high reputation as an industrial self- instructor. The Ladies Treasury is most varied, as usual, both as to text and illustrations. It is very superior as a sixpenny magazine of "Literature, education and, I fashion.

THE NEW CLERGY AT THE PARISH -CHURCH. Sir,—The force of circumstances must be my apology for seeking your aid in the matter of the Parish Church new clergy, namely, the programme of Ritualism they are so gracelessly unfolding to a congregation of worship- pers who, I believe, hate to have to begin, if necessary' to fight it down; but we must, not only for our own sale but for future generations, nip in the bud even by publicity, which one deeply regrets to have to do. The new order of things is repugnant to the feelings of Pro- testants, hence the alarm which is being sounded to-day. Peace is beautiful, but not at any price • we want no unnecessary bowings and scrapings; no adoration of of lifting on high the bread and wine in the communion; no frequent sights of the minister's back instead of his face ; no crossings of the person" in the name," &c.; and no spectacles of an institution of trained ladies to have to stand up and keep standing while the new clergy, forsooth, with the choristers, march to their places; in short, we want no Romanism.—yours, NOT A LOVER OF PEACE AT ANY PRICE.

THE LICENSING QUESTION AT WARRINGTON. Sir,—Will the magistrates of Warrington follow the example of the Liverpool justices and refuse to renew the licences of those houses where singing and dancing are carried on? It is well known that many houses in Warrington are "simply moral plague spots, whose extirpation should be remorselessly carried out," and it is altogether a mistaken idea that the magistrates have no power to refuse renewals of the licenses of such houses. Mr. Patterson pointed out yesterday—in Liver- pool—that the state of the law, as decided by the Court of Appeal, and which remained the law until it was repealed, was that the magistrates had absolute discretion alike over the renewal of liconsesNs well as the granting of new licenses." This being so, I think public opinion should be brought to bear upon the magis- trates, so that the licenses of these "plague spots," these "dens of infamy," these "haunts of the degraded of both sexes," these singing anddancing saloons, should be withdrawn. I hope the granting of any new licenses will be promptly refused. It is dreadful to think of the mis- chief that may be caused by a " house " in Battersby. lane—in close proximity to the Barracks—frequented, as it certainly would be, by military ruffians and the outcast degraded females of the town.—Yours, MORALITY.

Sir,—The refusal a tl}e I.!ice4sin Cqwpittee to grant pm increased number of licenses last yAar dod tit:A deter the 4pplicarits from coming forward In 1888, ahci town tails is anything to guide our opinions they do so with improved prOIDOCti. P. • •••• AA. . seems mxange "le new committee, so soon afterwards, should see the necessity of granting what their predecessors declined to

grant. Many brewery firms, of late, have been made limited m 403mpaes, and millions of money have been invested in shares. Some brewery companies have magistrates on the Board of Directors; one firm has three justices out of five directors ; another two out of four. For such instances we have not far to go. All investors of capital like large dividends, and increased sale of liquor means additional dividends; therefore we cannot expect per- sons interested in the liquor traffic to advocate a reduction in the number of licensed houses. An increased number of licenses will not tend to improve mankind, either mentally or morally. It must be evi- dent to all that there are too many licensed houses in Warrington already. The aymlica.nts promise to surren- der three licenses to obtain one in a new district. What a sacrifice ! Two indoor licenses in one street, and one outdoor else-where. How many people are there, who, having made a bad investment, would not like to get out of it and try again, even though they lost fifty per cent, by the change? Many. I wonder if the applicants at Warrington would have made this sacrificial offer if the compensation clauses had been retained in the Local Government Bill. It must be remembered that we have not yet heard the last of compensation. Therefore, if the justices have the taxpayers' interests at heart, they will be very chary in granting any new licenses. In conclusion let me say I am not a teetotaller, and do not condemn the use of a stimulant, but the increased facilities for abuse.

div.head: RUPERT.
div.p: RUPERT.

THE MARRIAGE QUESTION. Sir,—l don't know whether many of your readers have read or heard of Mrs. Mona Caird's article in this month's" Westminster Review," advocating a relaxa- tion of the marriage tie, which is evidently too tight and enduring for some men and women. Many people write about Mrs'. Caird's proposals, or rather suggestions —for she still honours Mrs. Grundy's dictum that a wo- man must not" propose," though she may suggest—as if they were something quite original. That, of course, is not the case, even.so far as recent years are concerned, and if we go further back we find that almost exactly 200 years ago "the grave and philosophic " Locke, in his Treatises of Civil Government," was arguing as to marriage that there was" no necessity in the nature of the thing, nor to the ends of it, that it should always be for life,' and that there was reason to inquire why the marriage compact might not be made determinable, "either by consent, or at certain time, or upon certain conditions, as well as any other voluntary compact." And in last century Hume contended that it was "mere superstition to imagine that marriage can be entirely uniform, and will admit of only one mode or form." As to practise, it is not necessary to say that conjugal en- gagements in time past or present have not been con- fined to one mode or form. It was said to be usual in Tonquin, for sailors, when their ship came into harbour, to marry for the season. When the male population of ancient Athens was reduced by war and pestilence, a law was passed to permit every man to have two wives. The poet, Euripides, was particularly unfortunate in his matrimonial ventures and after some experience of the much-married state became a professed woman-hater, and is said to be the only theatrical writer that ever did form an aversion to the fair sex. Coming nearer home, there are records to show that formerly marital arrange- ments called " hand-fisting" were entered into in Scot- land, the only ceremony being the shaking of hands, a couple thereby becoming man and wife for twelve months. So far from being regarded as mere illegal liasons were these arrangements that so late as the six- teenth century an offspring of one of them put in a claim to the Earldom of Sutherland, and his claim had to be bought off.—Yours, &c., RECLUSE.
Warrington, August 22, 1888. MR. GLADSTONE'S " INCONSISTENCY !" have, this last day or two, been considerably

amused by evidently strained efforts on the part of the Conservative party, or at least a section of that mongrel composition known by that title, to again convict Mr. Gladstone of "inconsistency." This seems to be a favourite pursuit on their part—what a pity they could not devote their energies to a better and more useful purpose! If Mr. Gladstone speaks or communicates in any form with the people of this country, some lynx- eyed gentleman on the opposite side whose prolific I imagination and cool assumption of infallibility place him far above the ordinary standard of humanity, is sure to discover some "inconsistency." and for some time afterwards the Tory Press gloat and glory over it, almost with the same delight as a pack of wolves would relish the carcase of some lost or strayed animal from the abodes ef civilisation. But when Mr. Gladstone again appears upon the scene the Tory bubbles of "inconsistency." " fallacy," and " mis-statement," are pricked, and fall to the ground, a discredit and discomfort to those who laboured so hard in securing their ascension. This has been the case on the present occasion. Mr. Gladstone, in speaking at Hawarden, last Monday, contrasted the treatment of political prisoners in Ireland with the cruelties under which the political prisoners in Italy suffered under King Bomba. He said that bad as the latter was, he did not put political prisoners into the company of felons. Two days later, in the leading organ of Tory cunning and forged letters, appears the conviction of Mr. Glad- stone for " inconsistency. " This was only to be expected—if Mr. Gladstone cannot be reruted by facts and truth something must be manufac- tured if there is the least ground to work upon. Mr. Gladstone's explanation has dispelled the charge of in- consistency. The fact that Mr. Gladstone, 37 years ago did see one political prisoner, who was convicted of the grave offence of high treason, imprisoned with other ' felons, out of the many thousands of political offenders, not so incarcerated, had escaped his memory, and this is the only foundation for the enormous bubble of " incon- sistency" which has been set afloat. It only proves how shallow and groundless are the devices and dodges upon which the Tory party claim support. Surely every man of common sense can see through them; and it is to be hoped that Mr. Gladstone's exposure of the abominable treatment of the Irish political prisoners will lead to their condition being greatly improved. If the Tory Govern- ment and party do not mend their ways of their own free will a day of reckoning will come, when the people of this country will arise and say "Away, you are un- worthy of the trust reposed in you, and we will have no more of you." What a sad day that will be for Salis- bury, Balfour, and Co. !—Yours, &c., A READER. St. Helens, August 23rd, 1888.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
OPERATIONS AT STOCKTON REAM

That part of the Ship Canal course which runs through Stockton Heath will probably soon be one of the busiest in the whole length, and, owing to the variety, of the work which has to be done here, it will certainly be one of the most interest- ing. From Stockton Heath to its western termina- tion at Runcorn, the Runcorn and Latchford Canal—which was completed in the early years of this century to facilitate navigation between the upper reaches and the estuary of the Mersey —will be abandoned, and already a number of navvies are busily engaged with spade and barrow in filling in the canal near Twenty-step and Tom Paine's Bridges. Part of the bed of the old canal lyingbet ween these two bridges will be absorbed in the Ship Canal channel. At this point the new canal will cut through the high-lying ground be- hind Wilderspool Brewery, once the site of a Roman station. The surface of the land here has been cleared for some weeks past, and already a steam navvy is in situ near Tom Paine's Bridge, and will very soon be in full operation. In this locality ex- cavation will be made on a very extensive scale, and some idea of the depth of the cutting , may be gathered from the fact that when the canal is completed the surface of its waters will be about thirty feet below the level of the ad- jacent ground. That part of the Runcorn and Latchford canal which runs between Stockton Heath and the Mersey at Howley will be left in- tact, and one of the works that will be carried out near Twenty-step bridge will be a lock to give access between the Ship Canal and this remaining part of the old navigation. Another of the works in the Stockton Heath locality is the making of a new road to branch off to the right just before reaching St. Thomas's Church, and to take a straight course across near Lower Walton. The making of this new road is already in full swing, at least at the Lower Walton end, but before it can be finished the filling in of the old Latchford canal between Stockton Heath and Tom Paine's Bridge will have to be completed. It is probable that as soon as this new road is made the present road to Chester over Tom Paine's Bridge will be stopped, and people travelling from Warrington in the direction of Walton and Darasbury will have to go straight on to Stockton Heath and pass along the substituted route. To make way for the canal and for this new road many houses on the south side of the Twenty-step Bridge have been pulled down within the last few days, and several others wili shortly be demolished. Another opera- tion that is being rapidly prosecuted is the laying of a line of rails along the old towing path, which will no doubt be largely used for the conveyance of materials from the Latchford Wharf to Stockton Heath and Lower Walton.

div.head: ELLESMERE PORT.
div.p: ELLESMERE PORT.

Recently two new cuttings have been started on the section between Ellesmere Port and Stanlow Point, and a steam navvy has been placed in each. The number of workmen has been increased, and additional huts for ther accommodation have been erected at Stanlovr Point. The soil. on this section is very heavy, and landslips are •• ' • ireqllent. EASTEIA.M. . , The Ane wettiii'Qr of Saturday ifidqi;ed thousands of people to visit the Ship Canal works at Eastham, which are now in full "swin..,r. The visitors included many be- longing to Iftnche.ster, Salford, and other Lancashire towns which are likely to be affected by the great under- taking. F..om mid-day until late in the afternoon, the steamers, plying between the Liverpool Landing-stage and Eastham Ferry, were crowded; in some instances there being scarcely comfortable standing room onboard. Notwithstanding this, however, the sail was an exceed- ingly pleasant one, and several of the trips were made in remarkably quick time. In order to cope with the re- turn traffic, boats were run half-hourly in the evening, and this enabled all the visitors to get 'back in good time for the late trains. The canal works have completely transformed the aspect of the country in the vicinity of Eastham Ferry, and to anyone who has not visited the place since these were commenced a great surprise is in store. The pretty field just beyond the Eastham gardens, which formerly sloped "'in verdure green" down almost to the water's edge, has been transformed into a yawning chasm, alongside of which are great heaps of earth, navvies' huts, locomotives, and all the other material and mechanical features incidental to the work of constructing the canal. The visitors showed much interest in the whole scene, and they were allowed to go over any portion of the works they liked, so long as they kept a good look-out for the numerous trains of waggons which are continually passing to and fro on the network of lines which intersect the works i and which are almost daily extended as the operations pro- ceed. Special interest seemed to be taken in the working of the ponderous steam navvies, close to which large crowds assembled to witness the rapidity and ease with which huge banks of earth disappeared under these triumphs of modern invention.

div.head: WESTON POINT AND NORTON.
div.p: WESTON POINT AND NORTON.

On section 3, Wt:enaini.fioinfnc-e to Weston Point, a German navvy and a steam crane excavator are at work. The work of making the basin at the mouth of the Weaver has also beea commenced, and employment is here found for a large number of people. The work on the section extending from Weston Point to Norton has been considerably delayed, in .consequence of the con- tractor not having had the consent of the Mersey Conser- vators to enter the river. The required consent to pFo- ceed with the river works has, however, been obtained. Opposite the offices at Norton, where the principal tips are, the embankments formed by the tips have in most places sunk as much as fifty feet. The ground is boggy here, and the soil tipped on it will serve to consolidate it, and thus make the sides of the canal firmer than they otherwise would have been. The principal cutting on this section is upwards of three miles in length, and is the longest yet made on the entire route. • RUNCORN.

During the week the river has been surveyed near to "No Man's Land," and preparations for the laying of a line of rails along the foreshore and certain streets from the Old Quay Docks through Runcorn Bridge are being made. Large consignments of material are being de- posited on the wharves at the Old Quay, ready for imme- diate use.

div.head: FRODSHAM MARSH.
div.p: FRODSHAM MARSH.

Six huts have been erected at Frodsham Marsh, and two are already tenanted. Preparations are being made for the erection of additional accommodation, and a coal stage has been provided. Two steam navvies are at work in this neighbourhood. THELWALL AND LYMM.

There are two steam navvies engaged on the site of the proposed Latchford Locks near Morris Brook, and a deep and wide cutting has been made. Many men are regularly at work along the length to Statham and Rix- ton, and at this latter place operations of the steam dig- ger are facilitated by blasting operations, in which such explosives as dynamite, tonite, and gunpowder are employed. One of the discoveries on the canal at Statham was that of a big tree on Saturday, which hooked on to the teeth of a bucket of one of the steam navvies. The tree was about 25 feet long and 5 feet in diameter, and had to be blown into two or three pieces with dynamite before it could be removed. It is said that the removal

of this unexpected obstacle cost about £2O. The tree was found at a depth of about 12 feet from the surface and it is said that a gentleman in Lymm claims to re- member its fall when he cropped it. In that case it , must have been covered up in the course by the silt de- posited by the Mersey at its overflows. THE LYMM FUSTIAN 'CUTTERS.

It is said that, mainly through wantof organisation amongst the men themselves, the arrangement whereby a considerable number of the unemployed fustian cutters were engaged on the canal, is nqt working very satisfac- torily It will be remembered that through the inter- position of two Lymm gentlemen, Mr. Walker, the con- tractor, agreed to give a number of fustian cutters piece jobs on the canal at 51 per cube yard of soil removed, the men being left to arrange amongst themselves as to the way the work should be carried on. It seems, how- ever, that the fustian cutters have shown a want of or- ganising tact, and many of the men have left the work. It his hoped that these difficulties will be smoothed so that the Lymm unemployed may still take full advan- tage of the opportunity offered them.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 25, 1888. WARRINGTON EMIGRANTS TO AMERICA. INTERESTING LETTER. The relatives of Mr. J. Winstanley, who, with his family,, recently left Warrington for America, have just received from him a very interesting letter. It is dated Salem, Oregon, August 7th, 1888, and in it Mr. Winstanley says that he and his family are in the enjoyment of good health. Mrs. Winstanley was very ill on leaving the boat at Quebec, but she quickly got better as they journeyed through a beau- tiful country and had warmer weather. The first stoppage they made was near Montreal, where they remained for three hours, and saw fire-flies and grasshoppers in abundance. Afterwards, the road lay through hundreds of miles of forest, of which scores of miles was burned and charred, and in many cases in flames, burning only as fnresta can.
", A GREAT COUNTRY."

"Truly this is a great country," remarks Mr. Win- stanley, "with immense prairies, flat and rolling, with lovely farms here and there, and with great herds of cattle feeding. Day after day it becomes wearisome riding, but worst of all was the sleep- ing on the hard car-beds. It made our bones sore, and yet we seemed to get along all right. We had lots of iced water, but were badly fixed sometimes for hot water to make tea. I tell you I paid as much as ten cents, for a pint of hot water, not boil- ing. There were no fires in the cars, as the weather was too warm, but I think the C.P.R. Railway people ought to provide it for immigrants. The dining cars, when they were attached, were kept too busy to supply hot water—even for money. They preferred supplying meals at 75 cents., which, of course, we could not afford. Winnipeg, in Mani- toba, is the best farming country that I have seen. If the winters were not so severe, I should say it is the best place in the country for a young man to come to. Here we parted with two-thirds of our fellow-passengers, a few of us going out West, and some going to California. Just take one of the maps and look at the little bit of Lake Superior, and, just fancy, it took the train six and a half hours to get round that small corner. I suppose they could put the whole of Great Britain in that great inland sea. The scenery was some- thing grand. On Thursday we reached the foot- hills of the Rockies. The scenery just baffles des- cription. The mountains were covered with snow, and the weather became very cold, as the train gradually ascended to the height of 5,296 feet above sea level. We reached Mount Stephen, 8,000 feet high, and saw a large glacier of ice, about 800 feet thick.

stances he thought that a case had been made out.—De- fendant was then formally charged, with the offtvice first stated, and also with having omitted to make en- tries of goods supplied to certain persons, with intent to defraud.—Mr. Davies said that he should like some of the evidence for the defence put on the depositions, and he called Robert Sutton (13), of 18, Chorley-st., who had been in the employ of Messrs. Sexton Brothers. Witness said that when he went to the Winwick-road shop to work the defendant and Stafford were there. Witness was errand boy, and saw James Sexton in the Winwick- road shop nearly once a week. Sometimes he looked over the book produced with Kenny. About February he noticed a string round part of the book. Witness, he believed in February, saw Stafford hold the book while Kenny cut the leaves out with a knife. Kenny said to Stafford—" Are they of any use?" and Stafford replied, "No." After they were cut out Stafford threw them into the fire. He had seen Jas. Sexton go through the book five or six times. He had seen deductions taken from Kenny's wages for groceries. —Evidence was also given by Annie Heathcote and Ann Smiler. The latter witness said that she had traded at Sexton's shop ev,..r since it was opened, but had never had credit allowed until Kenny came to the shop.—The defendant was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions, bail being allowed.—The hearing of the case occupied the court from soon after eleven o'clock in the morning until nearly six o'clock in the evening. During the afternoon Alderman Harrison was the only magistrate on the Bench.
LYNN. CONSERVATIVE PICNIC TO WARBURTON.—The Balfour Conservative Club, Manchester, consisting of about 80 members, held their annual picnic on Saturday, at the Saracen's Head, Warburton.

LYMM VOLUNTEERS.—The day for the shooting off of the company prizes has been postponed from August 25th to September Bth. The men will be conveyed to the Bollin range by 'bus and not as originally arranged by train. The cup, which is of the value of £lO, is at present on view ia the window of Mr. J. B. Taylor. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—A resolution was passed at the last meeting of the Altrincham Board of Guardians, at Knutsford, that the clerk to the Board be present to prosecute in the next flagrant case of school negligence that takes place in Lyinin, so that, if possible, an ex- ample may be made. This course has been considered necessary owing to the difficulty of getting convictions before the Lvmm Court. -

THE HAY AND CORN HARVEST AT LYMAL—But few farmers have entirely finished their hay getting, and in the meantime the corn has ripened quickly, and the somewhat strange spectacle is seen, of haymaking _in one field, and corn cutting in the next. During last week splendid harvest weather was experienced, of which the fullest advantage was taken, and great ad- vances have been made in gathering in the crops, though the last few days have been very detrimental to harvesting. BAPTIST SIns3AY SCHOOL.—On Thursday the annual treat was given to the children of this Sunday School. The children assembled to the number of 70, and were entertained by the teachers to a good substantial tea, after which they adjourned to a field for games and sports, during which about 40 friends sat down to tea in the schoolroom. After the school was cleared the children were regaled with sweets and nuts, and at seven o'clock they again sat down to supper, after which they were sent home, having spent a most enjoy- able day.

div.head: IRLAM.
div.p: IRLAM.

Two diggers of the American type have been got to work near Irlam. At this point there is springing up quite a village. In addition to the store-rooms, engine- shed, joiners' and blacksmiths' shops, and stabling for 20 horses, all of which are complete, there are in process of erection offices for the engineers and agents, and handsome houses for the various foremen. All these are on the north side of the cutting, and on the south side it is proposed to build twenty huts for the men, a mission room, and a hospital.

div.head: LOCAL ACCIDENTS.
div.p: LOCAL ACCIDENTS.

On Tuesday, just before noon, some blasting of shale rock was taking place immediately in front of the steam navvies at Rixton, on the Lymm section of the canal, and after the first and second charges of tonite had been exploded in the shot hole, the man proceeded to pour in the usual charge of about 501bs. of blasting powder for the purpose of "shaking up the rock," and the second man named England inserted the "swab" orlrammer to tightly drive home the charge, when the powder, by some unaccountable accident, exploded. The men were blown up with the mass of debris, the one who ' was ramming having his arm broken at the shoulder, and his face blackened and powder- marked, almost blinded, and; terribly shaken. The other man was little hurt. The injured man was at once removed to the hospital at Thelwall by means of a locomotive, which ran down on the canal line of rails. It is supposed that the charge of powder was put in be- fore the smouldering remnant of tonite had wholly ex- pired, or else that the iron-shod rammer struck the rock on which small particles of the powder had lodged in the pouring into the hole.—OnSaturday, whilst a navvy was engaged in removing a large tree which had been found in the course of the canal at Statham, he was accidentally jammed against it by a waggon and had his leg broken. He was also qnickly removed to the hospital at Thelwall.- From inquiries made yesterday we learn that both men are doing well. On Tuesday a man known by the name of "Cobbler Joe" was caught between the buffers of two wagons at Rixton, and was badly crushed. He vaS at once taken in a wagon to the Thelwall hospital. • • -

A GANGER'S CLAIM FOR WAGES. His Honour Judge Ffoulkes was occupied for a con- siderable time on Thursday in hearing a case in which John Bailey, a ganger, at present living at Stockton Heath, brought an action against Mr. T. A. Walker, the contractor for the Ship Canal, to recover £5 14s 7d, al- leged to beque as the balance of three different weeks' wages, and also a week's salary in lieu of notice. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Buckton, junr., represented defendant.-Mr Browne stated tht his client was a ganger, and had been employed in that capacity in various parts of the kingdom, and in France, for thirty years. In December last he went to the Acton Grange section of the Ship Canal, which was then sta:rting, and saw Mr. Squires, the manager for that section, who engaged him as ganger. He went to take up his duties on the following Monday, when he found that Mr. Squires had been dismissed. He was, however, engaged by Mr. Griffiths, the assistant mana- ger, and Mr. Grigson, who was appointed in Mr. Squire's place, to act as ganger at £2 2s a week. For about three months he worked as a ganger, and he then gave notice that he should leave, in consequence of what he considered wrong treatment on the part of oneof the officials. The manager, Mr. Griffiths, understanding that his services were useful, told him to take no notice of the person in question, and said that he would increase his wages 8s per week, making 50s. From that time until July he received that sum. On the 14th of July lie was paid 2s ld short. He asked what was the reason of that, and afterwards saw Mr. J. R. Walker, the nephew of the contractor, and agent for the Acton Grange sec- tion of the canal, who said that it was a mistake, and if plaintiff would go on with his work he would make it all right. The following week plaintiff again received a wage of 50s, but he did not receive the 2s ld. On the 28th July plaintiff was paid 12s 6d short. He complained to the cashier, who said that he had nothing to do with it. He then saw Mr. Griffiths, who said that it would be all right, and lie would get his money. On the Monday morning following he saw Mr. Walker. and asked him about the money. Mr. Walker then said—" I shall not pay you anything more. Let it be understood." He also said lie would see plaintiff " beggared " before he would pay the 2s. ld. that was short. A pay-off ticket was given to plaintiff, who con- sulted Mr. Browne on the matter.—Plaintiff was then called, and in his evidence he bpre out the remarks of his solicitor.—For the defence, it was stated that the 2s. ld. claimed was the amount of a fine inflicted on the plaintiff through not having his waggons well filled, but on plaintiff stating satisfactory reasons the fine was re- mitted, and the 2s. Id. was now paid into court with a further 10s. ld., being wages earned by the plaintiff up to the time of his leaving. As to the £5 also claimed, it was contended that there was a universal custom among the navvies and their gangers that they could leave and were liable to be dismissed at a moment's notice.—Mr. J. R. Walker, Bell-house farm, said that the matter re- garding the 2s. ld. deducted from the plaintiff's wages was satisfactorily explained. He told;plaintiff that he, could go to work nearer iAttchferti at the same rate of pay as the others working there received-1d a w Plaintiff said nothing, and left the office. a '• ' :mu witness by that understood that he cceptco - the terms. Afterwards he declined to work that rate and left. In cross-examination witness said that the £1 17s 61 only was paid because the work was of a different kind He denied having used the term "I'll see you beggared." He never heard the rule that standing gangers should be paid by the day questioned before. —Griffith Griffiths, sub-agent on the Acton Grange section, having given evidence for the defence, William Henry Golightly, walking ganger on the Moore section of the canal, sa d that he had been engaged in public works like that of the Ship Canal for thirty-two years. During that time he had engaged and dismissed many gangers. Plaintiff was a " standing " ganger, a "walking" ganger being a foreman of other gangers. He had never known of a " standing " ganger being paid weekly. No notice was, as far as his experience went, ever given or received where a " standing " gan- ger was concerned.—George Harding, ganger on the Ac- ton Grange section, also gave evidence to the effect that there was no custom of giving and receiving notice in respect to gangers.—Mr. Browne submitted that custom had nothing to do with the present case, as it had been shown that there was a weekly contract.—His: Honour, in summing up, said that the contract which appeared to have been made with the defendant was for two guineas per week. This was afterwards for some reason or other increased to 50s. The only evidence to show that there was not a weekly contract was that of Golightly and Harding, which was not strong enough to prove a uni- versal custom. The defendant, however, had not been dismissed by Mr. Walker, but had left because dissatis- fied with his pay, and -vas therefore, as he left on his own account, clearly not entitled to a week's notice. With regard to the other part of the claim, he could not see that plaintiff was entitled to success in the action on any ground whatever. He therefore gave judgment for the defendant, with costs.

div.head: BRICKLAYERS' BRAWL AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A BRICKLAYERS' BRAWL AT RUNCORN.

Before Major liazlehurst and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Frank An- trobus, bricklayer's labourer, of Nelson-st., was sum- moned for assaulting Lawrence Mullarney, also a bricklayer. There was a cress summons charging Mullarney with assaulting Antrobus. Mr. J. Burton appeared for Mullarney, and Mr. Wynne Humph- reys for Antrobus. Mullarney deposed that on Monday morning, about half-past nine, he was on his way to Pierpoint's Tannery, where Antrobus came from the Anchor Inn, and walking up to him, threatened to knock him off his feet. He told An- trobus that he wanted nothing to do with him. Upon this Antrolms struck witness on the facewith either a stone or a brick, and the latter attempted to get away, but Antrobus followed him, and struck him seve"al tides. Witness seized Antrobus by the scarf, butsome person cut it with a knife,'and Antrobus said he was sorry that be had not killed him.—John Regan, a boy,' gave confirmatory evi- dence.—Superintendent Hollingworth said Mul- larney came to the police station. He was bleeding from a wound on the head, but did not say any- thing about a brick or a stone.—The case for Antro- bus was that some feeling had arisen between the men because Mullarney had reported Antrobus to Mr. Coward, builder, for an alleged theft of bricks and mortar from the Public Hall. On the day in question Mullarney used threats to Antrobus, and commenced the assault. A free fight ensued, and Mullarney, who was the bigger and stronger man, dragged Antrobus eleven yards by his scarf, and struck him several times. He struck Mullarney on the face in self-defence, but no stone or brick was used.—After hearing the evidence the Bench said they considered both men equally to blame, and bound each over to keep the peace for six months in their own sureties of £5. Antrobus had to pay us 9d costs, and Mullarney 13s 6d, or in default 14 days' hard labour.

div.head: MEETING A WARILINOTON FRIEND.
div.p: MEETING A WARILINOTON FRIEND.

We reached Vancouver on Tuesday, having been just fifteen days out. I may say we had a near squeak, through one of those great pine trees slip- ping down the mountain, right through the top of a snow shed, and across the line. It threw the im- mense engine off the line, and thus delayed us for about two hours. The train had scarcely stopped at Vancouver before Mr. William Porter patted me on the back. and I tell you I was glad to see a friend's face in this stramge world. He took us to a very nice hotel; but I was disappointed with Van- couver. There is no land to .be got for farms, and the city land is dearer than the building lots in Bridge-st. I got an offer for work for Monday morning at 31 dollars (14s) a day, but we decided to move on to Portland in the States. Here I was pro- mised work, but our baggage had not come along with us (although I got it passed by the customs without being examined) and so I could not start.

div.head: PURCHASE OF A FARM.
div.p: PURCHASE OF A FARM.

I heard of a it;;;i-o—l-ii;sOld—at—S-a-le-m, and I came down and bought it. It consists of 44 acres, 33 of which are cultivated and the rest is forest, with some trees Oft, in diameter; plenty of cutting and fuel for years to come. I do not take possession until the first of October, and so I am in a cottage in Salem until then. There is a small house and barn, a good well, and some fruit on the farm. You should just see the fruit trees out here ! The prunes and pears, plums, peaches, apples, and vines are loaded, and in many dozen cases broken down with their load of fruit. I have .paid ao dollars an acre for the farm rather a good price—but I think it will soon be worth more. The land adjoining is offered at 76 dollars an acre. It is one and a half miles from Salem. The streets are lit up with electric light, but the roads are deep in dust. The weather is very hot, but cool at night. I have not got my luggage here yet, which is a great annoyance, as I cannot work without it. I got a job, however, this morning, in the office of a corn mill."

The following is an extract from a recent issue of an American journal :—James Winstanley and wife arrived here yesterday on the 11 o'clock train, having come direct to Salem from Liverpool, England, which city they left on the 12th ult. They had read such excellent reports of Salem and surrounding country from papers and pamph- lets that had reached them on the other side of the water that their minds had been fully made up to locate here if a suitable place could be found. Within four hours from the time they arrived here, they had selected the Arnold Myers place, one and a half miles north of town and purchased the same of the Oregon Land Co. They will make their home in Salem for a few weeks until they can get possession of the place, when they will go to work and meet with such success that they will never regret their prompt decision.

div.head: ALIATEP FALSIFWATION OF BOOKS,
div.p: THE ALIATEP FALSIFWATION OF BOOKS,

At the Ns'artiiigtoti tortitigh Court, yesterday morning, before Alderniati Harrison, Dr. Gornall, and Mr. R. Gallica, a respectable-looking man named John Francis Kenny, formerly in the em- ploy of Messrs Sexton Bros., provision dealers, ap- peared to answer a summons taken out at the in- stance of that firm, who alleged against him that, on or about the 30th July, he unlawfully mutilated a shop ledger, with intent to defraud. Mr. T. Swift, barrister, Liverpool, appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. P. Davies was for the defence.—ln stating the case for the prosecution, Mr. Swift said that it was brought under the Falsfication of Accounts Act, 1875. He then called Tames Sexton, one of the pro- secutors, who said that in December last the pri- soner was employed by him as a shopman. Soon afterwards be was appointed to the management of a branch establishment in Winwick-road. Prisoner was given a list containing the names of persons to whom credit was to be given. On no account was he to give credit to any customers not named on the list. On the 15th of the present month witness went to the shop, and noticed that several entries had not been made in the ledger, which, on further examination he found had been mutilated--tinee leaves having either been torn or cut out of the book. Subsequently he told his employer that he knew he had been doing what he should not have done,and asked for another chance. Some time later on witness said that he should take stock, where- upon defendant said that he would not wait for that. and went away saying, "If you want me you will have to follow me.' In the course of a long bross-examina- tio'n by Mr. Davies witness said that defendant's prede- cessor at the Winwick-road shop was a Mr. Williams. When prisoner went to the Winwick-road shop a number of the leaves in the book marked A were not tied down with a string. The first time he noticed the string was in June. He could, not tell whether the leaves which were tied down embraced the remains of those which had been torn out. The defendant did not inform him in February or March that he had torn the leaves out. The entries on the portion of the leaves remaining were not in Williams hand-writing. Williams' connection with the firm was closed on the Saturday before Christmas. The takings were about £75 a week. It was not correct that Williams wife dis- missed on account of any irregularities in the book marked A.—John Stafford a youth employed by Mr. Sexton, deposed that he had been employed at the Win- wick-road shop for about two years. He remembered noticing that some of the leaves had been cut or torn out of the book in question. He mentioned the matter to Kenny, who said—" It was me that cut them out. They stood in the way, and they were of no value to Mr. Sex- ton." Defendant also said that the leaves were in the ' Winwick-road shop, but they had been searched for and could not be found. On one occasion, witness said, he saw the defendant weigh a piece of ham. He then called t boy out of the street and sent him away with the ham o his (defendant's) home. It was not entered on the book, no money was put in the till. aid no account was kept of the transaction.—Michael Sexton, partner in the firm of Sexton Bros., provision dealers, deposed that he did not give any personal attention to the Winwick-road branch. Off Wednesday, 15th August, he was called by his brother, James Sexton, to where his brother and de- fendant were examining ;the books. His brother asked defendant who had cut mit those leaves. Defendant re- plied that he (defendant) had done so, and that the leaves were in the shop in Winwick-road.—lnspector Cox, of the borough police force, spoke to arresting the defendant at the " Three Pigeons" public-house. In answer to the charge the defendant said "It is wrong; I never touched the book."—For the defence Mr. Davies said that there was no intent to defraud. In the course of a lengthy address he contended that no prima .facie case had been made out, and referred to other charges against his client in regard to which evidence had not been called. Defendant did not make any secret to Stafford about having torn the leaves out. Had he intended to commit a fraud he would not have left the remaining portious of the leaves in the book.—Alderman Harrison admitted the reasonableness of that contention, but said that judging from all the circum-

MANSLAUGHTER.—At the Nenagh Assizes on Wedne..day the bailiff Sweeney, charged with the murder of a man named Kennedy at Templemore, was found guilty of manslaughter only. Sentence was deferred till the con- clusion of the trial onthe same charge of a young man named Lloyd, son of Mrs. Lloyd, Sweeney's em- ployer. STRIKE or MINERS.—The four thousand miners at the Murton and South Hetton Collieries. Durham, still re- main on strike. They have been warned that having come out without giving notice they have acted illegally, and summonses for damages under the Employers and Workmen Act have been issued against 300 of the men. The loss in wages to the men themselves and other workmen involved in the dispute amounts to about £BOO per day. For all kinds of domestic sewing. Bagley and Wright scott•n is the beet.—Advt.

LATEST NEWS.
Play between the English and Australians was stopped by heavy rain yesterday, the Australians being then 51 for two wickets.
A Grimsby smack has picked up in the North Sea the balloon which ascended from Belgium, and the occupants of which were rescued by the warship Warrior.

_ TRIPLE FATALITY.—Three of five lads injured ty a spirit lamp accident at Mold Green, near Huddersfietd, on Thursday night, died at Huddersfield Infirmary on Friday morning, The steamship Great Eastern parted from her tugs during a gale in the Irish Sea on Thursday night, and was last seen heading towards Ireland. The latest news is that she passed Llandudno, making for the Mersey, all safe.

COLLISION IN THE T/LCHES.—Lloyd's agent at Wapping states that the steamer Winston was proceeding down the Thames on Friday morning, and when in Limehouse Reach came into collision with and sunk the coal steamer Southmoor.

A BURY CASE FOR M. PASTEUR.—On Friday morning two children, who were bitten by a mad dog last week in Bury, started on their journey to M. Pasteur's Insti- tute, Paris, for treatment. They are accompanied by a doctor and nurse. The funds wherewith to send them have been raised by a public subscription promoted by the police. SUICIDE OF A FORGER.—Walter Scott Hammond was to have appeared at Marlborough•st. Police Court on Friday to e nswer a charge of forgery and uttering. Oh the case being called, it was announced that he had strangled himself in a cell in the house of detention. It was stated that deceased had forged bills to the amount of over £16,000.

RAILWAY COLLISION IN LONDON.—Seven persons were injured by a collision which occurred at Cannon-st. sta- tion, yesterday. One only, however, an employe of the company, was badly hurt. A good deal of damage was done to the company's property. One of the company's engineers, named William Coife, whilst engaged in re- moving the damaged vans, was crushed and internally injured.

-SUSPENSION OF TILE TOWN CLERK OF' SALFORD.—Re- cently certain irregularities were discovered in the Town Clerk's department of • the Salford Corporation. The matter was lengthily discussed at a meeting of the General Purposes Committee, and eventually the General Finance Committee were instructed to make a thorough investiption and report to the General Purposes Com- mittee, which consists of the whole of the members of the Council. A meeting of the Finance Committee was held on Tuesday, at which there was a large attendance, and they appointed several of their number as a sub- committee to draw up a report to the General Purposes Committee. That report was considered at an adjourned meeting of the General Finance Committee on Friday morning, and was unanimously adopted. Immediately after the meeting of the General Finance Committee the Mayor (Mr. Aid. Dickins) at once suspended the Town Clerk from his duties.

THE ROYAL VISIT TO GLASGOW. On Friday the weather in Glasgow was dull and threatening, but the city presented a gay aspect, large crowds having lined the palisades along the Royal route. Her Majesty drove first to the University, where she was received by the professors. The Queen next visited Queen Margaret's College, then proceeded to the Exhi- bition, where Sir Archibald Campbell, as Grand Master, presented her with an address from the Freemasons. The Queen gave the following reply to the address of the Scotch Grand Lodge of Freemasons :—" I received, with great pleasure, the dutiful address which you have pre- sented to me on the occasicn of my visit uo Glasgow. I fully recognise and heartily appreciate the value of the charitable works which it is the great object of your so- ciety to promote. I thank you cordially for the expres- sion of your loyalty and devotion." The Queen, sitting in a bath chair, was taken through the machinery an- nexe, and the Indian, Canadian, and other courts, and was highly pleased with all she witnessed. On leaving the Exhibition her Majesty drove to the University, where she had a splendid view of the city of Glasgow. The Town Clerk is to be knighted.

REPORTED CAPTURE OF DINIZULU. A "Times "telegram, dated Durban, Friday, says : " It is reported that Dinizulu and two minor chiefs, with a few hundred cattle, have been captured by the Transvaal Boers and handed over to the British authorities."

div.head: GREAT FIRE IN RUSSIA.-10,000 PEOPLE HOMELESS.
div.p: GREAT FIRE IN RUSSIA.-10,000 PEOPLE HOMELESS.

ORENBERG, THURSDAY:----A-47re:1-i fire occurred here to- day by which more than 1,000 houses, inhabited for the most part by factory operatives, were burned to the ground. Nearly 10,000 persons have been rendered homeless by the catastrophe. A CHINESE GUNPOWDER. PLOT.

The "Russian Official Messenger" iiuolishes the fol- lowing letter from Kuldja :—According to news just received here, there recently occurred at Urumtsi an affah which almost cost the governor of the new dominion his life. The soldiers, who had not received any pay for more than six months, and who were not allowed to address their complaints to the governor direct, determined to blow up the residence of the com- mander-in-chief. Eight soldiers chosen by lot-were en- trusted with this task. They laid a mine charged with 240 pounds of powder under the palace. Only half an hour before the time for putting the plot into execution it was divulged by one of the conspirators. The mine was immediately flooded with water. The guilty sol- diers declared that not only the whole garrison, but many of the chief officers, were implicated in the plot. A cruel punishment was promptly inflicted on the criminals, 30 soldiers being executed and 100 placed under arrest pending sentence.

A mail bag has been rifled on its way from Oregon to New Y9rk, and a package of the value of 10,000do1s. abstracted. A coroner's jury. on Thursday returned a verdict of wilful murder against some person unknown, in the case of a woman, supposed to be Martha Turner, a hawker, whose dead body, with 39 wounds from stabs upon it, was found on tlie 7th inst., on the landing of a model dwelling in Commercial-st Spitalfields. A MINISTER DROWNETI.-2A thrilling scene was with nessed at Montrose, on Wednesday. The Hey. Robert Milligan, minister of Chalmers Frce Church, Dundee, went down to the shore with his son and a nephew to bathe. About fifteen minutes after Mr. Milligan entered thelwater he was carried out a distance of 4hundred yards and was drowned, notwithstanding repeated and most heroic efforts on the part of the bathing attendant, a man named Robinson, to rescue him. A FATAL EVICTION.—An inquest was held at Moy- a.sta on Tuesday evening on the body of a woman of 60, who had died after being evicted from a farm on the Vandeleur estate. Dr. Hickey, of Kilkee, said the de- ceased had died of pneumonia, but he had no doubt that the circumstances of the eviction would accelerate her death. After hearing statements of members of her family, the jury found that the cause of the woman's death was excitement produced by the eviction, and anxiety resulting from her having formed the impression that her son, who was taken into custody at the time, was dead.

--- MR. GLADSTONE ON AGRICULTURE. Mr. Gladstone I was present on Thursday at a flower show held in the grounds of Hawarden Castle, and delivered .an interes- ting address upon agricultural topics. He said it had always been his opinion that there was a great deal to be done in this country in the cultivation of small par- cels and limited areas of ground, by what might be cal- led spade cultivation, using the phrase in the large sense of covering everything that was done by the human hand. In France what was called small culture was pur- sued by millions of the population, and there was no doubt that a large part of the wealth of France arose from that kind of work. As the result of the observa- tion of a tolerably long life, he believed there was an en- ormous economical importance in the cultivation of flowers, fruit, and vezetables, and in the application thereto of labour, care, skill, and vigilance. There was no doubt that the getting of the produce to the market was one of the most important subjects to to which agriculturists could apply their attehtion. He was extremely glad that Parliament had passed an Act upon the subject, and it was right that if there was any tendency on the part of the companies to do less than justice to the producer, that tendency should be checked. He believed farmers would do themselves a great deal of good if they would lay their heads together with a jew to getting their goods into the market in bulk, and thus enabling the railway companies to offer Moderate terms of carriage. THE NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF JOURNALISTS.—On Sat- urday evening a meetino. of journalists in the St. Helens district was held at the Royal Raven Hotel, St. Helens, to consider the desirability of forming a sub-district of the National Association. Mr. Dromgoole, the oldest newspaper proprietor and editor in the town, had very generously provided a substantial tea for all interested in the question, to which the following sat down :—Mr. G. Murdoch, editor of the "Warrington Guardian " ; Mr. Joseph Mason, Liverpool; and Mr. S. Harrison, "Warrington Examiner"; who formed the deputation; Mr. F. Dromgoole and Mr. P. J. Boylan, "St Helens Newspaper " ; Mr. G. Culshaw, proprietor of the "St. Helens Reporter " ; Mr. F. Hargreaves and Mr. R. H. Clulow, "St. Helens Reporter"; Mr. H. L. Riley and Mr. J. Ashton, "St. Helens Lantern " ; Mr. A. Kee and Mr. R. Schofield," St. Helens Chronicle"; Mr. J. Duxbury, "St. Helens Examiner " ; Mr. G. Marsh, "Liverpool Daily Post " ; and Mr. J. Mason, "Liverpool Courier." Mr. Dromgoole presided, and Mr. Culshaw occupied the vice-chair. Mr. Joseph Mason fully explained the objects of the association, and Mr. Murdoch urged all present to consider the personal advantages it offered to journalists. The Chairman proposed—" That this meet- ing of the St. Helens and Prescot journalists approve the formation of a chartered institute of journalists, and agrees to join the National Association under the title cf the St. Helens and Warrington sub-district of the Liver- pool district." Mr. Culshaw seconded the resolution, which was carried unanimously.—On the motion of Mr. Hargreaves, seconded by Mr. Clulow, Mr. James Dux- bury was appointed co-secretary pro tern, with Mr. S. Harrison, of Warrington. Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's, which for strength Is unequalled.—Advt.

FRODSHAM AND ' HELSBY DRAINAGE BOARD. I NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that a GENERAL MEETING of the'Ratepayers within the District of the Frodsham and Helsby Drainage Board will be held in the , ' TOWN lIALL, FRODSHAM, on MONDAY. THE 3RD DAY (XF SEP- , TEMBER, 1888, at half-part seven &clock in the evening, for the purpose of electing new members of the Board. The number of members to be elected is 15, and the qualifi- cations are as follows .—The proprietor of not less than 20 statute acres witnin the District ; The heir apparent of the , proprietor of an estate of not less than 20 statute acres within the District; The occupier, yearly or otherwise, of not less than 30 statute acres within the District; The Agent of a pro- prietor of an estate of not less than 20 statute acres within the District, such Agent acting under a written appointment. HENRY BESWICK, Returning Officer. Clerk's Office, Frodsham, 21st August, 1888.

GUY'S HOSPITAL MEDICAL SCHOOL. THE WINTER SESSION COMMENCES ON MONDAY, OCTOBER Ist. The Hospital contains 695 beds, of which 500 are in constant occupation. There are Wards for Obstetric and Opthalmic cases, and other special Departments. Special classes areheld in the Hospital for Students preparing for the Examinations of the University of London, and ether Higher Examina- tions. APPOINTMENTS.—The House-9urgeoncies, House-Phy- siciancies, Dresserships, and all other Appointments, are made strictly in accordance with the merits of the Candidates, and without extra payment. There are also a large number of Junior Appointments, every part of the Hospital practice bel ing systematically employed for instruction. eo that Students who have completed their preliminary studies elsewhere may enter at once upon the practice of the Hospital. ENTRANCE SCHOLA.RSHIPS.—Open Scholarship of 125 guineas in Clas- sics, Mathematics, and Modern Lauguages. Open Scholar- ship of 125 guineas in Chemistry. Physics, and Biology. PRIZES are open to Students in their various years amount- ing in the aggregate to more than £3OO. During the past year the accommodation in the PHYSIOLOGICAL AND PATHOLOGICAL Departments has been greatly increased, and a STUDENTS' CLUB has been opened in the Hospital, containing a Dining-room, Reading-rooms and ,a large Gym- nasium. COLLEGE.—A residential College is in the course of erec- tion upon a site immediately contiguous to the Hospital to accommodate about 50 Students in addition to the Resident Staff of the Hospital. For Prospectus and further information apply to the Dean, Dr. PERRY, Guy's Hospital, London, S.E.

MESSRS. BRUNNER, MOND, & CO. HALF-YEARLY MEETING. The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, & imited, Winning ton, Northwich, was held at Co.,die Law Association Rooms, Cook-st., Liverpool, on Monday. Mr. John Crosfield, the chairman of the board of directors. presided, and there was a good attendance of share- holders. Amongst those persons present were—Mr. J. T Brunner, M.P., Mr. L. Mond, Mr. H. Brunner, Mr. H. Coghill, Mr, C. M. Holland, Mr. E. Milner, Dr Ilewitt, and Mr, C. J. Galloway. Mr. T. H. FORGAN, the secretary, read the notice con- vening the meeting, after which the report of the direc- tors and balance-sheet, copies of which had been forwar- ded to all the shareholders, were taken as read. The report of the directors was as follows: The balance sheet and profit and loss account, Certified by the auditor, and now presented, show a balance to the credit of profit and loss account, on the working of the half-year en- ded on the 30th June, 1888, of £99,852 he 2d, which, with the amount of 34,988, 7s. brought forward from the previous half- year, makes a total of £134,840 12s 23. The directors propose to deal with the above balance as fol- lows: 2 s. d. Dividend on the preference capital, at 7 cent. per • annum Dividend on the ordinary capital. at 25 percent per annum Amount to be written off patents account 7,500 0 0 Amount to be placed to reserve fund 25,000 0 0 Balance to be carried forward £134,840 12 2 The above sum of £7,500 which it is proposed to write off Patents account will raise the amount written off this account to £B3, 558 2s 11d, and will leave the account standing at £27,962 12s; aud the above sum of £25,000 which it is pro- Posed to add to the reserve fund will bring that fund up to £126,500. The directors recommend the election of Mr. Gustav Jar- May, of Hartford, Cheshire, as a member of the Board of Directors. The auditor retires, but is eligible for re-election. The CHAIRMAN, after remarking that the directors had pleasure in presenting anothei satisfactory balance sheet, moved the following resolution That the directors' report and statement of accounts be adopted, and that a dividend be paid to the holders of the prefer- ence shares at the rate of 7 per cent. per-annum on the amount paid up on such shares; and that a dividend be Paid the holders of the ordinary shares at the rate of 25 Per cent, per annum on the amount paid up on such shares, free of income tax, for the half-year ended June 30th, 1888." ' Mr. H. Comma. seconded the resolution, which was unanimously carried. On the motion of Mr. Mom), seconded by Mr. Coo. 'SILL, Mr. G. Jarmay was unanimously elected a direc- tor of the company. Mr. W. SIMPSON moved, and Mr. MORROW seconded, that Mr. T. W. Read, chartered accountant, Liverpool, be re-appointed auditor.—Carried. ...With a vote of thanks to the Chairman, proposed by Jur, Dency, the proceedings ended.
